“Well then, my guess is that Mr. Willoughby goes hunting.”
Marianne was surprised and embarrassed, but could not help smiling at his gently teasing manner. After a moment's silence she said:
“Oh, Edward! How can you? But the time will come, I hope… I am certain you will like him.”

“I have no doubt I shall,” he replied, rather startled by her warmth and earnestness. He would never have ventured to mention the subject if he had not supposed it a joke generally shared by their acquaintances, based merely on something—or nothing—between Mr. Willoughby and herself.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Edward stayed at the cottage for a week. Mrs. Dashwood warmly urged him to remain longer, but he seemed determined, as though intent on depriving himself of pleasure, to leave just when he was enjoying his friends' company most. During the last two or three days his spirits, though still very uneven, had improved considerably. He grew increasingly fond of the house and its surroundings, never mentioned leaving without a sigh, declared he had no demands upon his time, and was unsure even where he would go next. Nevertheless, he must go. No week had ever passed so quickly; he could scarcely believe it was over. He said this repeatedly, and said other things too that revealed his feelings while contradicting his actions. Norland gave him no pleasure; he hated London. Yet he must go to one or the other. He valued their kindness above everything, and being with them made him happier than anything else. Still he must leave after a week, against both their wishes and his own, despite having no claim upon his time.

Elinor blamed his mother for everything puzzling in this conduct. Fortunately for her, she knew so little of Mrs. Ferrars's character that it could serve as a general excuse for every strange thing her son did. Yet despite her disappointment and vexation, and her occasional displeasure at his uncertain behaviour towards herself, Elinor was on the whole quite willing to interpret his actions with every generous allowance. These were the same allowances her mother had obtained from her with rather more difficulty on Willoughby's behalf. She usually attributed Edward's lack of cheerfulness, openness, and consistency to his dependence and his better knowledge of his mother's temperament and plans. His brief visit and firm decision to leave arose from the same restricted freedom, the same unavoidable need to accommodate his mother for the moment. The old, familiar conflict of duty against inclination, parent against child, explained everything. Elinor wished she knew when these difficulties would end and the opposition give way—when Mrs. Ferrars would reform and her son be free to be happy. But she had to turn from such useless wishes to the comfort of her renewed confidence in Edward's affection. She recalled every sign of regard in his words and looks at Barton, and above all the flattering evidence he always wore on his finger.

“I think, Edward,” Mrs. Dashwood said at breakfast on his last morning, “you would be happier with a profession to occupy your time and give purpose to your plans and actions. It might inconvenience your friends: you could not spend so much time with them. But,” she added with a smile, “you would gain at least one considerable advantage. When you left them, you would know where to go.”

“I assure you,” he replied, “that I have long thought just as you do about that. Having no necessary business, no profession to employ me or offer anything like independence, has been a great misfortune. It remains one, and probably always will. Unfortunately, my own fastidiousness and my family's have made me what I am: an idle, helpless creature. We could never agree on a profession. I always preferred the church, and still do. But that was not fashionable enough for my family. They recommended the army, which was far too fashionable for me. The law was considered sufficiently genteel. Plenty of young men with chambers in the Temple appeared to advantage in the best social circles and drove stylish gigs around London. But even this less demanding branch of legal study, the one my family approved, did not appeal to me. The navy was fashionable too, but by the time anyone suggested it, I was too old to enter. Eventually, since I had no need for a profession, and could be just as dashing and extravagant without a red coat as with one, idleness was declared the most advantageous and honourable course. A young man of eighteen is not generally so eager for work that he resists his family's urging to do nothing. So I was sent to Oxford and have remained properly idle ever since.”

“I suppose the result,” Mrs. Dashwood said, “since leisure has done so little for your own happiness, will be that your sons are brought up to as many occupations, professions, and trades as Columella's.”
“They will be brought up,” he answered in a serious voice, “to be as unlike me as possible—in their feelings, their actions, their circumstances, and everything else.”

“Come, Edward, that is only your present low spirits speaking. You are melancholy and imagine that anyone unlike yourself must be happy. But remember that everyone sometimes suffers when parting from friends, whatever their education or situation. Recognise your own happiness. You need only patience—or give it a more attractive name and call it hope. In time, your mother will grant the independence you want so much. It is her duty; soon it will, it must, become her pleasure to prevent your whole youth being wasted in discontent. How much might a few months change?”
“I think,” Edward answered, “I could challenge any number of months to bring me anything good.”

His despondency did not infect Mrs. Dashwood, but made the parting, which soon followed, more painful for everyone. It left a particularly unhappy impression on Elinor, which took time and effort to overcome. But she was determined to overcome it and not appear to suffer more at his departure than the rest of the family. She therefore did not follow the method Marianne had so wisely adopted on a similar occasion: seeking silence, solitude, and idleness to strengthen and prolong her grief. Their methods differed as much as their aims, and served those aims equally well.

As soon as he left the house, Elinor sat at her drawing table and kept herself busy all day. She neither invited nor avoided mention of his name, and seemed almost as interested as usual in the family's general affairs. If this behaviour did not lessen her sorrow, it at least prevented its needless increase, and spared her mother and sisters much anxiety about her.

To Marianne, behaviour so precisely opposite to her own appeared no more admirable than her own had seemed wrong. She settled the question of self-control very easily: strong feelings made it impossible, while with quiet feelings it deserved no credit. She could not deny that her sister's feelings were quiet, though she blushed to acknowledge it. She gave a striking demonstration of the strength of her own by continuing to love and respect Elinor despite this humiliating conviction.

Without shutting herself away from her family, deliberately going out alone to avoid them, or lying awake all night to reflect, Elinor found plenty of time each day to think about Edward and his conduct. As her spirits varied, she considered him with tenderness, pity, approval, criticism, and doubt. There were many moments when, even if her mother and sisters were present, their occupations prevented conversation and produced every effect of solitude. Her mind was inevitably free. Her thoughts could not be bound elsewhere, and on a subject so absorbing, the past and future must come before her, demand her attention, and occupy her memory, reflection, and imagination.

One morning soon after Edward's departure, visitors interrupted just such a reverie as she sat at her drawing table. She happened to be alone. The click of the little gate into the grassy courtyard made her look towards the window. She saw a large group of visitors walking up towards the front door. Sir John, Lady Middleton, and Mrs. Jennings were among them, with a gentleman and lady Elinor did not know. She was sitting near the window. The moment Sir John saw her, he left the others to the ceremony of knocking and crossed the grass, obliging her to open the casement so he could speak. Door and window were so close that it was scarcely possible to speak at either without being overheard by anyone waiting at the other.
“Well,” he said, “we have brought some new people for you to meet. How do you like them?”
“Hush! They will hear what you say.”
“Never mind if they do. They are only the Palmers. Charlotte is very pretty, I can tell you. Look this way and you will see her.”
Certain of seeing the lady in another minute or two without taking that liberty, Elinor begged to be excused.
“Where is Marianne? Has our coming frightened her away? I see her instrument has been left open.”
“I believe she has gone walking.”

Mrs. Jennings now joined them. She had too little patience to wait for the door to open before beginning her own story. She came calling to the window, “How are you, my dear? How is Mrs. Dashwood? And where are your sisters? What! Quite alone! You must be glad to have a little company. I have brought my other daughter and son-in-law to see you. Just imagine them arriving so unexpectedly! Last night, while we were having tea, I thought I heard a carriage, but it never occurred to me it might be theirs. I could think only that perhaps Colonel Brandon had returned. So I said to Sir John, I really think I hear a carriage; perhaps Colonel Brandon has come back—”

Elinor had to turn away in the middle of the story to welcome the others. Lady Middleton introduced the strangers. Mrs. Dashwood and Margaret came downstairs at the same moment, and everyone sat down to look at everyone else. Mrs. Jennings continued her story as she walked through the passage into the parlour, with Sir John beside her.

Mrs. Palmer was several years younger than Lady Middleton and entirely unlike her. Short and plump, she had a very pretty face with the most thoroughly good-humoured expression imaginable. Her manners were much less elegant than her sister's, but far more winning. She arrived smiling, smiled throughout the visit whenever she was not laughing, and smiled as she left. Her husband, a serious-looking young man of twenty-five or twenty-six, appeared more fashionable and intelligent than his wife, but less willing either to please or to be pleased. He entered with an air of importance, gave the ladies a slight bow without speaking, and briefly surveyed them and their rooms. Then he picked up a newspaper from the table and read it for the rest of his stay.

Mrs. Palmer, by contrast, had been richly endowed by nature with a disposition to be constantly pleasant and happy. She had scarcely sat down before bursting into admiration of the parlour and everything in it.

“Well! What a delightful room! I have never seen anything so charming! Think, Mama, how much better it looks than when I last came! I always thought it such a sweet place, ma'am,” she said, turning to Mrs. Dashwood, “but you have made it so charming! Just look, sister, how lovely everything is! How I would like a house like this for myself! Would you not, Mr. Palmer?”
Mr. Palmer gave no answer. He did not even lift his eyes from the paper.
“Mr. Palmer cannot hear me,” she said, laughing. “Sometimes he never does. It is so ridiculous!”
This was an entirely new idea to Mrs. Dashwood. She had never been accustomed to finding wit in someone's failure to pay attention, and could not help looking at them both in surprise.

Meanwhile Mrs. Jennings continued at the top of her voice, recounting their surprise at the visitors' arrival the evening before. She did not stop until she had told everything. Mrs. Palmer laughed heartily at the memory of their astonishment. Everyone agreed two or three times that it had been a very pleasant surprise.

“You can imagine how glad we all were to see them,” Mrs. Jennings added. She leaned towards Elinor and lowered her voice as though speaking for her alone, although they were on opposite sides of the room. “Still, I cannot help wishing they had not travelled so fast or made the journey so long. They came round through London because of some business. And you know,” she nodded significantly towards her daughter, “that was wrong in her condition. I wanted her to stay at home and rest this morning, but she insisted on coming. She was so eager to see you all!”
Mrs. Palmer laughed and said she was sure it would do her no harm.
“She is expecting her baby in February,” Mrs. Jennings continued.
Lady Middleton could endure the conversation no longer. She roused herself to ask Mr. Palmer whether the newspaper contained any news.
“No, nothing at all,” he answered, continuing to read.
“Here is Marianne,” Sir John called. “Now, Palmer, you will see an extraordinarily pretty girl.”

He immediately went into the passage, opened the front door, and brought her in himself. The moment she appeared, Mrs. Jennings asked whether she had been to Allenham. Mrs. Palmer's hearty laughter showed she understood the question. Mr. Palmer glanced up when Marianne entered, stared at her for several minutes, then returned to his paper. Mrs. Palmer now noticed the drawings hanging around the room and got up to inspect them.

“Oh! Dear, how beautiful! Well! How delightful! Look, Mama, how lovely! They really are quite charming. I could look at them for ever.” Then she sat down again and soon forgot that any drawings existed in the room.
When Lady Middleton stood to leave, Mr. Palmer also rose, put down the newspaper, stretched, and looked around at everyone.
“My love, have you been sleeping?” his wife asked, laughing.
He did not answer her. After inspecting the room once more, he merely remarked that it had a very low ceiling, which was crooked. Then he bowed and left with the others.

Sir John had urged them all to spend the next day at the park. Mrs. Dashwood, unwilling to dine there more often than the Middletons dined at the cottage, firmly refused for herself. Her daughters could do as they wished. But they felt no curiosity about watching Mr. and Mrs. Palmer eat dinner, and expected no pleasure from their company in any other way. They too tried to excuse themselves: the weather was unsettled and unlikely to be good. Sir John would not accept this. He would send the carriage; they must come. Lady Middleton, though she did not press their mother, urged the girls. Mrs. Jennings and Mrs. Palmer added their pleas. Everyone seemed equally anxious to avoid an exclusively family gathering, and the young ladies had to give way.

“Why must they invite us?” Marianne asked as soon as they left. “They say this cottage's rent is low, but the terms are very hard if we must dine at the park whenever anyone is staying either with them or with us.”

“They intend these frequent invitations to be just as kind and polite as the ones they gave us a few weeks ago,” Elinor said. “If their parties have become tedious and dull, they are not the ones who have changed. We must look elsewhere for the difference.”

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: When the Miss Dashwoods entered the park's drawing room the next day, Mrs. Palmer ran in through the opposite door, looking as cheerful and good-natured as ever. She took their hands with great affection and expressed her delight at seeing them again.

“I am so glad you came!” she said, sitting between Elinor and Marianne. “The weather is so bad that I feared you might stay away. That would have been dreadful, since we leave again tomorrow. We must go, you know, because the Westons are coming next week. Our visit here was quite sudden. I knew nothing about it until the carriage was coming to the door, and then Mr. Palmer asked if I wanted to go to Barton with him. He is so funny! He never tells me anything! I am terribly sorry we cannot stay longer. Still, I hope we shall meet again in London very soon.”
They had to disappoint her by explaining that they did not expect to go.

“Not coming to London!” Mrs. Palmer exclaimed with a laugh. “I shall be so disappointed if you do not. I could find you the nicest house imaginable, next to ours in Hanover Square. Really, you must come. I would be delighted to chaperon you whenever you liked until the baby comes, if Mrs. Dashwood did not want to go out into society.”
They thanked her, but had to refuse despite all her pleading.
“Oh, my love,” Mrs. Palmer called to her husband as he entered, “you must help persuade the Miss Dashwoods to come to London this winter.”
Her love gave no answer. After a slight bow to the ladies, he began complaining about the weather.

“How horrible this is!” he said. “Weather like this makes everything and everyone disgusting. Rain produces as much dullness indoors as outside. It makes one hate all one's acquaintances. What the devil does Sir John mean by having no billiard room? How few people understand comfort! Sir John is as stupid as the weather.”
The other members of the party soon came in.
“I fear, Miss Marianne,” Sir John said, “that you have not been able to take your usual walk to Allenham today.”
Marianne looked extremely serious and made no reply.

“Oh, do not be so secretive with us,” Mrs. Palmer said. “We know all about it, I assure you. I greatly admire your taste, for I think him extremely handsome. You know, we live quite near him in the country. No more than ten miles away, I dare say.”
“Closer to thirty,” her husband said.
“Oh, well! That makes very little difference. I have never been to his house, but people say it is a sweet, pretty place.”
“As dreadful a spot as I have ever seen,” Mr. Palmer said.
Marianne remained entirely silent, though her face revealed how much the subject interested her.
“Is it very ugly?” Mrs. Palmer went on. “Then I suppose I must be thinking of another place that is so pretty.”
Once they were seated in the dining room, Sir John regretfully observed that there were only eight of them.
“My dear,” he said to his wife, “it is very annoying to have so few people. Why did you not invite the Gilberts today?”
“Did I not explain, Sir John, when you first mentioned it, that it could not be done? They were the last to dine with us.”
“You and I, Sir John,” Mrs. Jennings said, “would not let such formalities stand in our way.”
“Then you would both be very ill bred,” Mr. Palmer declared.
“My love, you contradict everyone,” his wife said, laughing as usual. “Do you realise you are being quite rude?”
“I was not aware that calling your mother ill bred contradicted anyone.”
“Yes, you may abuse me all you like,” the good-natured old lady replied. “You have taken Charlotte off my hands, and you cannot give her back. I have the advantage of you there.”

Charlotte laughed heartily at the thought that her husband could not get rid of her. Triumphantly she declared that she did not care how cross he was, since they must live together. Nobody could have been more thoroughly good-natured, or more determined to be happy, than Mrs. Palmer. Her husband's studied indifference, rudeness, and discontent caused her no pain. When he scolded or insulted her, she found it highly amusing.
“Mr. Palmer is so funny!” she whispered to Elinor. “He is always in a bad temper.”

After observing him a little, Elinor was not inclined to believe him quite as naturally and sincerely bad-tempered or ill-mannered as he wished to appear. Perhaps his temper had been soured by discovering, like many other men, that an inexplicable preference for beauty had made him the husband of a very silly woman. But she knew this mistake was too common for any sensible man to remain wounded by it. She believed his contempt for everyone and criticism of everything arose more from a wish to distinguish himself—to appear superior to other people. The motive was too ordinary to surprise her. His method might establish his superiority in bad manners, but was unlikely to win anyone's affection except his wife's.

“Oh, my dear Miss Dashwood,” Mrs. Palmer said soon afterwards, “I have such a favour to ask of you and your sister. Will you come and stay at Cleveland this Christmas? Please do, and come while the Westons are there. You cannot imagine how happy it would make me! It would be delightful! My love,” she turned to her husband, “are you not longing for the Miss Dashwoods to visit Cleveland?”
“Certainly,” he replied with a sneer. “That was my only reason for coming to Devonshire.”
“There,” his wife said, “you see that Mr. Palmer expects you. You cannot possibly refuse now.”
Both sisters promptly and firmly declined the invitation she offered.

“But you really must come, and you shall. I am sure you will like it more than anything. The Westons will be with us, and it will be delightful. You cannot imagine what a lovely place Cleveland is. And we have such lively times now, because Mr. Palmer is always travelling around the county canvassing for the election. So many people I have never seen before come to dinner. It is charming! But poor man, it tires him dreadfully. He is obliged to make everyone like him.”
Elinor could scarcely keep a straight face as she agreed that such an obligation must be hard.

“How wonderful it will be when he is in Parliament!” Charlotte said. “Will it not? How I shall laugh! It will be so ridiculous seeing M.P. after his name on all his letters. But do you know, he says he will never frank my letters so they can go free? He insists he will not. Do you not, Mr. Palmer?”
Mr. Palmer paid no attention to his wife.
“You know, he cannot bear writing,” she continued. “He says it is quite shocking.”
“No,” he said, “I never said anything so irrational. Do not attribute all your misuse of language to me.”
“There, you see how funny he is. He is always like this! Sometimes he will not speak to me for half a day, and then he says something so funny about absolutely anything in the world.”
As they returned to the drawing room, she greatly surprised Elinor by asking whether she did not like Mr. Palmer exceedingly.
“Certainly,” Elinor answered. “He seems a very agreeable gentleman.”

“Well, I am so glad. I thought you would, he is so pleasant. And I can tell you that Mr. Palmer is extremely pleased with you and your sisters. You cannot imagine his disappointment if you do not come to Cleveland. I cannot understand why you object.”

Elinor once more found herself obliged to refuse the invitation, then changed the subject to end the pleading. Since Mrs. Palmer lived in the same county as Willoughby, she might know more about his general character than the Middletons, whose acquaintance with him was limited. Elinor was eager for any confirmation of his good qualities that would remove the possibility of anxiety about Marianne. She began by asking whether they saw much of Mr. Willoughby at Cleveland and knew him well.

“Oh dear, yes, I know him extremely well,” Mrs. Palmer answered. “Not that I have ever actually spoken to him, but I have seen him constantly in London. Somehow I have never happened to stay at Barton while he was at Allenham. Mama saw him here once before, but I was with my uncle at Weymouth. I dare say we should have seen a great deal of him in Somersetshire if we had not been so unfortunate as never to be in the country at the same time. I believe he spends very little time at Combe. But even if he were there constantly, I do not think Mr. Palmer would visit. You know, he supports the opposition, and besides, it is so far away. I know perfectly well why you are asking: your sister is to marry him. I am immensely glad, because then she will be a neighbour of mine.”
“Really,” Elinor replied, “if you have any reason to expect that marriage, you know much more about it than I do.”
“Do not pretend to deny it. You know everyone is talking about it. I assure you, I heard it on my way through London.”
“My dear Mrs. Palmer, really!”
“On my honour, I did. On Monday morning, just before we left London, I met Colonel Brandon in Bond Street. He told me immediately.”

“You surprise me very much. Colonel Brandon told you! Surely there is a mistake. Even if it were true, giving such news to someone with no particular concern in it is not what I would expect him to do.”

“But I assure you, that is how it happened, and I shall explain. When we met him, he turned and walked with us. We started talking about my brother-in-law and sister, and one thing and another. Then I said, ‘So, Colonel, I hear a new family has moved into Barton Cottage. Mama writes that they are very pretty, and that one is going to marry Mr. Willoughby of Combe Magna. Is it true? Of course you must know, since you have been in Devonshire so recently.’”
“And how did Colonel Brandon answer you?”
“Oh, he said very little. But he looked as though he knew it was true, so from that moment I considered it certain. It will be delightful, I declare! When will the wedding take place?”
“I hope Mr. Brandon was quite well?”
“Oh! Yes, perfectly well. And so full of praise for you! He did nothing but say fine things about you.”
“I am flattered that he thinks well of me. He seems an excellent man, and I find him unusually pleasing.”

“So do I. He is such a charming man that it is a great pity he is so serious and dull. Mama says he was in love with your sister too. If so, I assure you it was a great compliment, because he almost never falls in love with anyone.”
“Is Mr. Willoughby well known in your part of Somersetshire?” Elinor asked.

“Oh! Yes, very well. That is, I do not believe many people know him, because Combe Magna is so far away. But they all think him extremely agreeable, I assure you. Nobody is better liked than Mr. Willoughby wherever he goes. You may tell your sister that. On my honour, she is a tremendously lucky girl to get him. Though he is much luckier to get her, of course, because she is so handsome and agreeable that nothing could be good enough for her. Still, I hardly think her any prettier than you. I assure you, I think you both exceptionally pretty, and I am certain Mr. Palmer does too, though we could not make him admit it last night.”
Mrs. Palmer's information about Willoughby amounted to very little, but any favourable testimony, however slight, pleased Elinor.

“I am so glad we have finally met,” Charlotte continued. “Now I hope we shall always be great friends. You cannot imagine how much I wanted to see you! Your living at the cottage is so delightful! Nothing could compare with it! And I am so pleased your sister is going to marry well. I hope you will spend a great deal of time at Combe Magna. Everyone says it is a lovely place.”
“You have known Colonel Brandon for a long time, have you not?”

“Yes, a great while, ever since my sister married. He was a close friend of Sir John's. I believe,” she added quietly, “he would have been very glad to marry me if he could. Sir John and Lady Middleton wanted it very much. But Mama did not consider the match good enough. Otherwise Sir John would have mentioned it to the colonel, and we should have married at once.”
“Did Colonel Brandon know about Sir John's suggestion before he made it to your mother? Had he never declared his feelings to you?”

“Oh no. But if Mama had not objected, I dare say he would have liked it more than anything. He had seen me only once or twice then; it was before I left school. Still, I am much happier as I am. Mr. Palmer is the sort of man I like.”

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: The Palmers returned to Cleveland the next day, leaving the two Barton families once more to entertain one another. But this arrangement did not last long. Elinor had scarcely stopped thinking about their last visitors—wondering at Charlotte's happiness without a cause, Mr. Palmer's foolish behaviour despite his abilities, and the strange mismatch so often found between husband and wife—before Sir John and Mrs. Jennings, energetic champions of company, supplied fresh acquaintances for her to observe.

During a morning trip to Exeter, they had met two young women whom Mrs. Jennings was delighted to discover were relations of hers. Sir John needed no further reason to invite them to the park as soon as their Exeter engagements ended. Those engagements immediately gave way to the invitation. When Sir John returned, Lady Middleton was considerably alarmed to learn that two girls she had never seen were shortly to visit her. She could have no assurance of their elegance, or even of their reasonably good breeding: her husband's and mother's assurances counted for nothing. Being related to her made matters worse. Mrs. Jennings therefore chose an unfortunate ground for reassurance when she advised her daughter not to worry about their being fashionable, since they were all cousins and must tolerate one another. As preventing the visit was now impossible, Lady Middleton accepted it with all the philosophy of a well-bred woman. She contented herself with gently reproaching her husband five or six times a day.

The young women arrived, and neither their looks nor their dress suggested a lack of breeding or fashion. They were smartly dressed and very polite, delighted with the house and ecstatic over the furniture. They also happened to adore children so passionately that they won Lady Middleton's approval within an hour. She pronounced them very agreeable girls indeed, which from her amounted to enthusiastic admiration. This lively praise strengthened Sir John's confidence in his own judgment. He immediately went to the cottage to announce the Miss Steeles' arrival and assure the Dashwoods that they were the sweetest girls in the world. Such praise conveyed very little information. Elinor knew that the sweetest girls in the world could be found everywhere in England, with every imaginable kind of figure, face, temperament, and understanding. Sir John wanted the whole family to walk straight to the park to inspect his guests. Kind, public-spirited man! Keeping even a third cousin to himself gave him pain.

“Do come now,” he said. “Please come—you must come—I insist you shall come. You cannot imagine how much you will like them. Lucy is extraordinarily pretty, and so good-natured and agreeable! The children already cling to her as though they have known her for years. Both girls are desperate to see you. They heard in Exeter that you are the most beautiful creatures in the world, and I have told them that is entirely true and does not go far enough. I am sure you will be delighted. They filled the whole coach with toys for the children. How can you be so unkind as to refuse? They are your cousins, after a fashion. You are my cousins and they are my wife's, so you must be related.”

But Sir John could not persuade them. He obtained only a promise that they would visit within a day or two. Astonished by their indifference, he walked home to praise their attractions afresh to the Miss Steeles, just as he had already praised the Miss Steeles to them.

When the promised visit and introductions took place, the Dashwoods found nothing to admire in the elder sister's appearance. She was nearly thirty, with a very plain face that suggested little intelligence. The younger, no more than twenty-two or twenty-three, was undeniably attractive. Her features were pretty; her eyes were sharp and quick. A certain smartness in her manner distinguished her appearance, though it did not amount to elegance or grace. Both sisters were exceptionally polite. Elinor soon credited them with a kind of intelligence when she saw how steadily and judiciously they worked to please Lady Middleton. They were constantly enraptured by her children, praising their beauty, seeking their attention, and indulging their whims. Whatever time they could spare from the urgent demands this politeness created was spent admiring whatever her ladyship happened to be doing, if she was doing anything, or copying the pattern of some elegant new dress whose appearance the day before had thrown them into lasting delight. Fortunately for people who seek favour through such weaknesses, a doting mother is as credulous as she is greedy for praise of her children. Her demands are immense, but she will believe anything. Lady Middleton therefore viewed the Miss Steeles' excessive affection and patience with neither surprise nor suspicion. With maternal satisfaction she watched every intrusive demand and mischievous trick her cousins endured. She saw their sashes untied, their hair pulled about their ears, their workbags searched, and their knives and scissors carried off, without doubting that both sides enjoyed it equally. Her only surprise was that Elinor and Marianne could sit by so calmly without asking for a share.
“John is in such high spirits today!” she said as he took Miss Steele's handkerchief and threw it out of the window. “He is full of mischievous tricks.”
Soon afterwards, when the second boy pinched one of the same lady's fingers hard, she observed affectionately, “How playful William is!”

“And here is my sweet little Annamaria,” she added, tenderly stroking a three-year-old girl who had made no noise for two minutes. “She is always so gentle and quiet. There never was such a quiet little creature!”

Unfortunately, as she embraced her, a pin in her headdress lightly scratched the child's neck. This model of gentleness produced screams that scarcely any creature openly acknowledged as noisy could have surpassed. The mother's alarm was immense, but no greater than the Miss Steeles'. In this critical emergency, all three did everything affection could suggest to ease the little sufferer's agony. She was seated on her mother's lap and smothered in kisses. One Miss Steele knelt to bathe the wound with lavender water while the other filled her mouth with sugarplums. So generously rewarded for tears, the child was far too sensible to stop crying. She continued screaming and sobbing vigorously, and kicked both brothers when they tried to touch her. All their combined soothing failed until Lady Middleton fortunately remembered that, during a similar crisis the previous week, apricot marmalade had successfully treated a bruised temple. They eagerly proposed the same remedy for this unhappy scratch. A brief pause in the young lady's screams at the suggestion gave grounds for hoping she would accept it. Her mother therefore carried her out in search of the medicine. The boys chose to follow, despite earnest requests to stay, and the four young women were left in a silence the room had not enjoyed for hours.
“Poor little creatures!” Miss Steele said as soon as they had gone. “It might have been a very dreadful accident.”
“I can scarcely see how,” Marianne replied, “unless the circumstances had been completely different. But this is the usual way of increasing alarm where there is really nothing to fear.”
“What a lovely woman Lady Middleton is!” Lucy Steele said.

Marianne remained silent. However trivial the occasion, she could not say what she did not feel. The entire duty of lying when politeness required it therefore always fell to Elinor. She did her best when called upon, speaking of Lady Middleton more warmly than she felt, though far less warmly than Miss Lucy.
“And Sir John too!” the elder sister exclaimed. “What a wonderfully charming man!”
Here again, Miss Dashwood's praise made little impression because it was merely honest and reasonable. She said only that he was thoroughly good-natured and friendly.
“And what a charming little family! I have never seen such fine children. I declare I adore them already. Indeed, I am always madly fond of children.”
“I might have guessed that,” Elinor said with a smile, “from what I have seen this morning.”

“I suspect,” Lucy said, “you think the little Middletons are rather too indulged. Perhaps they do get a little more than enough. But it is so natural in Lady Middleton. For my part, I love children full of life and energy. I cannot bear them tame and quiet.”
“I confess,” Elinor replied, “that while I am at Barton Park, I never find the thought of tame, quiet children at all disagreeable.”

A brief silence followed. Miss Steele, who seemed eager to talk, was the first to break it. Rather abruptly she asked, “And how do you like Devonshire, Miss Dashwood? I suppose you were very sorry to leave Sussex.”
Somewhat surprised by the familiarity of the question, or at least by the way it was asked, Elinor answered that she was.
“Norland is an amazingly beautiful place, is it not?” Miss Steele added.
“We have heard Sir John praise it very highly,” Lucy said, apparently feeling some explanation was needed for her sister's freedom.
“I think anyone who has seen it must admire it,” Elinor replied. “Though of course one cannot expect anyone to value its beauties quite as we do.”
“And did you have plenty of fashionable young beaux there? I suppose you have fewer in this part of the world. For myself, I always think they add a great deal.”
“Why should you suppose,” Lucy asked, looking ashamed of her sister, “that Devonshire has fewer well-bred young men than Sussex?”

“Now, my dear, I am sure I never meant to say that. Exeter has plenty of smart beaux, certainly. But how could I know how many there were around Norland? I only feared the Miss Dashwoods might find Barton dull if they had fewer than they were used to. Perhaps you young ladies do not care for beaux, though, and would be just as happy without them. I find them very agreeable myself, provided they dress well and behave politely. But I cannot bear seeing them dirty and untidy. Take Mr. Rose in Exeter, for instance: such a smart young man, quite a beau, Mr. Simpson's clerk, you know. Yet if you meet him in the morning, he is not fit to be seen. I suppose your brother was quite a beau before his marriage, Miss Dashwood, being so rich?”

“Really,” Elinor answered, “I cannot tell you, since I do not entirely understand what the word means. But I can say this: if he was a beau before he married, he remains one, for he has not changed in the slightest.”
“Oh! Dear! Nobody thinks of married men as beaux. They have other things to occupy them.”

“Lord, Anne!” her sister exclaimed. “You talk about nothing but beaux. You will make Miss Dashwood think you have no other thoughts.” Then, to change the subject, she began admiring the house and furniture.

This sample of the Miss Steeles was enough. The elder sister's vulgar familiarity and foolishness offered nothing to recommend her. Nor did the younger's beauty and shrewd expression blind Elinor to her lack of true elegance and unaffected simplicity. She left without any wish to know them better.

The Miss Steeles felt differently. They had arrived from Exeter with ample admiration to distribute among Sir John, his family, and every relation. His pretty cousins now received a generous portion. They pronounced them the most beautiful, elegant, accomplished, agreeable girls they had ever seen, and were particularly eager to know them better. Elinor soon discovered that knowing them better was unavoidable. Sir John firmly supported the Miss Steeles, making their combined force too strong to oppose. She must accept the sort of intimacy that consists of sitting together in the same room for an hour or two almost every day. Sir John could achieve no more, but did not know more was necessary. In his opinion, being together meant being intimate. As long as his constant plans to bring them together succeeded, he never doubted they were established friends.

To do him justice, he did everything possible to encourage openness. He told the Miss Steeles everything he knew or imagined about the circumstances of his cousins' lives, including the most delicate details of their personal affairs. Elinor had met them no more than twice before the elder congratulated her on Marianne's good fortune in winning such a fashionable beau since coming to Barton.

“It will be a fine thing to see her married so young,” she said. “I hear he is quite a beau and extraordinarily handsome. I hope you have equally good luck soon. Though perhaps you already have someone in reserve.”

Elinor could not imagine Sir John being more delicate about announcing his suspicions of her affection for Edward than he had been about Marianne. Indeed, hers was his favourite of the two jokes, being newer and more speculative. Since Edward's visit, they had never dined together without his drinking to her dearest affections with enough meaningful nods and winks to attract everyone's attention. He invariably introduced the letter F as well. It produced so many jokes that Elinor had long accepted its reputation as the wittiest letter in the alphabet.

As she expected, the Miss Steeles now enjoyed the full benefit of these jokes. They made the elder sister eager to learn the gentleman's name. She expressed her curiosity impertinently and often, entirely in keeping with her usual prying into the family's concerns. Sir John did not keep her in suspense for long. He enjoyed revealing the name at least as much as Miss Steele enjoyed hearing it.
“His name is Ferrars,” he said in a whisper everyone could hear. “But please do not repeat it. It is a tremendous secret.”
“Ferrars!” Miss Steele repeated. “So Mr. Ferrars is the fortunate man? Your sister-in-law's brother, Miss Dashwood? A very agreeable young man, certainly. I know him extremely well.”

“How can you say that, Anne?” Lucy exclaimed, as she generally corrected whatever her sister asserted. “We have seen him once or twice at my uncle's, but it is rather much to claim we know him very well.”

Elinor listened with attention and surprise. Who was this uncle? Where did he live? How had they met Edward? She badly wanted the subject to continue, though she did not choose to join in herself. Nothing more was said. For the first time in her life, she found Mrs. Jennings deficient either in curiosity about small details or in willingness to share them. Miss Steele's manner of speaking about Edward increased her curiosity: it had sounded rather unkind, suggesting that the lady knew, or thought she knew, something against him. But Elinor's curiosity achieved nothing. Miss Steele paid no further attention to Mr. Ferrars's name when Sir John hinted at it, or even mentioned it openly.

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Marianne had never had much patience with impertinence, vulgarity, inferior intelligence, or even tastes different from her own. Her present low spirits made her particularly unwilling to like the Miss Steeles or encourage their attentions. Her consistently cold behaviour stopped every attempt at intimacy. Elinor chiefly attributed to this the preference both sisters soon showed for herself, especially Lucy. Lucy never missed a chance to draw her into conversation or strengthen their acquaintance through an apparently easy and frank disclosure of her feelings.

Lucy was naturally clever. Her observations were often sound and amusing, and Elinor frequently found her pleasant company for half an hour. But education had done nothing to develop her abilities. She was ignorant and poorly read. Despite her continual effort to appear at her best, she could not hide from Elinor her lack of intellectual cultivation or her ignorance of the most ordinary information. Elinor recognised and pitied the neglect of talents that education might have made highly respectable. She felt less sympathy for the complete absence of delicacy, uprightness, and integrity revealed by Lucy's attentions, efforts, and flattery at the park. She could find no lasting pleasure in someone who combined ignorance with insincerity. Lucy's lack of education kept them from conversing as equals, while her behaviour towards others made every show of respect and consideration for Elinor herself entirely worthless.
“I dare say you will think this an odd question,” Lucy said one day as they walked from the park to the cottage, “but do you happen to know your sister-in-law's mother, Mrs. Ferrars, personally?”
Elinor did think it very odd. Her expression showed as much when she answered that she had never met Mrs. Ferrars.
“Really!” Lucy replied. “That surprises me. I thought you must sometimes have seen her at Norland. Then perhaps you cannot tell me what sort of woman she is?”
“No,” Elinor answered, careful not to reveal her real opinion of Edward's mother and unwilling to gratify what seemed an impertinent curiosity. “I know nothing about her.”

“I am sure you think it very strange of me to ask about her like this,” Lucy said, watching Elinor closely. “But perhaps there are reasons. I wish I could venture—but in any case, I hope you will do me the justice of believing I do not mean to be impertinent.”
Elinor gave her a polite reply, and for the next few minutes the two of them continued walking without speaking. Lucy broke the silence by returning hesitantly to the same subject:

“I cannot bear to have you think me rudely inquisitive. I would rather do anything than have someone whose good opinion matters as much as yours think that of me. And I am sure I could trust you without the slightest fear. Indeed, I should be very glad of your advice about managing such an uncomfortable situation as mine. Still, there is no need to trouble you. I am sorry you do not happen to know Mrs. Ferrars.”

“I am sorry too,” Elinor said in great astonishment, “if knowing my opinion of her could be useful to you. But I had no idea that you had any connection with the family. I confess I am therefore rather surprised by such a serious inquiry into her character.”

“I dare say you are, and I certainly do not wonder. But if I dared tell you everything, you would be less surprised. Mrs. Ferrars is nothing to me at present, of course. But the time may come—how soon depends on her—when we shall be very closely connected.”
She lowered her eyes as she spoke, looking prettily shy, with only a sideways glance at Elinor to observe the effect.
“Good heavens!” Elinor exclaimed. “What do you mean? Do you know Mr. Robert Ferrars? Can you possibly know him?” She found the thought of such a sister-in-law far from pleasing.
“No,” Lucy answered, “not Mr. Robert Ferrars. I have never seen him. But,” she fixed her eyes on Elinor, “his elder brother.”

What did Elinor feel then? An astonishment that would have hurt as much as it overwhelmed her, if disbelief had not accompanied it at once. She turned to Lucy in silent amazement, unable to understand the reason or purpose of this declaration. Her colour changed, but her disbelief remained firm. She felt in no danger of either hysterics or fainting.

“You may well be surprised,” Lucy continued. “Of course you could never have guessed. I dare say he has never hinted at it to you or anyone in your family. It was always meant to be a great secret, and I have faithfully kept it until this moment. Not one of my relations knows except Anne. I would never have mentioned it to you unless I had the greatest possible confidence in your discretion. I also thought my asking so many questions about Mrs. Ferrars must seem strange enough to need explaining. And I do not believe Mr. Ferrars can be displeased when he learns I have trusted you. I know he thinks the world of your whole family, and regards you and the other Miss Dashwoods just as his own sisters.” She paused.

For a few moments Elinor said nothing. At first her astonishment was too great for words. Eventually she forced herself to speak, and to choose her words carefully. With a calm manner that concealed her surprise and anxiety fairly well, she asked, “May I ask whether you have been engaged for long?”
“We have been engaged for four years now.”
“Four whole years!”
“Yes, four.”
Though deeply shocked, Elinor still could not bring herself to believe it.
“Until the other day,” she said, “I did not even know you were acquainted.”
“But we have known each other for years. You know, he spent a considerable time under my uncle's care.”
“Your uncle, you say!”
“Yes, Mr. Pratt. Have you never heard him speak about Mr. Pratt?”
“I believe I have,” Elinor replied, making a greater effort to remain composed as her emotion increased.

“He spent four years with my uncle, who lives at Longstaple, near Plymouth. That was where we met, because my sister and me often stayed there. It was where we became engaged too, though not until a year after he had finished being a pupil. He was almost always with us afterwards. As you can imagine, I was very reluctant to agree without his mother's knowledge and approval. But I was too young and loved him too much to be as prudent as I ought. Though you do not know him as well as I do, Miss Dashwood, you must have seen enough to realise how deeply he can make a woman love him.”

“Certainly,” Elinor answered, scarcely knowing what she said. After a moment's reflection, however, her confidence in Edward's honour and love, and in Lucy's falsehood, revived. “Engaged to Mr. Edward Ferrars! I admit I am so completely astonished by what you tell me that really—forgive me—but surely there must be some confusion over a person or a name. We cannot be speaking of the same Mr. Ferrars.”

“We can mean nobody else,” Lucy cried, smiling. “I mean Mr. Edward Ferrars, eldest son of Mrs. Ferrars of Park Street and brother to your sister-in-law, Mrs. John Dashwood. You must admit I am unlikely to mistake the name of the man on whom all my happiness depends.”
“How strange,” Elinor replied in painful bewilderment, “that I have never even heard him mention your name.”

“No, it is not strange when you consider our position. Keeping it secret has been our first concern. You knew nothing about me or my family, so there was never any occasion to mention my name. Besides, he was always particularly afraid his sister might suspect something. That alone was reason enough not to speak of it.”
She stopped. Elinor's confidence faltered, but her self-control did not.
“You have been engaged for four years,” she said in a steady voice.

“Yes, and Heaven knows how much longer we may have to wait. Poor Edward! It quite discourages him.” Taking a small miniature from her pocket, she added, “To prevent any possibility of mistake, please look at this face. It certainly does not do him justice, but I think you can have no doubt who sat for it. I have had it for more than three years.”

She placed it in Elinor's hands. Whatever doubts might still linger in her mind because Elinor feared judging too quickly or hoped to discover a lie, she could not doubt that the painting showed Edward's face. She returned it almost immediately, acknowledging the resemblance.

“I have never managed,” Lucy continued, “to give him my portrait in exchange. It vexes me very much, because he has always been so eager to have it! But I am determined to sit for one at the first opportunity.”
“You are quite right,” Elinor answered calmly. They walked a few more steps in silence before Lucy spoke again.

“I am certain you will faithfully keep our secret. You must understand how important it is that his mother should not hear of it. I dare say she would never approve. I shall have no fortune, and I believe she is an exceedingly proud woman.”

“I certainly did not ask for your confidence,” Elinor said. “But you are quite right to believe you can depend on me. Your secret is safe. Forgive me, however, if I express some surprise at your telling me when there was no need. Surely you must have realised that my knowing could not make it any safer.”
As she spoke, she studied Lucy’s face intently, hoping to discover some sign in it—perhaps a sign that most of what she had been saying was untrue. But Lucy’s expression did not change.

“I feared you would think me too familiar in telling you all this,” she said. “Certainly I have not known you long in person. But I have heard descriptions of you and your family for a long time, and almost felt I knew you already when we met. Besides, after asking such particular questions about Edward's mother, I really thought I owed you an explanation. And I am so unfortunate that I have nobody to ask for advice. Anne is the only person who knows, and she has no judgment. Indeed, she does me much more harm than good. I am constantly afraid she will give me away. As you must have noticed, she cannot hold her tongue. The other day, when Sir John mentioned Edward, I was terrified she would reveal everything. You cannot imagine all the distress this whole affair causes me. I only wonder I am still alive after suffering so much for Edward during these four years. Everything remains so uncertain, and we see one another so seldom—scarcely more than twice a year. I wonder my heart has not completely broken.”
She took out her handkerchief, but Elinor felt little sympathy.

“Sometimes,” Lucy continued after wiping her eyes, “I wonder whether it would be better for both of us to end the engagement altogether.” She looked straight at Elinor. “But at other times I cannot find the courage. I cannot bear to make him as miserable as I know even mentioning it would do. And for myself too, loving him as I do, I do not think I could manage it. What would you advise, Miss Dashwood? What would you do in my place?”
“Forgive me,” Elinor replied, startled by the question, “but I cannot advise you in such circumstances. You must follow your own judgment.”

“Of course,” Lucy continued after they had both been silent for a few minutes, “his mother must provide for him eventually. But poor Edward is so discouraged! Did you not find him dreadfully low-spirited at Barton? He was so miserable when he left us at Longstaple to visit you that I feared you would think him quite ill.”
“Then he came from your uncle's house when he visited us?”
“Oh yes. He had been with us for a fortnight. Did you think he came straight from London?”

“No,” Elinor replied, painfully aware of each new detail supporting Lucy's truthfulness. “I remember his telling us he had spent a fortnight with friends near Plymouth.” She also remembered being surprised then that he had said nothing more about those friends, not even their names.
“Did you not find him terribly low-spirited?” Lucy asked again.
“We certainly did, especially when he first came to us.”

“I begged him to make an effort, so that you would not suspect the trouble. But being unable to stay more than a fortnight, and seeing how upset I was, made him so melancholy. Poor fellow! I fear he is just the same now, because his letters are terribly low-spirited. I heard from him just before leaving Exeter.” She took a letter from her pocket and casually showed Elinor the address. “I dare say you know his handwriting. Such a lovely hand, though this is not as well written as usual. He was probably tired: he had just filled the sheet for me as closely as possible.”

Elinor recognised his handwriting and could doubt no longer. She had allowed herself to suppose that Lucy might have acquired the portrait by chance, that Edward might not have given it. But they could exchange letters only under a definite engagement; nothing else would justify it. For a few moments she was almost overcome. Her heart sank, and she could scarcely stand. Yet she absolutely had to make an effort. She struggled so determinedly against her feelings that she mastered them quickly and, for the moment, completely.

“Writing is our only comfort during these long separations,” Lucy said, returning the letter to her pocket. “Yes, I have one other comfort in his portrait, but poor Edward does not even have that. He says he would be content if only he had mine. The last time he was at Longstaple, I gave him a lock of my hair set in a ring. He said it comforted him somewhat, but not as much as a portrait. Perhaps you noticed the ring when he was with you?”
“I did,” Elinor said. Her composed voice concealed greater distress and emotion than she had ever experienced. She felt humiliated, shocked, and bewildered.

Fortunately, they had reached the cottage and could continue the conversation no further. After sitting with the family for a few minutes, the Miss Steeles returned to the park. Elinor was then free to think and be miserable.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: However little Elinor generally trusted Lucy's truthfulness, serious reflection made it impossible to doubt her in this case. No imaginable advantage could justify the foolishness of inventing a lie of this kind. Elinor could therefore no longer doubt—could not dare to doubt—that Lucy's account was true. Every probability and every piece of evidence supported it; nothing contradicted it except her own wishes. Their opportunities to know each other at Mr. Pratt's house provided an undeniable and alarming foundation for everything else. Edward's visit near Plymouth, his sadness, his dissatisfaction with his prospects, his uncertain behaviour towards herself, the Miss Steeles' surprisingly intimate knowledge of Norland and its family connections, the portrait, the letter, the ring: together these made up a body of evidence that overcame every fear of judging him unfairly. His ill-treatment of her became an established fact which no affection could explain away. For a little while, resentment at his behaviour and indignation at having been deceived left her able to feel only for herself. But other thoughts and considerations soon followed. Had Edward deliberately deceived her? Had he pretended to feel affection which he did not feel? Was his engagement to Lucy founded on love? No: whatever it might once have been, she could not believe that it was now. His love belonged entirely to herself. About that she could not be mistaken. Her mother, her sisters, Fanny—everyone had recognised his affection for her at Norland. It had not been an illusion created by her own vanity. He certainly loved her. How that conviction softened her heart! How powerfully it persuaded her to forgive! He had been wrong, very wrong, to remain at Norland after he first realised that her influence over him was becoming stronger than it should. That could not be defended. But if he had hurt her, how much more deeply had he hurt himself? If her situation deserved pity, his was beyond hope. His lack of judgement had made her unhappy for a time; it seemed to have deprived him of any chance of ever being anything else. She might eventually recover her peace of mind; but what could _he_ look forward to? Could he ever be reasonably happy with Lucy Steele? Even leaving his love for herself entirely aside, could a man of his honesty, his sensitivity, and his cultivated understanding be content with such a wife—uneducated, calculating, and selfish?

The infatuation of a nineteen-year-old would naturally have blinded him to everything except her beauty and good temper. But the four years since then—years which, if sensibly spent, do so much to develop the understanding—must have opened his eyes to the shortcomings of her education. The same years, spent by Lucy in less cultivated company and more frivolous occupations, had perhaps taken away the simplicity which might once have given her beauty an appealing character.

When Elinor had imagined him wanting to marry herself, the difficulties his mother might raise had seemed great enough. How much greater would they be now, when the woman he was engaged to unquestionably had humbler connections, and probably less money, than she had herself? With his heart so far removed from Lucy, these obstacles might indeed make little demand on his patience. But how miserable must someone be when the prospect of opposition and unkindness from his family could come as a relief!

As these thoughts passed painfully through her mind, one after another, she wept more for him than for herself. The knowledge that she had done nothing to deserve her present unhappiness sustained her; the belief that Edward had done nothing to lose her respect consoled her. Even now, while the heavy blow was still fresh, she believed she could control herself well enough to keep her mother and sisters from suspecting the truth. And she fulfilled her own expectations so completely that, when she joined them at dinner only two hours after all her dearest hopes had been destroyed, nobody looking at the sisters could have guessed their feelings. Elinor was secretly mourning the obstacles that must separate her for ever from the man she loved. Marianne was privately considering the perfections of a man whose heart she believed entirely her own, and whom she expected to see in every carriage that came near their house.

Having to hide from her mother and Marianne what had been confided to her, though it demanded constant effort, did not make Elinor's distress worse. On the contrary, she was relieved to be spared telling them something that would cause them such pain. She was also spared hearing them condemn Edward, as their excessive affection for her would probably lead them to do; and that was more than she felt capable of bearing.

She knew that neither their advice nor their conversation could help her. Their tenderness and sorrow would increase her distress, while their example would do nothing to encourage her self-control, and neither would their praise. Alone, she was stronger. Her own good sense supported her so effectively that her resolution remained as steady, and her outward cheerfulness as consistent, as feelings so painful and so recent could possibly allow.

Painful as her first conversation with Lucy on the subject had been, she soon began earnestly wishing to renew it, and for several reasons. She wanted to hear many of the details of the engagement again. She wanted a clearer understanding of what Lucy really felt for Edward, and whether there was any sincerity in her declarations of tender affection. Above all, she wanted her willingness to return to the subject, and her calm manner in discussing it, to convince Lucy that she took only a friend's interest in it. She greatly feared that her involuntary agitation during their morning conversation must have left at least some doubt about that. It seemed very likely that Lucy was inclined to be jealous of her. Edward had plainly always spoken of her with high praise: that was clear not just from Lucy's own account, but from her willingness, after so short an acquaintance, to trust Elinor with a secret which she admitted, and which plainly was, so important. Even Sir John's joking information must have carried some weight. Indeed, while Elinor felt so certain within herself that Edward truly loved her, she needed no other calculation of probabilities to understand why Lucy should be jealous. The confidence itself proved that she was. What other reason could there have been for revealing the affair, except to make Elinor aware of Lucy's stronger claim on Edward, and teach her to avoid him in future? She found little difficulty in understanding this much of her rival's purpose. She was firmly determined to treat Lucy as every principle of honour and honesty required, to struggle against her own love for Edward, and to see him as little as possible. But she could not deny herself the comfort of trying to persuade Lucy that her heart had suffered no wound. And since she could now hear nothing more painful on the subject than she had heard already, she did not doubt her ability to listen calmly to the details a second time.

An opportunity did not immediately present itself, though Lucy was just as willing as Elinor to take advantage of one. The weather was seldom fine enough for a walk together, which would have given them the easiest way of separating from the others. And although they met at least every other evening, either at the park or at the cottage, and usually at the park, nobody could suppose that they met for conversation. Such an idea would never have entered the heads of Sir John or Lady Middleton. They were consequently allowed very little time for general conversation, and none at all for private discussion. They met to eat, drink, and laugh together, to play cards, or consequences, or any other game that made enough noise.

One or two such gatherings had passed without giving Elinor a chance to speak privately with Lucy when Sir John called at the cottage one morning. He begged them, as an act of charity, to dine with Lady Middleton that day. He had to attend his club at Exeter, and otherwise she would be entirely alone, apart from her mother and the two Miss Steeles. Elinor foresaw a better opportunity for her purpose in a gathering of this kind. Under Lady Middleton's quiet, well-bred direction, they would have more freedom among themselves than when her husband united them all in a single noisy activity. She accepted at once. Margaret, with her mother's permission, agreed just as readily. Marianne, though always reluctant to join any of their parties, was persuaded to go as well by her mother, who could not bear to see her shut herself away from any possible amusement.

The young ladies went, and Lady Middleton was happily rescued from the dreadful solitude that had threatened her. The gathering was exactly as dull as Elinor had expected. It produced not one new thought or expression, and nothing could have been less interesting than everything they said, both in the dining room and afterwards in the drawing room. The children followed them into the latter, and while they stayed there, Elinor was too certain of the impossibility of securing Lucy's attention even to try. They left only when the tea things were taken away. The card table was then set out, and Elinor began to wonder how she could ever have hoped to find time for conversation at the park. Everyone rose to prepare for a round game.

“I am pleased,” Lady Middleton said to Lucy, “that you are not planning to finish poor little Annamaria's basket tonight. I am sure working at paper filigree by candlelight must be bad for your eyes. We shall find some way tomorrow to make up to the darling little creature for her disappointment, and then I hope she will not mind it very much.”

The hint was sufficient. Lucy immediately remembered what was expected of her and answered, “Oh, you have quite misunderstood me, Lady Middleton. I am only waiting to find out whether you can make up your party without me; otherwise I should already have started my filigree. I would not disappoint the little angel for anything in the world. And if you need me at the card table now, I am determined to finish the basket after supper.”

“That is very good of you. I hope your eyes won't suffer. Will you ring for some candles to work by? I know my poor little girl would be terribly disappointed if the basket were not finished tomorrow. Although I told her it certainly would not be ready, I am sure she is counting on having it done.”

Lucy immediately pulled her work table towards her and sat down again with a readiness and good humour which suggested that she could imagine no greater pleasure than making a paper-filigree basket for a spoiled child.

Lady Middleton suggested a rubber of Casino for the others. Nobody objected except Marianne, who, with her usual disregard for the ordinary forms of politeness, exclaimed, “Your Ladyship must kindly excuse _me_. You know how I hate cards. I shall go to the piano; I haven't touched it since it was tuned.” Without any further ceremony, she turned from them and walked over to the instrument.
Lady Middleton's expression suggested that she thanked heaven _she_ had never said anything so rude in her life.

“You know Marianne can never stay away from that instrument for very long, ma'am,” Elinor said, trying to soften the offence. “And I can hardly wonder at it myself: it has the finest tone of any piano I have ever heard.”
The five who remained were now ready to draw cards.

“Perhaps,” Elinor went on, “if I draw a card that leaves me out, I could help Miss Lucy Steele by rolling some of her papers. There is still so much to do on the basket that I really think she cannot possibly finish it tonight by working alone. I should enjoy it very much, if she would let me have a share in the work.”
“I should be extremely grateful for your help,” Lucy exclaimed. “I find there is more work left than I expected, and it would be dreadful to end by disappointing dear Annamaria after all.”
“Oh, it really would be dreadful!” said Miss Steele. “The dear little creature—how fond I am of her!”

“That is most kind of you,” Lady Middleton said to Elinor. “Since you really enjoy the work, perhaps you would be just as happy to wait until another rubber before joining us. Or would you rather take your chance now?”

Elinor gladly accepted the first suggestion. With a little of the tact Marianne could never lower herself to use, she had secured her own wish and pleased Lady Middleton at the same time. Lucy attentively made room for her at once. The two young rivals were thus seated next to each other at the same table, working in perfect harmony on the same task. Fortunately, Marianne's piano was very close to them. Absorbed in her music and her own thoughts, she had by now forgotten that anyone else was in the room. Elinor therefore decided that, protected by its sound, she could safely introduce the subject that interested her, with no danger of being overheard by the people at the card table.

chapters.title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: Elinor began to speak in a steady but careful voice.
“If I had no wish for you to continue the confidence you have honoured me with, and no further interest in the subject, I should hardly deserve it. So I shall not apologise for bringing it up again.”
“Thank you for speaking first!” Lucy exclaimed warmly. “You have really set my mind at rest. Somehow I had begun to fear that what I told you on Monday had offended you.”

“Offended me! How could you think that? Believe me”—and Elinor spoke with perfect sincerity—“nothing was further from my intention than to let you think so. Could you have had any reason for trusting me that was not honourable, and flattering to me?”

“But I assure you,” Lucy answered, her small, sharp eyes full of meaning, “there seemed to be something cold and displeased in your manner, and it made me very uncomfortable. I was sure you was angry with me. Ever since then I have been blaming myself for taking such a liberty, troubling you with my own affairs. But I am so pleased to discover that it was only my imagination, and that you really do not blame me. If you knew what a comfort it was to unburden my heart by talking to you about the thing I think of every moment of my life, I am sure your kindness would make you forgive everything else.”

“I can certainly believe that it was a great relief to tell me about your situation. And you may be sure that you will never have cause to regret it. Your position is a very unfortunate one. Difficulties seem to surround you, and you will need all your affection for each other to sustain you through them. I believe Mr. Ferrars depends entirely on his mother.”

“He has only two thousand pounds of his own. It would be madness to marry on that, though for myself I could give up every hope of more without a sigh. I have always been used to a very small income, and for his sake I could struggle with any degree of poverty. But I love him too much to be the selfish cause of his losing, perhaps, everything his mother might give him if he married to please her. We must wait, possibly for many years. With almost any other man in the world that would be a frightening prospect. But I know that nothing can take Edward's love and faithfulness away from me.”

“That certainty must mean everything to you. And no doubt he is sustained by the same confidence in your love. If your attachment to each other had weakened—as it naturally would between many people, in many circumstances, over a four-year engagement—your position really would have been pitiable.”
At this Lucy looked up, but Elinor carefully kept her face free of any expression that might give her words a questionable meaning.

“Edward's love for me,” Lucy said, “has certainly been tested by the long, very long periods we have spent apart since our engagement began. It has stood the test so well that I should have no excuse for doubting it now. I can safely say he has never given me a moment's anxiety about it, from the very beginning.”
Elinor could hardly decide whether that assertion called for a smile or a sigh.

Lucy continued. “Besides, I am rather jealous by nature. With our different positions in life, and his going so much more into society than I do, and our being constantly apart, I was quite ready to be suspicious. I should have discovered the truth immediately if there had been the slightest change in his behaviour when we met, or any depression that I could not explain; if he had talked more about one lady than another, or seemed in any way less happy at Longstaple than before. I don't mean that I am generally particularly observant or quick to notice things. But in a case like this I am certain nobody could deceive me.”
“That is all very prettily said,” Elinor thought, “but neither of us can be taken in by it.”

“But what are your plans?” she asked after a brief silence. “Or have you none except to wait for Mrs. Ferrars to die? That is a sad and shocking last resort. Is her son determined to accept it, and all the weariness of the many years of uncertainty it may mean for you, rather than tell her the truth and risk displeasing her for a time?”

“If only we could be sure it would be for a time! But Mrs. Ferrars is a very proud, stubborn woman. In her first burst of anger when she heard, she would very likely settle everything on Robert. For Edward's sake, the thought of that puts me off any idea of acting hastily.”
“And for your own sake as well, surely, unless your selflessness goes beyond anything reasonable.”
Lucy gave Elinor another look, but said nothing in reply.
“Are you acquainted with Mr. Robert Ferrars?” Elinor asked.
“Not in the least. I have never met him. But I imagine he is quite different from his brother—foolish, and terribly vain.”
“Terribly vain!” repeated Miss Steele, who had caught the words when Marianne's music suddenly paused. “Oh, I expect they are talking about their favourite young men.”
“No, sister,” Lucy exclaimed, “you have that quite wrong. Our favourite young men are _not_ terribly vain.”

“I can certainly answer for Miss Dashwood's,” said Mrs. Jennings with a hearty laugh. “He is one of the most modest, well-mannered young men I have ever seen. But Lucy is such a sly little thing that nobody can discover who _she_ likes.”
“Oh!” Miss Steele exclaimed, looking meaningfully round at them. “I dare say Lucy's young man is every bit as modest and well-mannered as Miss Dashwood's.”

Elinor could not help blushing. Lucy bit her lip and gave her sister an angry look. For some time neither of them spoke. Lucy broke the silence first, lowering her voice, although Marianne was now protecting them very effectively with an extremely magnificent concerto.

“I will frankly tell you one plan that has occurred to me lately for bringing things to a conclusion. In fact, I ought to let you into the secret, because you have a part in it. You have surely seen enough of Edward to know that he would rather enter the church than any other profession. My idea is that he should be ordained as soon as possible. Then, through your influence—which I am sure you would kindly use out of friendship for him, and, I hope, some affection for me—your brother might be persuaded to give him the Norland living. I understand that it provides a very good income, and that the clergyman who holds it now is unlikely to live much longer. That would give us enough to marry on, and we could leave the rest to time and chance.”

“I should always be glad,” Elinor replied, “to show my regard and friendship for Mr. Ferrars in any way. But surely you see that my influence would be entirely unnecessary in such a case? He is Mrs. John Dashwood's brother. _That_ must be recommendation enough to her husband.”
“But Mrs. John Dashwood would not be very pleased about Edward becoming a clergyman.”
“Then I rather think my influence would achieve very little indeed.”
For several more minutes they were both silent. At last Lucy gave a deep sigh and exclaimed,

“I believe the wisest thing would be to end it all at once by breaking off the engagement. There seem to be difficulties surrounding us on every side. Although it would make us miserable for a while, perhaps we should be happier in the end. But will you not give me your advice, Miss Dashwood?”

“No,” Elinor answered, with a smile that hid considerable agitation, “I certainly will not advise you on such a subject. You know perfectly well that my opinion would carry no weight with you unless it agreed with what you wished yourself.”

“You really do misjudge me,” Lucy replied with great solemnity. “There is nobody whose judgement I value as highly as yours. I honestly believe that if you was to tell me, ‘I strongly advise you to break off your engagement to Edward Ferrars; it will make you both happier,’ I should decide to do it at once.”

Elinor blushed at the dishonesty of Edward's future wife. “That compliment would be quite enough to frighten me away from giving an opinion, even if I had formed one,” she replied. “It gives me far too much influence. The power to separate two people so deeply in love is too much for someone with no personal interest.”

“It is precisely because you have _no personal interest_,” Lucy said, a little sharply, giving the words particular emphasis, “that your judgement could rightly mean so much to me. If there were any reason to think your own feelings might influence you, your opinion would be worth nothing.”

Elinor thought it wiser not to answer. Otherwise they might provoke each other into speaking with a degree of freedom and frankness that would be quite inappropriate. She even half decided never to mention the subject again. Another silence of several minutes followed Lucy's speech, and once more it was Lucy who ended it.
“Will you be in London this winter, Miss Dashwood?” she asked, with all her customary pleasantness.
“Certainly not.”

“I am sorry to hear it,” Lucy replied, her eyes brightening at the news. “It would have been such a pleasure to see you there! But I expect you will go all the same. Your brother and his wife will surely ask you to stay with them.”
“If they do invite me, it will not be possible for me to accept.”

“How unfortunate! I had quite counted on seeing you there. Anne and me are going towards the end of January to stay with some relations who have been wanting us to visit for several years. But I am only going to see Edward. He will be there in February. Otherwise London would hold no attraction for me at all; I have no spirits for it.”

The first rubber soon ended, and Elinor was called to the card table. Their confidential conversation was therefore over, an ending neither woman regretted. Nothing either had said had made them dislike each other any less than before. Elinor took her place at the table with the sad conviction that Edward not only felt no love for the woman who was to become his wife, but lacked even that prospect of reasonable happiness in marriage which sincere love on _her_ side might have offered him. Only self-interest could make a woman hold a man to an engagement when she so clearly understood that he was tired of it.

After this, Elinor never brought the subject up again. When Lucy introduced it, as she seldom missed an opportunity of doing, Elinor dealt with it calmly and carefully, then dismissed it as soon as politeness allowed.
