Lucy was particularly determined to tell her confidante how happy she was whenever a letter arrived from Edward. But Elinor felt that allowing these conversations was an indulgence Lucy did not deserve, and one that was dangerous to herself.

The Miss Steeles' stay at Barton Park stretched far beyond the period originally intended. They became greater favourites every day; nobody could spare them; Sir John would not hear of their leaving. Despite their numerous, long-standing engagements in Exeter, despite the absolute necessity of returning immediately to fulfil them—a necessity which was just as urgent at the end of every week—they were persuaded to remain at the park for nearly two months. They thus helped to celebrate, with all due ceremony, that festival whose importance must be proclaimed by an unusually large number of private balls and substantial dinners.

chapters.title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Although Mrs. Jennings generally spent much of the year staying with her children and friends, she had a permanent home of her own. Since her husband's death—he had been a successful businessman in a less fashionable part of London—she had spent every winter in a house in one of the streets near Portman Square. As January approached, her thoughts began to turn towards it. One day she abruptly invited the two elder Miss Dashwoods to accompany her, taking them completely by surprise. Elinor did not notice her sister's changing colour, or the eager look which showed how far she was from indifferent to the proposal. She immediately declined for them both, gratefully but firmly, believing that she spoke for them equally. The reason she gave was their settled determination not to leave their mother at that time of year. Mrs. Jennings was rather surprised by the refusal, and immediately renewed her invitation.

“Oh, Lord! I am certain your mother can spare you perfectly well, and I _do_ beg you to give me the pleasure of your company. I have quite set my heart on it. Don't imagine you will cause me any inconvenience, for I shan't put myself out at all on your account. All I shall have to do is send Betty by the coach, and I hope I can afford _that_. The three of us can travel very comfortably in my chaise. And when we are in London, if you don't want to go everywhere I go, well and good: you can always go with one of my daughters. I am sure your mother won't object. I've been so fortunate in getting my own children off my hands that she will consider me just the person to look after you. And if I don't have at least one of you well married before I've finished with you, it won't be for lack of trying. You may depend on me to put in a good word for you with all the young men.”

“I have an idea,” said Sir John, “that Miss Marianne would have no objection to the plan if her elder sister agreed to it. It really is very hard that she should lose a little pleasure because Miss Dashwood doesn't want it. My advice to you two is to set off for London whenever you grow tired of Barton, without telling Miss Dashwood a word about it.”

“Well,” Mrs. Jennings exclaimed, “I shall be enormously pleased to have Miss Marianne with me, whether Miss Dashwood comes or not. Only, I always say the more the merrier, and I thought they would be happier together. If they grew tired of me, they could talk to each other and laugh at my odd ways behind my back. But I must have one of them, if I cannot have both. Bless me! How am I supposed to live shut up there on my own, when until this winter I have always been used to having Charlotte with me? Come, Miss Marianne, let us shake hands on it. And if Miss Dashwood changes her mind later, so much the better.”

“Thank you, ma'am, I sincerely thank you,” Marianne said warmly. “Your invitation has made me grateful to you for ever. To accept it would make me so happy—yes, almost as happy as I could possibly be. But my mother, my dearest, kindest mother! I know Elinor is right in what she says. If our absence would make her less happy, less comfortable—oh, no! Nothing could tempt me to leave her. There should not, there must not, be any struggle about that.”

Mrs. Jennings again assured them that Mrs. Dashwood could spare them perfectly well. Elinor now understood her sister. She saw how her longing to be with Willoughby again made her indifferent to almost everything else, and no longer directly opposed the plan. She simply left the decision to their mother. From her, however, she scarcely expected any support in trying to prevent a visit which she could not approve for Marianne, and which she had particular reasons of her own for avoiding. Whatever Marianne wanted, their mother would eagerly encourage. Elinor could hardly hope to make her act cautiously in an affair about which she had never been able to persuade her to feel any doubt; and she dared not explain her own reason for disliking the idea of London. Marianne was so particular, knew Mrs. Jennings's manners so well, and was so consistently disgusted by them. That she should overlook every inconvenience of that kind, and disregard everything most likely to offend her sensitive feelings, in pursuit of a single object, was a proof of that object's importance to her so strong and so complete that, despite all that had happened, Elinor had not been prepared to see it.

When Mrs. Dashwood heard of the invitation, she was convinced that the trip would provide both her daughters with a great deal of enjoyment. Through all Marianne's affectionate concern for her, she could see how deeply the girl wanted to go. She refused to hear of their declining on _her_ account, insisted that they both accept immediately, and then began, with her usual optimism, to foresee all sorts of advantages that the separation would bring to every one of them.

“I am delighted with the idea,” she exclaimed. “It is exactly what I would have wished. Margaret and I shall benefit from it as much as you will. When you and the Middletons have gone, we shall live so quietly and happily together, with our books and our music! You will find Margaret wonderfully improved when you return. I have a small plan for altering your bedrooms, too, which can now be carried out without inconveniencing anyone. It is quite right that you _should_ go to London. I would like every young woman in your position to know its manners and amusements. You will be looked after by a good, motherly woman, whose kindness to you I cannot doubt. And you will probably see your brother. Whatever his faults may be, or his wife's, when I remember whose son he is, I cannot bear to think of you becoming such complete strangers to one another.”

“With your usual concern for our happiness,” Elinor said, “you have been clearing away every difficulty in the plan that has occurred to you. But there is still one objection which I do not think can be disposed of so easily.”
Marianne's face fell.
“And what,” Mrs. Dashwood asked, “is my dear, sensible Elinor about to suggest? What terrible obstacle will she produce this time? I will not hear a single word about the expense.”
“My objection is this: I think very highly of Mrs. Jennings's good heart, but we cannot enjoy her company, and being under her care will give us no social standing.”
“That is perfectly true,” her mother replied. “But you will hardly ever have her company without other people's as well. And when you go out in public, you will almost always be with Lady Middleton.”

“If Elinor's dislike of Mrs. Jennings frightens her away,” Marianne said, “it need not stop ME from accepting the invitation. I have no such objections, and I am sure I could endure every unpleasantness of that kind with very little trouble.”

Elinor could not help smiling at this indifference to the manners of a woman towards whom she had often struggled to make Marianne behave with even reasonable politeness. She privately decided that, if her sister insisted on going, she would go too. She did not think it right to leave Marianne guided entirely by her own judgement, or to leave Mrs. Jennings dependent on Marianne's mercy for any comfort in her hours at home. She accepted this decision more easily when she remembered that, according to Lucy, Edward Ferrars would not reach London until February. Their own visit might end before then without being cut unreasonably short.

“I mean you _both_ to go,” Mrs. Dashwood said. “These objections are nonsense. You will have a great deal of pleasure in London, particularly because you will be together. If Elinor would ever lower herself to look forward to enjoyment, she could foresee it there from all sorts of sources. She might perhaps expect some pleasure from getting to know her sister-in-law's family better.”

Elinor had often wished for an opportunity to weaken her mother's confidence in the attachment between Edward and herself, so that the shock would be less severe when the whole truth came out. Now, at this direct reference, she forced herself to begin, although she had almost no hope of success. As calmly as she could, she said, “I like Edward Ferrars very much, and I shall always be pleased to see him. But as for the rest of his family, I am completely indifferent to whether they ever know me or not.”
Mrs. Dashwood merely smiled. Marianne raised her eyes in astonishment, and Elinor decided that she might just as well have said nothing at all.

Very little more discussion was needed before they finally agreed to accept the invitation in full. Mrs. Jennings received the news with great delight, and many promises of kindness and care. Nor was she the only person pleased. Sir John was delighted too: to a man whose chief anxiety was the fear of being alone, adding two people to London's population meant something. Even Lady Middleton made the effort to be delighted, which took her rather out of her usual way. As for the Miss Steeles, and Lucy in particular, they had never in their lives been so happy as this news made them.

Elinor accepted an arrangement so contrary to her wishes with less reluctance than she had expected. For herself, it now seemed a matter of little importance whether she went to London or stayed away. And when she saw her mother so thoroughly pleased, and her sister's joy showing in her face, her voice, and her manner—restoring all her usual animation and raising her spirits beyond their ordinary gaiety—she could not be dissatisfied with what had caused it. She would hardly even allow herself to fear what might follow.

Marianne's joy almost went beyond happiness, so violently were her spirits stirred, and so impatient was she to leave. Only her reluctance to part with her mother could restore any calm. When the moment of departure came, her grief on that account was extreme. Her mother's distress was scarcely less; of the three, Elinor alone appeared to regard the separation as anything short of permanent.
They left during the first week of January. The Middletons were to follow about a week later. The Miss Steeles remained established at the park and would leave only when the rest of the family did.

chapters.title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: Elinor could hardly sit in the carriage with Mrs. Jennings, setting out for London as her guest and under her care, without being astonished at her own position. They had known the woman for so short a time; their ages and temperaments were so entirely unsuited; and only a few days earlier Elinor had raised so many objections to this very arrangement! But the joyful enthusiasm of youth, shared equally by Marianne and her mother, had either overcome those objections or ignored them. Despite her occasional doubts about Willoughby's faithfulness, Elinor could not look at the delighted anticipation filling Marianne's whole being and shining in her eyes without feeling how empty her own prospects were, and how dreary her own state of mind seemed beside them. Gladly would she have accepted the anxieties of Marianne's position for the sake of the same inspiring purpose, the same possibility of hope. A little time, a very little time, must now reveal Willoughby's intentions. He was probably already in London. Marianne's eagerness to leave showed that she counted on finding him there. Elinor resolved not only to gather every fresh insight into his character that her own observation or other people's information could supply, but also to watch his behaviour towards her sister with such close attention that, before they had met many times, she would know what he was and what he intended. If her observations proved unfavourable, she was determined, whatever happened, to open her sister's eyes. If they proved otherwise, her efforts must take a different form. She must learn to resist every selfish comparison, and dismiss every regret that might diminish her pleasure in Marianne's happiness.

Their journey took three days. Marianne's behaviour on the road provided an encouraging sample of the consideration and companionship Mrs. Jennings could expect in future. She sat silent almost the whole way, absorbed in her own thoughts. She scarcely spoke of her own accord unless some picturesque feature of the landscape prompted an exclamation of delight, addressed exclusively to her sister. To make up for this, Elinor immediately took up the post of politeness she had assigned herself. She gave Mrs. Jennings the greatest attention, talked with her, laughed with her, and listened whenever she could. Mrs. Jennings, for her part, treated them both with every possible kindness, considering their comfort and enjoyment at every opportunity. Her only trouble was that she could not make them choose their own dinners at the inns, or extract an admission that they preferred salmon to cod, or boiled chicken to veal cutlets. They arrived in London at three o'clock on the third day, glad after such a journey to escape the confinement of the carriage, and ready to appreciate all the luxury of a good fire.

The house was handsome and well furnished, and the young ladies were immediately given a very comfortable room. It had once been Charlotte's. Above the mantelpiece still hung a landscape she had worked in coloured silks, proving that seven years at an expensive London school had not been entirely wasted on her.

Dinner would not be ready for at least two hours after their arrival, so Elinor decided to spend the interval writing to her mother, and sat down to do so. A few moments later Marianne followed her example. “_I_ am writing home, Marianne,” Elinor said. “Wouldn't it be better to leave your letter for another day or two?”

“I am _not_ writing to my mother,” Marianne answered quickly, as though anxious to prevent further questions. Elinor said nothing more. It struck her at once that Marianne must therefore be writing to Willoughby; and she immediately concluded that, however mysterious they chose to be about it, they must be engaged. Though not entirely satisfied, she was pleased by this conviction, and continued her letter with greater energy. Marianne finished in only a few minutes: it could have been no more than a note. She folded, sealed, and addressed it with eager speed. Elinor thought she could make out a large W in the address. The moment it was ready, Marianne rang the bell and asked the footman who answered to have it taken to the two-penny post. That settled the question at once.

Her spirits remained very high, but there was a nervous excitement in them that kept her sister from taking much pleasure in them. As evening approached, her agitation increased. She could scarcely eat any dinner, and when they returned to the drawing room afterwards, she seemed to be listening anxiously for every carriage.

Elinor was much relieved that Mrs. Jennings, occupied in her own room, saw little of what was happening. The tea things had been brought in, and Marianne had already been disappointed more than once by a knock at a neighbour's door, when suddenly there came a loud knock that could belong to no other house. Elinor felt certain that it announced Willoughby's arrival. Marianne sprang up and went towards the door. Everything was silent. After a few unbearable seconds, she opened the door and took several steps towards the stairs. She listened for half a minute, then returned to the room in all the agitation that naturally followed her conviction that she had heard him. In the joy of that moment she could not help crying, “Oh, Elinor, it is Willoughby! It really is!” She seemed almost ready to throw herself into his arms when Colonel Brandon appeared.

The shock was too great for her to bear calmly, and she immediately left the room. Elinor was disappointed as well, but her affection for Colonel Brandon ensured that she welcomed him. It particularly distressed her that a man so fond of her sister should see that his appearance caused her only grief and disappointment. She saw at once that he had noticed. Indeed, he watched Marianne leave with such astonishment and concern that he almost forgot the politeness he owed to Elinor herself.
“Is your sister unwell?” he asked her.

Rather distressed, Elinor answered that she was. She spoke of headaches, low spirits, and excessive tiredness—of anything that might reasonably provide a respectable explanation for her sister's behaviour.

He listened with the closest attention. Then, seeming to recover himself, he let the subject drop and began at once to express his pleasure at seeing them in London. He asked the usual questions about their journey and the friends they had left behind.

Their conversation continued in this quiet way, with very little interest on either side. Both were dispirited, and both had their thoughts elsewhere. Elinor very much wanted to ask whether Willoughby was in London, but feared hurting him by asking about his rival. At last, simply to say something, she asked whether he had stayed in London ever since she had last seen him. “Yes,” he answered with some embarrassment, “nearly all the time. I have been down to Delaford once or twice for a few days, but I have never been able to return to Barton.”

His answer, and the manner in which he gave it, immediately reminded her of all the circumstances of his departure from Barton, and the anxiety and suspicions they had caused Mrs. Jennings. She feared her question had suggested far more curiosity about the matter than she had ever felt.

Mrs. Jennings soon joined them. “Oh, Colonel!” she said with her usual loud good humour. “I am enormously pleased to see you. Sorry I couldn't come sooner—do forgive me—but I had to look round a little and get my affairs in order. It is a long time since I was last at home, and you know there are always a thousand little odds and ends to attend to after one has been away. And then I had to settle accounts with Cartwright. Lord, I have been as busy as a bee ever since dinner! But do tell me, Colonel, how did you manage to discover that I should be in London today?”
“I had the pleasure of hearing the news at Mr. Palmer's, where I dined today.”
“Oh, did you? Well, and how is everyone there? How is Charlotte? I expect she must be getting very large by now.”
“Mrs. Palmer seemed perfectly well. She asked me to tell you that you may certainly expect to see her tomorrow.”

“Yes, of course, I thought so. Well, Colonel, you see I have brought two young ladies with me—or rather, you can see only one at present, but there is another somewhere. Your friend Miss Marianne, too; you won't be sorry to hear that. I don't know how you and Mr. Willoughby will settle things between you about her. Ah, it is a fine thing to be young and pretty! Well, I was young once, though never particularly pretty, worse luck for me. Still, I found a very good husband, and I don't know what more the greatest beauty can do. Ah, the poor man! He's been dead more than eight years now. But Colonel, where have you been since we parted? And how is your business getting on? Come, come, friends should have no secrets from one another.”
He answered every question with his usual gentleness, without satisfying her curiosity about any of them. Elinor began to make the tea, and Marianne was obliged to return.

Once she had come in, Colonel Brandon grew more thoughtful and quieter than before. Mrs. Jennings could not persuade him to stay very long. Nobody else called that evening, and all the ladies agreed that an early night would be best.

Marianne got up the next morning with her spirits restored and happiness in her face. The previous evening's disappointment seemed forgotten in her expectations of the day ahead. They had barely finished breakfast when Mrs. Palmer's barouche stopped outside. A few minutes later she came laughing into the room, so delighted to see them all that it was impossible to tell whether meeting her mother or the Miss Dashwoods again gave her more pleasure. She was so surprised that they had come to London, although she had rather expected it all along! So angry that they had accepted her mother's invitation after refusing her own, although she would never have forgiven them if they had stayed away!
“Mr. Palmer will be so pleased to see you,” she said. “What do you think he said when he heard you were coming with Mama? I can't remember now, but it was something wonderfully funny!”

An hour or two passed in what her mother called a comfortable chat. This meant, on Mrs. Jennings's side, every possible question about all their acquaintances, and, on Mrs. Palmer's, laughter without any reason. Mrs. Palmer then suggested that they should accompany her to some shops where she had business that morning. Mrs. Jennings and Elinor readily agreed, having purchases of their own to make. Marianne at first declined, but was eventually persuaded to join them too.

Everywhere they went, she was plainly keeping watch. Her eyes were constantly searching, especially in Bond Street, where they had much of their business. Whichever shop they entered, her mind remained equally remote from everything before them, from everything that interested and occupied the rest of the party. She was restless and dissatisfied everywhere. Her sister could never get an opinion from her on anything they were buying, even when it concerned them both equally. Nothing gave her any pleasure. She wanted only to be home again, and could scarcely control her irritation at Mrs. Palmer's delays. Every pretty, expensive, or novel object caught that lady's eye. She was desperate to buy everything, unable to decide on anything, and wasted her time in delight and indecision.

It was late in the morning when they got home. The moment they entered the house, Marianne hurried eagerly upstairs. Elinor followed and found her turning away from the table with a sorrowful expression that made it clear Willoughby had not called.

“Hasn't a letter been left for me while we were out?” she asked the footman, who came in just then with their parcels. He said there had been none. “Are you quite sure?” she asked again. “Are you certain no servant or porter has brought any letter or note?”
He repeated that nobody had brought one.
“How very strange!” she said quietly, disappointment in her voice, as she turned away and went to the window.

“Strange indeed!” Elinor repeated to herself, watching her sister uneasily. “If she had not known he was in London, she would not have written to him here; she would have written to Combe Magna. And if he is here, how strange that he should neither visit nor write! Oh, my dear mother, you must be wrong to allow an engagement between so young a daughter and so little-known a man to continue in this uncertain, mysterious way! _I_ long to ask questions; and how will _my_ interference be received?”

After some thought, she decided that if things continued to look so unpromising for many more days, she would write to her mother and urge, as strongly as possible, the need for a serious inquiry into the affair.

Mrs. Palmer dined with them, along with two elderly ladies whom Mrs. Jennings knew intimately and had met and invited that morning. Soon after tea Mrs. Palmer left for her evening engagements, and Elinor had to help make up a table for whist with the others. Marianne was useless on such occasions, since she would never learn the game. But although her time was therefore entirely her own, the evening gave her no more pleasure than it gave Elinor. She passed it in anxious expectation and painful disappointment. Sometimes she tried to read for a few minutes, but soon tossed the book aside and returned to the more absorbing occupation of pacing up and down the room. Every time she reached the window, she paused for a moment, hoping to make out the knock she had waited for so long.

chapters.title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: “If this mild weather lasts much longer,” Mrs. Jennings said at breakfast the next morning, “Sir John won't like leaving Barton next week. It is a dreadful thing for a sportsman to miss a day's pleasure. Poor creatures! I always feel sorry for them when it happens. They seem to take it so much to heart.”
“That's true,” Marianne exclaimed cheerfully, going to the window as she spoke to inspect the day. “I hadn't thought of _that_. Weather like this will keep plenty of sportsmen in the country.”

It was a fortunate thought, and restored all her good spirits. “It really is delightful weather for _them_,” she continued, sitting down to breakfast with a happy face. “How they must be enjoying it! But”—a little anxiety returned—“we cannot expect it to last. At this time of year, and after so much rain, we shall certainly have very little more of it. The frosts will soon begin, and probably severe ones. Perhaps in another day or two. This extraordinary mildness can hardly continue any longer. Indeed, it might even freeze tonight!”

“In any case,” Elinor said, hoping to prevent Mrs. Jennings from reading her sister's thoughts as clearly as she could herself, “I expect Sir John and Lady Middleton will be in London by the end of next week.”
“Yes, my dear, you may be sure of that. Mary always gets her own way.”
“And now,” Elinor thought to herself, “she will write to Combe by today's post.”

But if she _did_, she wrote and sent the letter so secretly that all Elinor's watchfulness failed to establish the fact. Whatever the truth might be, and far as Elinor was from feeling entirely satisfied, she could not be very unhappy herself while she saw Marianne in good spirits. And Marianne was in good spirits: happy because the weather was mild, and happier still because she expected it to freeze.

They spent most of the morning leaving visiting cards at the houses of Mrs. Jennings's acquaintances to announce her arrival in London. Throughout the outing Marianne busied herself with noting the wind's direction, watching every change in the sky, and imagining a change in the air.

“Don't you think it is colder than it was this morning, Elinor? There seems a very definite difference to me. I can hardly keep my hands warm even inside my muff. I don't think it was like that yesterday. And the clouds seem to be breaking up. The sun will be out in a moment, and we shall have a clear afternoon.”

Elinor was amused one moment and distressed the next. But Marianne persisted, discovering every evening in the brightness of the fire, and every morning in the look of the air, unmistakable signs that a frost was coming.

The Miss Dashwoods had no more cause to complain of Mrs. Jennings's way of living or her circle of acquaintances than of her treatment of them, which was consistently kind. Her household was run with the greatest generosity. Apart from a few old friends from the City whom, to Lady Middleton's regret, she had never given up, she visited nobody to whom her young companions could have felt embarrassed to be introduced. Elinor was pleased to find her circumstances in this respect more comfortable than she had expected. In exchange, she was quite willing to accept the lack of much real enjoyment at their evening parties. Whether at home or elsewhere, these were organised entirely around cards, and offered little to entertain her.

Colonel Brandon had a standing invitation and came almost every day. He came to look at Marianne and talk to Elinor. She often found more satisfaction in their conversations than in anything else the day brought, but at the same time she watched his continuing affection for her sister with considerable concern. She feared it was growing stronger. It pained her to see the intensity with which he often watched Marianne, and his spirits were certainly lower than they had been at Barton.
About a week after their own arrival, they had definite proof that Willoughby too was in London. When they returned from their morning drive, his visiting card lay on the table.

“Good heavens!” Marianne cried. “He has called while we were out.” Delighted to be certain that he was in London, Elinor ventured to say, “You may be sure he will come again tomorrow.” But Marianne hardly seemed to hear her. As Mrs. Jennings came in, she escaped with the precious card.

This incident lifted Elinor's spirits, but brought back all Marianne's former agitation, and more. From that moment her mind was never at rest. Expecting him every hour of the day made her incapable of anything else. The following morning, when the others went out, she insisted on staying behind.

Throughout their absence, Elinor's thoughts were occupied with what might be happening in Berkeley Street. But one glance at her sister on their return told her that Willoughby had made no second visit. Just then a note was brought in and placed on the table.
“For me!” Marianne exclaimed, moving quickly towards it.
“No, ma'am. It is for my mistress.”
Still unconvinced, Marianne immediately picked the note up herself.
“It really is for Mrs. Jennings. How annoying!”
“Then you are expecting a letter?” Elinor asked, unable to keep silent any longer.
“Yes—a little. Not very much.”
After a brief pause, Elinor said, “You do not trust me, Marianne.”
“Oh, Elinor! Such a reproach from _you_, who never confide in anybody!”
“I?” Elinor answered, rather embarrassed. “Really, Marianne, there is nothing I can tell you.”
“Nor is there anything I can tell you,” Marianne replied emphatically. “So our positions are the same. Neither of us has anything to say: you because you share nothing, and I because I hide nothing.”
Distressed by this accusation of secrecy, which she was not free to clear away, Elinor did not know how, in such circumstances, she could urge Marianne to be more open with her.

Mrs. Jennings soon appeared. They gave her the note, and she read it aloud. Lady Middleton wrote to announce that they had arrived in Conduit Street the previous evening, and to invite her mother and cousins for the following night. Sir John's business and a severe cold of her own prevented them from calling in Berkeley Street. They accepted the invitation. But as the appointed time drew near, Elinor found it difficult to persuade her sister to go, although ordinary courtesy to Mrs. Jennings required them both to accompany her on such a visit. Marianne had still seen nothing of Willoughby. She was as unwilling to risk his calling again while she was out as she was disinclined to seek amusement elsewhere.

By the end of the evening, Elinor had discovered that a change of address does little to alter a person's character. Though scarcely settled in London, Sir John had managed to gather nearly twenty young people around him and entertain them with a dance. Lady Middleton, however, did not approve of the arrangement. An unplanned dance was perfectly acceptable in the country. In London, where a reputation for elegance mattered more and was harder to acquire, it was too great a risk merely to please a few girls. People might learn that Lady Middleton had given a little dance for eight or nine couples, with only two violins and a simple supper set out on a sideboard.

Mr. and Mrs. Palmer were there. The sisters had not seen him since arriving in London: he carefully avoided any appearance of paying attention to his mother-in-law, and therefore never came near her. When they entered, he gave no sign of recognising them. He glanced at them as though he did not know who they were, and merely nodded to Mrs. Jennings from across the room. Marianne took one look round as she entered. It was enough: _he_ was not there. She sat down equally unwilling to enjoy herself or make herself pleasant to anyone else. About an hour after they had gathered, Mr. Palmer strolled over to the Miss Dashwoods to express surprise at seeing them in London. This was despite Colonel Brandon having first heard of their arrival at his house, and despite his own extremely funny remark when he had learnt they were coming.
“I thought you were both still in Devonshire,” he said.
“Did you indeed?” Elinor replied.
“When are you going back there?”
“I don't know.” That brought their conversation to an end.
Never in her life had Marianne felt so unwilling to dance as she did that evening, or found the exercise so exhausting. On the way back to Berkeley Street, she complained of her tiredness.

“Yes, yes,” Mrs. Jennings said, “we know perfectly well what accounts for that. If a certain person, whom I won't name, had been there, you wouldn't be tired at all. And to tell the truth, it was not very nice of him to miss meeting you when he had been invited.”
“He was invited?” Marianne exclaimed.

“So my daughter Middleton told me. Apparently Sir John ran into him somewhere in the street this morning.” Marianne said nothing further, but looked deeply hurt. Elinor longed to do something that might relieve her sister's distress. She decided to write to their mother the next morning, hoping that by alarming her about Marianne's health she could bring about the inquiries that had been put off so long. She became still more determined when, after breakfast the next day, she saw Marianne once again writing to Willoughby; she could not imagine the letter being addressed to anyone else.

Around midday, Mrs. Jennings went out alone on business, and Elinor immediately began her letter. Too restless to occupy herself and too anxious to talk, Marianne moved from one window to another, or sat by the fire lost in unhappy thought. Elinor wrote very earnestly to her mother. She related everything that had happened and her suspicions that Willoughby's affection had changed, appealing to every consideration of duty and love to persuade her mother to ask Marianne exactly how matters stood between them.

She had barely finished when a knock announced a visitor, and Colonel Brandon's name was brought in. Marianne had seen him from the window. Disliking company of any kind, she left the room before he entered. He looked more serious than usual. Although he expressed pleasure at finding Miss Dashwood alone, as if he had something particular to tell her, he sat for some time without speaking. Elinor was convinced that he had something to communicate about her sister, and waited impatiently for him to begin. It was not the first time she had felt this. More than once before, after a remark such as “Your sister looks unwell today,” or “Your sister seems low in spirits,” he had appeared about to reveal, or ask, something specific concerning her. After several minutes, he broke the silence by asking, in an agitated voice, when he might congratulate her on acquiring a brother. Elinor was unprepared for the question. With no answer ready, she was obliged to resort to the simple and familiar expedient of asking what he meant. He attempted a smile as he replied, “Your sister's engagement to Mr. Willoughby is very widely known.”
“It cannot be widely known,” Elinor answered, “because even her own family knows nothing of it.”
He looked surprised. “Forgive me. I am afraid my question was intrusive. But I had not imagined they intended any secrecy, since they write to each other openly and everyone talks of their marriage.”
“How can that be? Who have you heard speaking about it?”

“Many people. Some you do not know at all, others who are among your closest friends: Mrs. Jennings, Mrs. Palmer, the Middletons. Even so, I might not have believed it. When the mind is unwilling to accept something, it can always find reasons for doubt. But today, as the servant let me in, I happened to see a letter in his hand addressed to Mr. Willoughby in your sister's writing. I came to ask, but I was convinced before I could put the question. Is everything finally settled? Is it impossible to—? But I have no right, and no chance of success. Forgive me, Miss Dashwood. I believe I have said too much. I hardly know what to do, and I have the utmost trust in your discretion. Tell me that it is absolutely decided, that any attempt—that, in short, concealment, if concealment is possible, is all that remains.”

To Elinor, these words were a direct confession of his love for her sister, and they moved her deeply. At first she could not speak. Even after recovering herself, she considered for a little while what answer would be most appropriate. She knew so little of the actual understanding between Willoughby and Marianne that, in trying to explain it, she might just as easily say too much as too little. Yet she was certain that Marianne's love for Willoughby left Colonel Brandon no hope of success, whatever its eventual outcome. She also wanted to protect her sister's behaviour from criticism. After some thought, she decided that the wisest and kindest course was to say more than she really knew or believed. She therefore admitted that, although neither of them had ever told her exactly where they stood with each other, she had no doubt of their mutual affection and was not surprised to hear that they corresponded.

He listened attentively without speaking. As soon as she finished, he rose from his chair. “I wish your sister every possible happiness,” he said in a voice full of feeling, “and I hope Willoughby will try to deserve her.” Then he took his leave and went away.

The conversation gave Elinor no comforting thoughts to ease her other anxieties. Instead, it left her with a painful sense of Colonel Brandon's unhappiness. She could not even wish it ended, since she herself so anxiously desired the very event that must make it certain.

chapters.title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: Over the next three or four days, nothing happened to make Elinor regret having appealed to her mother. Willoughby neither visited nor wrote. Towards the end of that time, they were due to accompany Lady Middleton to a party. Mrs. Jennings could not go, because her younger daughter was unwell. Marianne prepared for the evening in complete dejection, indifferent to her appearance and apparently equally indifferent to going or staying. Not a hopeful look or a pleased expression escaped her. After tea she sat beside the drawing-room fire until Lady Middleton arrived, never once moving from her chair or changing her position. She was lost in thought, unaware of her sister's presence. When they were finally told that Lady Middleton was waiting at the door, she started as though she had forgotten they were expecting anyone.

They reached their destination in due course. As soon as the line of carriages ahead allowed, they got out, climbed the stairs, heard their names loudly announced from one landing to the next, and entered a brilliantly lit room that was crowded and unbearably hot. Having paid their tribute to politeness by curtsying to their hostess, they were free to join the crowd and take their share of the heat and discomfort to which their arrival must inevitably add. After some time spent saying little and doing even less, Lady Middleton sat down to Casino. Marianne had no inclination to move about. She and Elinor were fortunate enough to secure chairs, and settled themselves fairly close to the card table.

They had not been sitting there long when Elinor noticed Willoughby a few yards away, deep in conversation with a very fashionably dressed young woman. She soon caught his eye. He immediately bowed, but made no attempt to speak to her or approach Marianne, whom he could not possibly have failed to see. Instead, he continued talking to the same young woman. Elinor involuntarily turned towards her sister to discover whether she had noticed. At that very moment Marianne first saw him. Her whole face lit up with sudden joy, and she would immediately have gone to him if Elinor had not caught her arm.
“Good heavens!” she cried. “There he is—there he is! Oh, why doesn't he look at me? Why can't I speak to him?”
“Please, please, control yourself,” Elinor urged. “Don't let everyone here see what you are feeling. Perhaps he hasn't noticed you yet.”

But she could not believe that herself. To be calm at such a moment was not merely beyond Marianne's ability; it was beyond her wishes. She sat in an agony of impatience that showed in every feature of her face.

At last he turned again and looked at them both. Marianne sprang up, spoke his name affectionately, and held out her hand. He came towards them, but addressed Elinor rather than Marianne, as though anxious to avoid her eyes and determined not to notice her outstretched hand. He hurriedly asked after Mrs. Dashwood and inquired how long they had been in London. Such a greeting deprived Elinor of all composure, and she could not speak. Her sister, however, expressed her feelings immediately. Her face flushed crimson, and in a voice of intense emotion she cried, “Good heavens, Willoughby! What does this mean? Haven't you received my letters? Won't you shake hands with me?”

He could no longer avoid it, but her touch seemed to hurt him, and he held her hand for only a moment. Throughout the encounter he was plainly struggling to compose himself. Elinor watched his face and saw it gradually grow calmer. After a brief pause, he spoke steadily.
“I had the honour of calling in Berkeley Street last Tuesday, and was very sorry not to have the good fortune of finding you and Mrs. Jennings at home. I hope my card was not mislaid.”

“But haven't you received my notes?” Marianne cried in frantic anxiety. “There must be a mistake—some dreadful mistake. What can it mean? Tell me, Willoughby. For heaven's sake, tell me what is wrong!”

He did not answer. His colour changed, and all his embarrassment returned. But he caught the eye of the young woman he had been talking to, and seemed suddenly to feel the need for an immediate effort. Recovering himself once more, he said, “Yes, I had the pleasure of receiving the news of your arrival in London, which you were kind enough to send me.” Then, with a slight bow, he turned quickly away and rejoined his friend.

Marianne had turned terribly pale. Unable to stand, she sank into her chair. Elinor expected her to faint at any moment and tried to shield her from other people's attention while reviving her with lavender water.

“Go to him, Elinor,” she cried as soon as she could speak, “and make him come to me. Tell him I must see him again—must speak to him immediately. I cannot rest. I shall not have a moment's peace until this is explained. There is some dreadful misunderstanding. Oh, go to him at once!”
“How could I do that? No, my dearest Marianne, you must wait. This is no place for explanations. You need only wait until tomorrow.”

Even so, she could hardly stop Marianne from going after him herself. It was impossible to persuade her to restrain her agitation, or even appear calm while she waited until they could speak more privately and to better effect. Marianne continually gave voice to her misery in quiet exclamations of distress. Before long, Elinor saw Willoughby leave through the door leading to the stairs. She told Marianne he had gone and used the impossibility of speaking to him again that evening as a fresh reason for calm. Marianne immediately begged her to ask Lady Middleton to take them home. She was too miserable to remain another minute.

Although Lady Middleton was in the middle of a rubber, she was too polite to raise the slightest objection when told that Marianne was unwell and wished to leave. She handed her cards to a friend, and they departed as soon as their carriage could be found. Hardly a word passed between them on the way back to Berkeley Street. Marianne suffered in silence, too overwhelmed even to cry. Fortunately, Mrs. Jennings had not yet returned, so they could go straight to their own room. There, smelling salts brought Marianne a little back to herself. She was soon undressed and in bed. Since she seemed to want to be alone, Elinor left her. While waiting for Mrs. Jennings, she had plenty of time to reflect on everything that had happened.

She could not doubt that some sort of engagement had existed between Willoughby and Marianne. It seemed equally clear that Willoughby had grown tired of it. However much Marianne might continue to encourage her own hopes, _Elinor_ could not explain such behaviour by any mistake or misunderstanding. Only a complete change of feeling could account for it. Her indignation would have been still greater if she had not seen his embarrassment. It seemed to show an awareness of his own wrongdoing, and prevented her from believing him so utterly without principle that he had played with her sister's feelings from the beginning, without any honourable intention. Absence might have weakened his affection, and convenience might have persuaded him to conquer it. But she could not bring herself to doubt that such affection had once existed.

As for Marianne, Elinor could not think without the deepest concern of the pain this unhappy meeting must already have caused her, or the still greater suffering that its probable consequences might bring. Her own position looked better by comparison. However far she and Edward might be separated in future, her unchanged _respect_ for him could always sustain her. But every circumstance that could make such a loss more bitter seemed to combine to deepen Marianne's misery in a final separation from Willoughby—an immediate breach that could never be repaired.

chapters.title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: The next morning, before the housemaid had lit their fire or the sun had made any impression on the cold January gloom, Marianne was already kneeling against a window seat, still only half dressed. She was trying to catch what little light it offered, and writing as quickly as her constant tears would allow. Elinor, woken by her restless movements and sobbing, first saw her in this position. After watching her for a few moments in silent anxiety, she spoke with the greatest tenderness and care.
“Marianne, may I ask you—?”
“No, Elinor,” she answered. “Don't ask anything. You will know everything soon.”

The desperate calm with which she said this lasted only as long as the words themselves, and immediately gave way to the same overwhelming grief. Several minutes passed before she could resume her letter. Even then, repeated bursts of sorrow forced her to stop writing. They showed clearly enough that she felt how very likely it was that this would be her last letter to Willoughby.

Elinor gave her every quiet, unobtrusive comfort she could. She would have tried still harder to soothe her, but Marianne begged her, with all the urgency of strained and irritable nerves, not to speak to her on any account. In these circumstances, it was better for both that they should not remain together for long. Marianne's restlessness prevented her from staying in the room for a moment after she had dressed. Needing both solitude and constant movement, she wandered through the house until breakfast, avoiding everyone she might meet.

At breakfast she ate nothing and made no attempt to eat. Elinor devoted all her attention, not to urging her, pitying her, or seeming to watch her, but to keeping Mrs. Jennings's notice entirely fixed on herself.

Breakfast was one of Mrs. Jennings's favourite meals, and lasted a considerable time. Afterwards, they were just settling themselves round the table where they worked when a letter arrived for Marianne. She snatched it eagerly from the servant, turned deathly pale, and immediately ran out of the room. Elinor knew as certainly as if she had read the address that it must be from Willoughby. Her heart sank so painfully that she could barely hold up her head, and she trembled so much that she feared Mrs. Jennings must notice. That good lady, however, saw only that Marianne had received a letter from Willoughby. She considered this an excellent joke and treated it accordingly, laughing as she hoped Marianne would find it to her liking. She was too busy measuring lengths of wool for her rug to notice anything of Elinor's distress. As soon as Marianne had disappeared, she calmly continued talking.

“Upon my word, I have never in my life seen a young woman so desperately in love! _My_ girls were nothing beside her, though they could be foolish enough. But Miss Marianne is quite a different creature from what she was. I sincerely hope he won't keep her waiting much longer. It is really painful to see her looking so ill and miserable. Tell me, when are they to be married?”

Elinor had never felt less able to talk, but she forced herself to answer so direct an attack. Trying to smile, she said, “Have you really talked yourself into believing that my sister is engaged to Mr. Willoughby, ma'am? I thought you were only joking. But such a serious question seems to mean more, and I must ask you not to continue deceiving yourself. I assure you that nothing would surprise me more than to hear they intended to marry.”

“For shame, Miss Dashwood, for shame! How can you say such a thing? Don't we all know it must end in marriage, and that they were head over heels in love from the moment they met? Didn't I see them together every day in Devonshire, all day long? And don't I know that your sister came to London with me expressly to buy her wedding clothes? Come, come, that won't do. Because you are so secretive about it yourself, you imagine nobody else has any sense. But I can tell you that is not the case. It has been known all over London for ages. I tell everybody, and so does Charlotte.”
“You really are mistaken, ma'am,” Elinor said very seriously. “It is extremely unkind of you to spread the story. You will discover that for yourself, although you do not believe me now.”

Mrs. Jennings laughed again. Elinor had no strength to say more, and in any case was desperate to know what Willoughby had written. She hurried to their room. Opening the door, she found Marianne stretched on the bed, almost choking with grief, one letter in her hand and two or three more beside her. Elinor approached without speaking. She sat on the bed, took her sister's hand, kissed her affectionately several times, and then burst into tears herself, at first almost as violently as Marianne. Though unable to speak, Marianne seemed to feel the full tenderness of these actions. After they had shared their sorrow for some time, she put all the letters into Elinor's hands. Then she covered her face with her handkerchief and almost screamed in anguish. Elinor knew that such grief, terrible as it was to witness, had to run its course. She stayed beside her until the worst of the suffering had spent itself a little, then eagerly turned to Willoughby's letter and read:
“Bond Street, January.

MY DEAR MADAM, “I have just had the honour of receiving your letter, for which I offer my sincere thanks. I am very sorry to learn that anything in my behaviour last night failed to meet with your approval. Although I cannot discover how I could have been unfortunate enough to offend you, I ask your forgiveness for what I assure you was entirely unintentional. I shall always remember my acquaintance with your family in Devonshire with the greatest gratitude and pleasure, and I hope that no mistake or misunderstanding of my actions will bring it to an end. My regard for your entire family is perfectly sincere. But if I have unfortunately encouraged you to believe that I felt, or intended to express, anything more, I must blame myself for not being more cautious in expressing that regard. You will recognise that I could never have intended more when I explain that my affections have long been committed elsewhere. I believe it will be only a few weeks before that engagement ends in marriage. With great regret, I comply with your request to return the letters you have honoured me by writing, and the lock of hair you were so kind as to give me.
“I remain, dear Madam, “Your most obedient “and humble servant, “JOHN WILLOUGHBY.”

It is easy to imagine the indignation with which Elinor read such a letter. Before beginning, she had known it must admit that his affection had changed and confirm their permanent separation. But she had not imagined that anyone could announce it in such language. Nor could she have believed Willoughby capable of abandoning so completely even the appearance of honour and sensitivity, or the ordinary courtesy expected of a gentleman, as to send a letter of such shameless cruelty. Instead of asking to be released from his promise with some expression of regret, it acknowledged no broken promise and denied that he had ever felt any particular affection. Every line was an insult. The whole letter declared its writer a thoroughly hardened villain.

For some time she stared at it in astonishment and anger, then read it again and again. Each reading only increased her disgust for him. Her feelings were so bitter that she dared not trust herself to speak, for fear of hurting Marianne still more. She might have described the broken engagement, not as the loss of any possible happiness, but as an escape from the worst and most incurable of evils: being bound for life to a man without principles. She might have called it a true deliverance, an immense blessing.

Absorbed in the letter, in the corruption of a mind that could compose it, and probably in the very different mind of a very different person—someone who had no connection with the affair except the connection her heart gave him with everything that happened—Elinor forgot her sister's immediate suffering. She forgot the three unread letters in her lap. She forgot so completely how long she had been in the room that, on hearing a carriage draw up, she went to the window to see who could be calling so unreasonably early. To her astonishment, it was Mrs. Jennings's carriage, which she knew had not been ordered until one o'clock. Although she had no hope of comforting Marianne just then, she was determined not to leave her. She hurried downstairs to excuse herself from accompanying Mrs. Jennings because her sister was unwell. With thoroughly kind concern for the cause, Mrs. Jennings readily accepted the excuse. After seeing her off, Elinor returned to Marianne and found her trying to get out of bed. She reached her just in time to stop her falling to the floor. Marianne was weak and dizzy from prolonged lack of proper food and rest. For many days she had had no appetite; for many nights she had not really slept. Now that the fever of uncertainty no longer sustained her, she felt the consequences in an aching head, an unsettled stomach, and a general trembling faintness. Elinor immediately brought her a glass of wine. It helped her feel more comfortable, and at last she could show some appreciation of her sister's kindness by saying,
“Poor Elinor! How miserable I am making you!”
“I only wish,” her sister answered, “that there were something I _could_ do to bring you a little comfort.”
This, like anything else she might have said, was too much for Marianne. “Oh, Elinor, I really am miserable!” was all she could cry out in her anguish before her voice dissolved completely into sobs.
Elinor could no longer watch this unchecked flood of grief without speaking.

“Try to control yourself, dearest Marianne,” she cried, “unless you mean to kill yourself and everyone who loves you. Think of your mother; think how miserable _your_ suffering makes her. You must make an effort for her sake.”

“I can't, I can't!” Marianne cried. “Leave me if I upset you. Leave me, hate me, forget me! But don't torment me like this. Oh, how easy it is for people with no sorrow of their own to talk about making an effort! Happy, happy Elinor! _You_ cannot imagine what I am suffering.”
“Do you call _me_ happy, Marianne? Ah, if only you knew! And can you really believe I am happy while I see you so wretched?”

“Forgive me, forgive me!” She threw her arms round her sister's neck. “I know you feel for me. I know how loving your heart is. But you are happy—you must be. Edward loves you. What, oh what, could take away happiness like that?”
“A great many things,” Elinor answered gravely.
“No, no, no!” Marianne cried wildly. “He loves you, and only you. You _cannot_ have anything to grieve about.”
“I cannot take pleasure in anything while I see you like this.”
“And you will never see me any other way. Nothing can take away my misery.”

“You must not speak like that, Marianne. Have you no comforts left? No friends? Has your loss left no possibility of consolation? Much as you suffer now, think how much worse it would have been if you had discovered his character later—if he had allowed your engagement to continue for months and months, as he might have done, before choosing to end it. Every extra day of that unhappy trust on your part would have made the eventual blow more dreadful.”
“Engagement!” Marianne exclaimed. “We have never been engaged.”
“Never engaged?”
“No. He is not as dishonourable as you think. He has broken no promise to me.”
“But he did tell you he loved you.”
“Yes—no—not in so many words. It was implied every day, but never explicitly declared. Sometimes I thought he had said it, but he never did.”
“And yet you wrote to him?”
“Yes. After everything that had happened, could that be wrong? But I cannot talk about it.”

Elinor said nothing more. She turned back to the three letters, now far more curious about them than before, and quickly read them all. The first, which Marianne had sent on their arrival in London, ran as follows.
Berkeley Street, January.

“How surprised you will be to receive this, Willoughby! And I think you will feel more than surprise when you learn that I am in London. We could not resist the opportunity to come, even though it meant coming with Mrs. Jennings. I hope you get this in time to visit us tonight, though I shall not count on it. In any case, I shall expect you tomorrow. Goodbye for now.
Her second note, written on the morning after the dance at the Middletons', contained these words:

“I cannot tell you how disappointed I am to have missed you the day before yesterday, or how astonished I am to have received no answer to the note I sent more than a week ago. Every hour of the day I have been expecting to hear from you, and still more to see you. Please come again as soon as you can, and explain why I have been waiting in vain. You had better call earlier next time, because we are usually out by one. Last night we went to Lady Middleton's, where there was a dance. I have been told you were invited. But can that be true? If you could have been invited and stayed away, you must have changed very much since we parted. I will not believe that possible, and hope very soon to hear you assure me yourself that it is not so.
The last note she had sent him read as follows:

“What am I to understand from your behaviour last night, Willoughby? Once again I ask you to explain it. I was ready to greet you with the pleasure that naturally followed our separation, and with the familiarity that our closeness at Barton seemed to justify. How thoroughly I was rejected! I have spent a miserable night trying to excuse behaviour that can hardly be called anything less than insulting. Although I have not yet found any reasonable explanation for it, I am perfectly willing to hear your justification. Perhaps you have been given mistaken information about me, or deliberately deceived about something that has lowered me in your opinion. Tell me what it is. Explain why you acted as you did, and I shall be content if I can satisfy you. It would indeed grieve me to be forced to think badly of you. But if I must—if I am to discover that you are not the man we have believed you, that your affection for us all was insincere, and that you meant only to deceive me by your behaviour—let me know as soon as possible. My feelings are in a dreadful state of uncertainty. I want to believe you innocent, but certainty either way would be a relief compared with what I suffer now. If your feelings have changed, return my notes and the lock of my hair that you have.

For Willoughby's sake, Elinor would have preferred not to believe that letters so full of affection and trust could receive such an answer. But her condemnation of him did not blind her to the impropriety of writing them at all. She silently regretted the recklessness that had risked such uninvited proofs of tenderness, justified by nothing that had gone before and most severely condemned by the outcome. Seeing that Elinor had finished reading, Marianne remarked that the letters contained nothing which anyone in the same position would not have written.
“I felt,” she added, “as solemnly bound to him as if the strictest legal agreement had committed us to each other.”
“I can believe that,” Elinor said. “Unfortunately, he did not feel as you did.”

“He _did_ feel as I did, Elinor. For weeks and weeks he felt it. I know he did. Whatever has changed him now—and only the darkest plotting against me could have done it—I was once as dear to him as my heart could wish. This lock of hair, which he can now give up so easily, he begged me for with the most earnest pleading. If only you had seen his expression, his manner, heard his voice at that moment! Have you forgotten our last evening together at Barton? And the morning we parted! When he told me it might be many weeks before we met again—his distress! Could I ever forget his distress?”
For a moment or two she could say nothing more. When the rush of feeling had passed, she continued in a steadier voice.
“Elinor, I have been treated cruelly, but it was not Willoughby who did it.”
“My dearest Marianne, who else could it be? Who could have urged him to it?”

“The whole world, rather than his own heart. I would sooner believe that everyone I know had joined together to destroy his good opinion of me than that he could be capable of such cruelty. This woman he writes about, whoever she is—or anyone, in fact, except your own dear self, Mama, and Edward—may have been cruel enough to tell lies about me. Apart from you three, is there anyone alive whom I would not sooner suspect of wrongdoing than Willoughby, whose heart I know so well?”

Elinor would not argue. She only said, “Whoever has made themselves your enemy so despicably, my dear sister, deny them their malicious triumph. Let them see how nobly the knowledge of your own innocence and good intentions supports you. The pride that resists such malice is reasonable and deserves respect.”

“No, no!” Marianne cried. “Misery like mine has no pride. I do not care who knows how unhappy I am. The whole world may have the triumph of seeing it. Elinor, people who suffer little may be as proud and independent as they please. They may resist insults, or repay humiliation with humiliation. But I cannot. I must feel, I must be miserable, and anyone who can enjoy knowing it is welcome to do so.”
“But for our mother's sake, and for mine—”
“I would do more than for my own. But to look happy when I am so miserable—oh, who could demand that?”

They both fell silent again. Elinor walked thoughtfully between the fire and the window, and back again, unaware of the warmth from one or the view through the other. Marianne sat at the foot of the bed, her head resting against one of its posts. She picked up Willoughby's letter once more, shuddered over every sentence, and exclaimed,

“It is too much! Oh, Willoughby, could you have written this? Cruel, cruel! Nothing can excuse you. Nothing, Elinor. Whatever he might have heard against me, should he not have withheld his belief? Should he not have told me, and given me a chance to clear myself? ‘The lock of hair you were so kind as to give me’”—she repeated the words from the letter—“that is unforgivable. Willoughby, where was your heart when you wrote those words? Oh, such brutal insolence! Elinor, can anything justify him?”
“No, Marianne. Nothing could possibly justify him.”

“And yet this woman—who knows what tricks she has used? How long she may have planned it, how carefully she may have plotted! Who is she? Who can she be? Which of his female acquaintances did I ever hear him describe as young and attractive? Oh, nobody, nobody! He spoke to me only about myself.”
Another silence followed. Marianne was deeply agitated, and at last broke it with these words.
“Elinor, I must go home. I must go back and comfort Mama. Could we not leave tomorrow?”
“Leave tomorrow, Marianne?”
“Yes. Why should I stay here? I came only because of Willoughby. And now who cares about me? Who feels for me?”
“We could not possibly leave tomorrow. We owe Mrs. Jennings much more than mere politeness; and even the most ordinary politeness would prevent us from making such a hurried departure.”

“Well, perhaps in another day or two, then. But I cannot stay long. I cannot remain here to endure all these people's questions and remarks. The Middletons and Palmers—how am I to bear their pity? To be pitied by a woman like Lady Middleton! Oh, what would _he_ say to that?”

Elinor urged her to lie down again, and for a moment she did. But no position brought relief. Restless with pain in both mind and body, she shifted continually from one posture to another. As she grew increasingly distraught, Elinor could barely keep her on the bed and for some time feared she would have to call for help. At last Marianne was persuaded to take some lavender drops, which helped her. From then until Mrs. Jennings returned, she lay quietly on the bed without moving.

chapters.title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: As soon as Mrs. Jennings returned, she came to their room. She asked to be let in, but without waiting for an answer opened the door and entered, looking genuinely concerned.
“How are you feeling, my dear?” she asked Marianne with great sympathy. Marianne turned her face away, making no attempt to answer her.

“How is she, Miss Dashwood? Poor thing, she looks very ill. And no wonder! Yes, it is all too true. He is getting married very soon—the worthless fellow! I have no patience with him. Mrs. Taylor told me half an hour ago, and she heard it from a close friend of Miss Grey herself. Otherwise I should never have believed it. As it was, I nearly dropped on the spot. Well, I said, if this is true, all I can say is that he has treated a young lady I know abominably, and I hope with all my heart his wife makes his life a misery. And you may depend on it, my dear, that is what I shall always say. I cannot stand men behaving like this. If ever I meet him again, I shall give him a scolding such as he hasn't had in many a day. But there is one comfort, my dear Miss Marianne: he is not the only young man in the world worth having. With your pretty face, you will never be short of admirers. Well, poor creature, I won't disturb her any longer. She had better have her cry out and be done with it. Fortunately, the Parrys and Sandersons are coming tonight, you know, and that will cheer her up.”
She went away, tiptoeing out of the room as though she imagined that noise might add to her young friend's distress.

To Elinor's surprise, Marianne decided to join them for dinner. Elinor even advised against it. But no: she would go down, she could bear it perfectly well, and there would be less fuss about her. Elinor was pleased to see her guided, even briefly, by such a consideration. Though she hardly believed Marianne could remain through the meal, she said no more. While her sister still lay on the bed, she straightened her dress as well as she could, then stood ready to help her into the dining room when they were called.

Once there, though looking utterly miserable, Marianne ate more and remained calmer than Elinor had expected. If she had tried to speak, or noticed half Mrs. Jennings's well-meant but ill-judged attentions, she could not have kept that calm. But not a word passed her lips, and her absorption in her own thoughts kept her unaware of everything happening around her.

Elinor fully appreciated Mrs. Jennings's kindness, though its expressions often caused distress and sometimes came close to being ridiculous. She offered the thanks and returned the courtesies which Marianne could neither offer nor return for herself. Their good friend saw that Marianne was unhappy, and felt she deserved everything that might make her less so. She therefore treated her with all the indulgent affection a parent shows a favourite child on the last day of the holidays. Marianne must have the best seat by the fire; every delicacy in the house must tempt her to eat; all the day's news must be related for her entertainment. Had her sister's sorrowful face not checked every impulse to laugh, Elinor might have been amused by Mrs. Jennings's attempts to cure disappointed love with sweets, olives, and a good fire. But once the constant repetition of these attentions forced them upon Marianne's notice, she could stay no longer. With a hurried cry of misery, and a gesture telling her sister not to follow, she rose and rushed from the room.

“Poor soul!” Mrs. Jennings cried once she had gone. “How it hurts me to see her! And just look, she has left without finishing her wine! Or her dried cherries! Lord, nothing seems to help her at all. If I knew anything she wanted, I would send all over London to find it. Well, I cannot understand how a man can treat such a pretty girl so badly. But when there is plenty of money on one side and next to none on the other, bless you, they care nothing about such things!”
“So the lady—Miss Grey, I think you called her—is very wealthy?”

“Fifty thousand pounds, my dear. Have you ever seen her? They say she is smart and fashionable, though not beautiful. I remember her aunt very well, Biddy Henshawe. She married a very rich man. But the whole family has money. Fifty thousand pounds! And from everything one hears, it won't arrive a moment too soon, for they say he is quite ruined. No wonder, racing about with his curricle and his hunting horses! Well, there is no use talking. But when a young man, whoever he may be, courts a pretty girl and promises to marry her, he has no right to go back on his word simply because he becomes poor and a richer girl will take him. Why doesn't he sell his horses, rent out his house, dismiss his servants, and reform his whole way of living at once? I am sure Miss Marianne would have waited until his affairs improved. But that will not do nowadays. The young men of this age cannot give up a single pleasure.”
“Do you know what Miss Grey is like as a person? Do people say she is pleasant?”

“I have never heard anything against her. Indeed, I have hardly heard her mentioned, except that Mrs. Taylor said this morning that Miss Walker once hinted to her that she believed Mr. and Mrs. Ellison would be glad to see Miss Grey married, because she and Mrs. Ellison could never get along.”
“And who are Mr. and Mrs. Ellison?”

“Her guardians, my dear. But she is of age now and can choose for herself. And a fine choice she has made!” After a moment's pause, she continued, “Well, I suppose your poor sister has gone to her room to grieve alone. Is there nothing we can get to comfort her? Poor dear, it seems positively cruel to leave her by herself. We shall have a few friends here later, and that will entertain her a little. What shall we play? I know she hates whist, but isn't there some round game she enjoys?”
“My dear ma'am, you need not go to all this trouble. I doubt Marianne will come out of her room again tonight. If I can, I shall persuade her to go to bed early. I am sure she needs rest.”

“Yes, I believe that will be best. Let her choose her own supper and go to bed. Lord, no wonder she has looked so ill and so low these last couple of weeks! I suppose this has been hanging over her all that time. And today's letter finished it! Poor soul! If I had had the least idea, I would not have teased her about it for all the money I possess. But how could I have guessed? I was certain it was only an ordinary love letter, and you know young people like being laughed at about those. Lord, how distressed Sir John and my daughters will be when they hear! If I had been thinking properly, I could have called in Conduit Street on my way home and told them. But I shall see them tomorrow.”

“I am sure you need hardly warn Mrs. Palmer and Sir John against mentioning Mr. Willoughby, or making the slightest reference to what has happened, in front of my sister. Their own kindness must show them how cruel it would be to appear to know anything about it in her presence. And the less that is said to me on the subject, the more my own feelings will be spared, as I know you will readily understand, dear ma'am.”

“Oh, Lord, yes, of course I do! It must be dreadful for you to hear people discussing it. And as for your sister, I would not say a word to her about it for the world. You saw that I never did throughout dinner. Neither would Sir John or my daughters, for they are all very thoughtful and considerate, particularly if I give them a hint, which I certainly shall. For myself, I think the less said about such things, the better: they blow over and are forgotten all the sooner. And what good does talking ever do?”

“In this case it can only do harm, perhaps more than in many similar cases. There are circumstances which, for the sake of everyone involved, make it especially unsuitable for public discussion. I must do Mr. Willoughby _this_ justice: he has broken no definite engagement with my sister.”
“Good gracious, my dear, don't try to defend him! No definite engagement, indeed! After taking her all over Allenham House and choosing the very rooms they were to live in together!”

For Marianne's sake, Elinor could not pursue the subject. She hoped she was not obliged to do so for Willoughby's, since insisting on the precise truth could benefit him very little and cost Marianne a great deal. They were both silent for a short time. Then Mrs. Jennings burst out again with all her natural good humour.

“Well, my dear, the saying about an ill wind is true enough, for all this will be better for Colonel Brandon. He will have her in the end, yes, he will. Mark my words, they will be married by midsummer. Lord, how he will chuckle at the news! I hope he comes tonight. He would be a far better match for your sister. Two thousand a year, without debts or deductions—except that little child of his born out of wedlock; yes, I had forgotten her. But an apprenticeship could be found for her at very little expense, and then what would it matter? Delaford is a lovely place, I can tell you. Exactly what I call a lovely, old-fashioned place, full of comforts and conveniences. Great garden walls enclose it, covered with the finest fruit trees in the country. And there is such a mulberry tree in one corner! Lord, how Charlotte and I ate the only time we visited! Then there is a dovecote, some delightful fish ponds, and a very pretty canal—everything one could wish for, in short. Besides, it is close to the church and only a quarter of a mile from the toll road. It is never dull: you have only to sit in an old yew-tree arbour behind the house, and you can watch all the passing carriages. Oh, it is a lovely place! A butcher close by in the village, and the parsonage within a stone's throw. To my mind, it is a thousand times prettier than Barton Park, where they have to send three miles for meat and have no neighbour nearer than your mother. Well, I shall encourage the Colonel as soon as I can. One shoulder of mutton drives another down, as they say. If only we _can_ put Willoughby out of her mind!”

“Yes, ma'am, if we can do _that_,” Elinor said, “we shall do very well, with or without Colonel Brandon.” She rose and went to join Marianne. As she expected, she found her in their room, leaning in silent misery over the remains of a small fire, which had been her only light until Elinor entered.
“You had better leave me alone,” was the only acknowledgement Marianne gave of her sister's arrival.

“I will leave you if you go to bed,” Elinor answered. At first Marianne refused, with the momentary stubbornness of someone made impatient by suffering. But her sister's earnest, gentle persuasion soon softened her resistance. Before leaving her, Elinor saw her lay her aching head on the pillow and hoped that she was at last ready for some quiet sleep.
Elinor then went to the drawing room. Mrs. Jennings soon joined her, carrying a wineglass filled with something in her hand.

“My dear,” she said as she entered, “I have just remembered that there is some of the finest old Constantia wine imaginable in the house, so I have brought your sister a glass. My poor husband was so fond of it! Whenever his old gout troubled his stomach, he said it did him more good than anything else in the world. Do take it up to her.”

“How kind you are, dear ma'am,” Elinor replied, smiling at the difference between the ailments for which it was recommended. “But I have just left Marianne in bed, and I hope she is nearly asleep. Nothing could help her as much as rest, I think. So, if you will allow me, I shall drink the wine myself.”

Mrs. Jennings regretted being five minutes too late, but accepted the compromise. As Elinor drank most of the glass, she reflected that, although its effect on gout of the stomach mattered little to her at present, its power to heal a disappointed heart might as reasonably be tested on herself as on her sister.

Colonel Brandon arrived while they were having tea. From the way he looked round the room for Marianne, Elinor immediately suspected that he neither expected nor wished to find her there, and that he already knew the reason for her absence. Mrs. Jennings had no such thought. Soon after he entered, she crossed to the tea table, where Elinor was serving, and whispered, “You see, the Colonel looks as solemn as ever. He knows nothing about it. Do tell him, my dear.”
Shortly afterwards he drew a chair beside Elinor's and asked after her sister, with an expression that left her in no doubt that he already knew.
“Marianne is unwell,” she said. “She has felt ill all day, and we have persuaded her to go to bed.”
“Then perhaps,” he answered hesitantly, “what I heard this morning may be—there may be more truth in it than I could at first believe possible.”
“What have you heard?”
“That a gentleman whom I had reason to think—in short, that a man whom I _knew_ to be engaged—but how can I tell you? If you already know, as surely you must, perhaps you can spare me.”

“You mean Mr. Willoughby's marriage to Miss Grey,” Elinor answered with forced calm. “Yes, we _do_ know everything. This seems to have been a day of revelations for everyone, since we first learnt of it this very morning. Mr. Willoughby is impossible to understand! Where did you hear the news?”

“In a stationer's shop in Pall Mall, where I had business. Two ladies were waiting for their carriage. One was telling the other about the proposed marriage in a voice so plainly unconcerned with secrecy that I could not avoid hearing everything.
