Though she often expressed pity for Marianne to Elinor, and more than once remarked in Marianne's hearing on the unfaithfulness of young men, she achieved only a look of indifference from one sister or disgust from the other. An even smaller effort might have won her friendship: if only they had teased her about the Doctor! But they were no more inclined to oblige than anyone else. When Sir John dined away from home, she might pass a whole day without hearing a single joke on the subject except those she kindly supplied herself.

Mrs. Jennings suspected none of these jealousies and grievances. She thought it delightful for the girls to spend time together, and usually congratulated her young friends each night on having escaped a tiresome old woman for so long. Sometimes she joined them at Sir John's, sometimes at her own house. Wherever they met, she arrived in excellent spirits, full of happiness and importance. She attributed Charlotte's good recovery to her own care, and was ready to give a report so precise and detailed that only Miss Steele had enough curiosity to welcome it. One thing _did_ trouble her, and she complained of it daily. Mr. Palmer held the opinion, common among men but unfatherly, that all babies looked alike. At different moments she could plainly see striking likenesses between this baby and every relation on both sides of the family. Yet nothing could persuade his father that he was not exactly like every other infant of the same age. He could not even be brought to acknowledge the simple fact that this was the finest child in the world.

I must now describe a misfortune that befell Mrs. John Dashwood about this time. During her sisters-in-law's first visit to Harley Street with Mrs. Jennings, another acquaintance had happened to call. In itself, that circumstance hardly seemed likely to harm her. But while other people's imaginations lead them into mistaken judgements of our behaviour, based on the slightest appearances, our happiness must always be partly at the mercy of chance. In this instance, the new arrival allowed imagination to run so far beyond truth and probability that, merely on hearing the Miss Dashwoods' name and learning that they were Mr. Dashwood's sisters, she immediately assumed they were staying in Harley Street. A day or two later, this mistake produced invitations for them, as well as their brother and his wife, to a small musical party at her house. Mrs. John Dashwood consequently had to endure not only the enormous inconvenience of sending her carriage for the sisters, but the still greater unpleasantness of appearing to pay them attention. And who could be sure they might not expect to accompany her a second time? Certainly, she would always have the power to disappoint them. But that was not enough. When people have resolved on conduct they know is wrong, they feel injured by any expectation that they might behave better.

By now Marianne had gradually become so accustomed to going out every day that she no longer cared whether she went or stayed. She prepared quietly and mechanically for each evening's engagement, expecting no pleasure from any of them, and often not knowing until the last moment where she was going.

She had become so indifferent to her clothes and appearance that, during the whole process of dressing, she gave them less than half the attention Miss Steele bestowed in the first five minutes after seeing her ready. Nothing escaped _that_ lady's close observation and general curiosity. She saw everything and asked about everything, never resting until she knew the price of every part of Marianne's outfit. She could have estimated the total number of her gowns more accurately than Marianne herself. She also hoped, before they parted, to discover the weekly cost of her laundry and her annual allowance for personal expenses. These intrusive investigations generally ended with a compliment intended to soften them, but which Marianne considered the greatest intrusion of all. After an examination of the cost and making of her gown, the colour of her shoes, and the arrangement of her hair, she was almost certain to hear that “upon her word, she looked wonderfully smart, and would surely make a great many conquests.”

With encouragement of this kind, Marianne was sent to her brother's carriage on the present occasion. Both sisters were ready to enter it within five minutes of its arrival. Their punctuality did not please their sister-in-law, who had gone ahead to her acquaintance's house and was hoping they would delay enough to inconvenience either her or her coachman.

Nothing very remarkable happened that evening. Like other musical parties, it contained many people who genuinely appreciated the performance, and many more who did not appreciate it at all. The performers, as usual, were in their own opinion and that of their closest friends the finest amateur musicians in England.

Elinor was not musical and did not pretend to be. She therefore felt no hesitation in looking away from the grand piano whenever she wished. Even the presence of a harp and cello could not restrain her from directing her eyes towards any other object in the room. During one such wandering glance, she noticed among a group of young men the very gentleman who had lectured them on toothpick cases at Gray's. Soon afterwards she saw him looking at her and speaking familiarly with her brother. She had just decided to ask John his name when both men approached, and Mr. Dashwood introduced him as Mr. Robert Ferrars.

He addressed her with easy politeness, twisting his head into a bow that confirmed, as clearly as words could, that he was exactly the conceited fool Lucy had described. How fortunate for Elinor if her love for Edward had depended less on his own worth than on the worth of his closest relations! His brother's bow would then have completed the work begun by his mother's and sister's bad temper. But, though she wondered at the difference between the brothers, she did not find that one's emptiness and vanity destroyed her affection for the other's modesty and goodness. Robert himself explained why they _were_ so different in the course of fifteen minutes' conversation. Speaking of Edward and regretting the extreme social awkwardness which he truly believed kept him out of proper society, Robert candidly and generously attributed it less to any natural defect than to the misfortune of private education. He himself, though probably not born with any particular or substantial superiority, had become as fit for society as any man simply through attending a public school.

“Upon my soul,” he added, “I believe that is the whole explanation. I often tell my mother so when she worries about it. ‘My dear mother,’ I always say, ‘you must stop troubling yourself. Nothing can mend it now, and it is entirely your own doing. Why did you let my uncle Sir Robert persuade you, against your own judgement, to place Edward with a private tutor at the most important stage of his life? If you had sent him to Westminster with me instead of to Mr. Pratt's, none of this would have happened.’ That is how I always see the matter, and my mother is thoroughly convinced of her mistake.”
Elinor did not challenge his opinion. Whatever she thought in general of the advantages of a public school, she could take no satisfaction in Edward's having lived with Mr. Pratt's family.
“You live in Devonshire, I believe,” he next observed, “in a cottage near Dawlish.”

Elinor corrected him about its location. He seemed rather surprised that anyone could live in Devonshire without living near Dawlish. He nevertheless gave his hearty approval to their choice of a cottage.

“For my part,” he said, “I am excessively fond of cottages. They are always so comfortable, so elegant. I declare that, if I had money to spare, I would buy a little land and build one myself not far from London. I could drive down whenever I liked, gather a few friends round me, and be happy. I tell everyone who plans to build to build a cottage. My friend Lord Courtland came expressly to ask my advice the other day and showed me three different designs by Bonomi. I was to choose the best. ‘My dear Courtland,’ I said, immediately throwing all three into the fire, ‘don't use any of them. Whatever you do, build a cottage.’ And I imagine that will settle it.

“Some people think a cottage cannot have any space or conveniences, but they are quite wrong. Last month I visited my friend Elliott near Dartford. Lady Elliott wanted to give a dance. ‘But how can we manage it?’ she asked. ‘My dear Ferrars, do tell me what to do. No room in this cottage will hold ten couples, and where could we serve supper?’ _I_ saw at once that there was no difficulty. ‘My dear Lady Elliott,’ I said, ‘don't trouble yourself. The dining room will easily hold eighteen couples; put the card tables in the drawing room; open the library for tea and other refreshments; and have supper laid out in the saloon.’ She was delighted. We measured the dining room and found that it held exactly eighteen couples. Everything was arranged precisely according to my plan. So you see, provided people know how to go about it, a cottage can offer every comfort just as well as the largest house.”
Elinor agreed with everything. She did not consider him worth the compliment of a reasoned disagreement.

John Dashwood enjoyed music no more than his eldest sister, so his mind was equally free to occupy itself elsewhere. During the evening an idea occurred to him which he put to his wife for approval when they returned home. Mrs. Dennison's mistaken assumption that his sisters were their guests had suggested that it might be proper to invite them to become so while Mrs. Jennings was kept away from home. It would cost nothing and cause no more inconvenience. Altogether, it was an attention which his sensitive conscience considered necessary to release him completely from his promise to his father. Fanny was startled by the proposal.

“I don't see how we could do it without offending Lady Middleton,” she said. “They spend every day with her. Otherwise I would be delighted. You know I am always ready to show them any kindness in my power, as taking them out tonight proves. But they are Lady Middleton's guests. How can I ask them away from her?”

Very humbly, her husband failed to understand the force of this objection. They had already spent a week of days in Conduit Street; Lady Middleton surely could not object to their giving the same number to such close relations.
Fanny paused briefly, then spoke again with renewed energy.

“My dear, I would invite them with all my heart if I could. But I had just decided to ask the Miss Steeles to stay with us for a few days. They are very well-behaved, good sort of girls, and I think we owe them the attention, since their uncle did so well by Edward. We can invite your sisters another year. The Miss Steeles may never come to London again. I am sure you will like them. Indeed, you _do_ like them very much already, you know, and so does my mother. And Harry is so fond of them!”

Mr. Dashwood was convinced. He saw the need to invite the Miss Steeles immediately. Resolving to invite his sisters another year soothed his conscience, though he privately suspected that another year would remove the need for any invitation: Elinor would come to London as Colonel Brandon's wife, and Marianne as _their_ guest.

Delighted at her escape and proud of the quick thinking that had secured it, Fanny wrote to Lucy the next morning. She invited her and her sister to spend several days in Harley Street as soon as Lady Middleton could spare them. This gave Lucy real and reasonable cause for happiness. Mrs. Dashwood seemed actually to be working on her behalf, encouraging every hope and advancing every plan. Nothing could matter more to her interests than such an opportunity to be with Edward and his family; nothing could flatter her feelings more than this invitation. No gratitude could be too great, and no acceptance too prompt. Their visit to Lady Middleton, whose duration had previously been unfixed, was immediately discovered to have been intended all along to end in two days.

The note was shown to Elinor within ten minutes of its arrival. For the first time it led her to share some of Lucy's hopes. Such unusual kindness, offered after so short an acquaintance, seemed to show that their goodwill towards Lucy arose from more than mere spite against Elinor. With time and skilful management, it might achieve everything Lucy wanted. Her flattery had already overcome Lady Middleton's pride and gained entry into Mrs. John Dashwood's closed heart. Such results opened the possibility of still greater ones.

The Miss Steeles moved to Harley Street. Everything Elinor heard about their influence there strengthened her expectation of the outcome. Sir John called more than once and brought back accounts of their favour which must have impressed anyone. Mrs. Dashwood had never liked any young women so much in her life. She had given each a needle case made by an emigrant, called Lucy by her first name, and did not know whether she could ever bear to part with them.

chapters.title: Chapter 37
paragraphs: By the end of a fortnight, Mrs. Palmer was so well that her mother no longer felt obliged to devote all her time to her. Content now to visit once or twice a day, she returned to her own home and habits. The Miss Dashwoods were very willing to resume their former share in that routine.

On about the third or fourth morning after they had settled back into Berkeley Street, Mrs. Jennings returned from her usual visit to Mrs. Palmer and entered the drawing room, where Elinor was alone. Her air of hurried importance prepared Elinor for something extraordinary. She had barely time to form the thought before Mrs. Jennings confirmed it.
“Lord, my dear Miss Dashwood! Have you heard what has happened?”
“No, ma'am. What is the news?”

“Something so extraordinary! But you shall hear everything. When I arrived at Mr. Palmer's, Charlotte was in a terrible fuss about the baby. She was certain he was very ill: he cried and fretted and was covered in spots. I looked at him immediately. ‘Lord, my dear,’ I said, ‘it is only the red gum, an ordinary infant's rash.’ The nurse said exactly the same. But Charlotte would not be satisfied, so we sent for Mr. Donavan. Fortunately, he had just returned from Harley Street and could come straight over. The moment he saw the baby, he said just what we had: nothing but the red gum. Then Charlotte was satisfied. As he was about to leave, it occurred to me—I really cannot think what put it into my head—to ask whether there was any news. At that he smiled and smirked, then looked serious, and seemed to know something. At last he whispered, ‘In case any worrying report about their sister-in-law's illness reaches the young ladies staying with you, I think I ought to say that there is no great cause for alarm. I hope Mrs. Dashwood will recover very well.’”
“What! Is Fanny unwell?”

“That is exactly what I said, my dear. ‘Lord,’ I said, ‘is Mrs. Dashwood ill?’ Then the whole story came out. From everything I can gather, this is the long and short of it. Mr. Edward Ferrars—the very young man I used to tease you about, though I am enormously glad now that there was never anything in it—Mr. Edward Ferrars has apparently been engaged to my cousin Lucy for more than a year! What do you think of that, my dear? And nobody knew a word except Nancy! Could you have believed it possible? It is no great wonder that they should like each other, but that things should have gone so far without anyone suspecting—that _is_ strange. I never happened to see them together, or I am sure I should have discovered it immediately. Well, they kept it all a great secret for fear of Mrs. Ferrars. Neither she nor your brother or his wife suspected a thing until this very morning, when poor Nancy, who is well-meaning but no genius, blurted it all out. ‘Lord,’ she must have thought, ‘they are all so fond of Lucy, surely they won't object.’ Off she went to your sister-in-law, who was sitting alone at her carpet-work, little imagining what was coming. Only five minutes earlier she had been telling your brother she meant to arrange a marriage between Edward and some lord's daughter—I forget whose. You can imagine the blow to all her pride and vanity. She immediately went into violent hysterics, screaming so loudly that your brother heard from his dressing room downstairs, where he was considering writing to his steward in the country. He rushed up, and there was a dreadful scene. Lucy had joined them by then, without the least idea of what was happening. Poor creature, I pity _her_. I must say she was treated very harshly. Your sister-in-law raged like a fury and soon made her faint. Nancy went down on her knees, crying bitterly, while your brother walked about saying he did not know what to do. Mrs. Dashwood declared they should not stay in the house another minute. Your brother had to kneel as well to persuade her to let them remain long enough to pack their clothes. _Then_ she had another fit of hysterics, and he was so frightened that he insisted on sending for Mr. Donavan. He found the whole house in an uproar. The carriage was at the door to take my poor cousins away, and they were getting into it as he left. He says poor Lucy could scarcely walk, and Nancy was nearly as bad. I declare I have no patience with your sister-in-law, and I sincerely hope the marriage takes place in spite of her. Lord, how upset poor Mr. Edward will be when he hears! To have his beloved treated with such scorn! They say he is terribly fond of her, as he well may be. I shouldn't wonder if he flies into a furious rage. Mr. Donavan thinks so too. We talked a great deal about it. And the best part is that he has gone back to Harley Street to be close at hand when Mrs. Ferrars hears. They sent for her the moment my cousins left, because your sister-in-law was certain _she_ would have hysterics too. Well, she may, for all I care. I pity neither of them. I cannot stand people making such a fuss over money and rank. There is no reason on earth why Edward and Lucy should not marry. Mrs. Ferrars can certainly afford to provide very handsomely for her son. Lucy may have next to nothing, but nobody knows better how to make the most of everything. If his mother would allow him just five hundred a year, I dare say Lucy could make as good a showing as anyone else on eight hundred. Lord, how comfortably they could live in a cottage like yours, or a little larger, with two maids and two menservants! I believe I could find them a housemaid, too. My Betty has a sister out of work who would suit them perfectly.”

Mrs. Jennings stopped. Elinor had had plenty of time to collect her thoughts and was able to make a reply and offer comments as the subject naturally required. She was glad that nobody suspected her of any special interest in it; glad that Mrs. Jennings had stopped imagining her in love with Edward, as she had lately often hoped; and, above all, glad that Marianne was absent. She felt quite able to discuss the affair without embarrassment and to judge, as she believed impartially, the conduct of everyone involved.

She could scarcely decide what outcome she herself expected. She earnestly tried to banish any notion that it might ultimately end otherwise than in Edward's marriage to Lucy. She wanted to hear what Mrs. Ferrars would say and do, though the nature of her response could not be doubted. Still more, she wanted to know how Edward would behave. For _him_ she felt great compassion. For Lucy she felt very little, and had to work to find even that little. For the rest of the party she felt none at all.

Since Mrs. Jennings could discuss nothing else, Elinor soon realised that Marianne must be prepared to hear it. There was no time to lose in correcting her mistake, telling her the truth, and trying to make her able to hear others discuss it without betraying distress for her sister or resentment towards Edward.

It was a painful duty. Elinor was about to take away what she truly believed was Marianne's chief comfort, reveal facts about Edward that might destroy him for ever in her good opinion, and make her relive her own disappointment through a likeness between their situations which _she_ would find striking. Unwelcome as the task was, however, it had to be done, and Elinor hurried to do it.

She had no desire to dwell on her own feelings or present herself as deeply suffering. The only exception was that the self-control she had practised since learning of Edward's engagement might show Marianne what was possible. Her account was clear and simple. She could not give it without feeling, but there was no violent agitation or passionate grief. _Those_ belonged to her listener: Marianne heard her with horror and wept bitterly. Elinor had to comfort others in her own distress as much as in theirs. She readily offered every reassurance her own calm could supply, and defended Edward earnestly against every charge except lack of judgement.

For some time, Marianne would believe neither the reassurance nor the defence. Edward seemed another Willoughby. Since Elinor admitted that she _had_ loved him deeply, how could she suffer less than Marianne herself? As for Lucy Steele, Marianne considered her so utterly unlovable, so incapable of attracting an intelligent man, that at first she could not believe Edward had ever loved her, and afterwards could not forgive him for it. She would not even admit that it was natural. Elinor left her to be persuaded by the only thing that could persuade her: a better understanding of human nature.

In her first account, Elinor had got no further than the fact of the engagement and how long it had existed. Marianne's feelings had then interrupted, making an orderly explanation impossible. For some time Elinor could only soothe her distress, ease her fears, and resist her indignation. The first question that led to further details was,
“How long have you known this, Elinor? Has Edward written to tell you?”
“I have known for four months. When Lucy first came to Barton Park last November, she told me about the engagement in confidence.”
Marianne's eyes expressed an astonishment her lips could not put into words. After a pause of wonder, she exclaimed,
“Four months! Have you known all this for four months?”
Elinor said she had.
“What! While you were caring for me through all my misery, you had this on your heart? And I reproached you for being happy!”
“It would not have been right for you to know then how far I was from happiness.”
“Four months!” Marianne cried again. “So calm, so cheerful! What has kept you going?”

“The knowledge that I was doing my duty. My promise to Lucy required secrecy. I owed it to her to give no hint of the truth. And I owed it to my family and friends not to make them anxious about me when I could offer no explanation to relieve that anxiety.”
Marianne looked deeply affected.
“I have often wanted to correct your expectations and our mother's,” Elinor added. “Once or twice I even tried. But I could never convince you without betraying the confidence placed in me.”
“Four months! And you still loved him!”

“Yes. But he was not the only person I loved. Because other people's comfort mattered to me, I was glad to spare them the knowledge of how much I felt. Now I can think and talk about it with little agitation. I do not want you to suffer for me, because I assure you I no longer suffer greatly myself. Many things sustain me. I know of no foolishness of my own that brought this disappointment about. I have borne it as far as possible without making others share it. I do not believe Edward guilty of any fundamental wrongdoing. I wish him every happiness, and I am so certain he will always do his duty that, whatever regrets he may have now, he must become happy in the end. Lucy is not without intelligence, and that is a foundation on which every good quality may be built. After all, Marianne, however enchanting the idea of one unchanging love, and whatever we may say about our happiness depending entirely on one particular person, it is not intended—it is not right—it is not possible that this should be so. Edward will marry Lucy. He will marry a woman more attractive and more intelligent than half her sex. Time and habit will teach him to forget that he ever thought another woman superior to _her_.”

“If that is how you think,” Marianne said, “if losing what you value most can be so easily compensated for by something else, perhaps your determination and self-control are a little less astonishing. I can understand them rather better.”

“I understand you. You don't believe I have ever felt very much. For four months, Marianne, all this has weighed on my mind without my being free to speak of it to a single person. I knew it would make you and our mother deeply unhappy whenever you learnt it, yet I could do nothing to prepare you. It was told to me—almost forced on me—by the very woman whose earlier engagement destroyed all my hopes. And she told me, I thought, triumphantly. I have had to counter her suspicions by trying to seem indifferent where I cared most deeply. Not just once: again and again I have had to listen to her hopes and her triumph. I have known I was separated from Edward for ever without hearing a single fact that could make me want him less. Nothing has shown him unworthy, and nothing has shown that he is indifferent to me. I have had to bear his sister's unkindness and his mother's insolence, suffering the penalties of an attachment without enjoying its advantages. All this has happened at a time when, as you know only too well, it has not been my only unhappiness. If you can believe me capable of feeling anything at all, surely you can believe I have suffered _now_. The calm with which I can at last consider it, the comfort I have allowed myself to accept, are the results of constant, painful effort. They did not appear by themselves. They did not come to relieve me at the beginning. No, Marianne. _Then_, if I had not been bound to silence, perhaps nothing—not even what I owed my dearest friends—could have entirely prevented me from showing openly that I was _very_ unhappy.”
Marianne was completely humbled.

“Oh, Elinor!” she cried. “You have made me hate myself for ever. How cruel I have been to you! You have been my only comfort, endured me through all my misery, seemed to suffer only for me. Is this my gratitude? Is this all I can give you in return? Because your goodness condemns me, I have tried to deny it.”

The confession was followed by the most affectionate embraces. In Marianne's present state of mind, Elinor had no difficulty in obtaining any promise she asked. At her request, Marianne undertook never to discuss the affair with anyone in the slightest tone of bitterness; to meet Lucy without revealing any increase in dislike; and even, if chance brought them together, to see Edward with all her usual warmth. These were great concessions. But when Marianne felt she had wronged someone, no effort to make amends could be too great.

She kept her promise of discretion admirably. She listened to everything Mrs. Jennings said without changing colour, disagreed with nothing, and was heard three times to say, “Yes, ma'am.” She heard Lucy praised with no response beyond moving from one chair to another. When Mrs. Jennings spoke of Edward's love, it cost her only a tightening in the throat. Such progress towards heroism in her sister made Elinor feel capable of anything herself.
The next morning brought a further test. Their brother arrived, wearing an expression of the utmost seriousness, to discuss the dreadful affair and report on his wife's condition.
“I suppose you have heard,” he said with great solemnity as soon as he sat down, “of the shocking discovery made under our roof yesterday.”
Their expressions showed that they had. The moment seemed too terrible for anyone to speak.

“Your sister-in-law has suffered dreadfully,” he continued. “Mrs. Ferrars too. In short, there has been such a complicated scene of distress—but I hope we may weather the storm without any of us being entirely overcome. Poor Fanny! She was in hysterics all day yesterday. Still, I must not alarm you too much. Donavan says there is no serious cause for concern. She has a strong constitution and resolution equal to anything. She has borne it all with the courage of an angel. She says she will never think well of anyone again. Who could wonder, after such deception, such ingratitude, where so much kindness and trust had been shown? She invited these young women entirely out of the goodness of her heart, simply because she thought they deserved attention, were harmless, well-behaved girls, and would make pleasant company. Otherwise we had both very much wanted to invite you and Marianne while your kind friend here was caring for her daughter. And now this is the reward! ‘I wish with all my heart,’ poor Fanny says in her affectionate way, ‘that we had invited your sisters instead.’”
He stopped here to receive their thanks. Once they had supplied them, he continued.

“It is impossible to describe what poor Mrs. Ferrars suffered when Fanny first told her. While she had been lovingly planning such an excellent marriage for him, who could have imagined he was secretly engaged to someone else all along? Such a suspicion could never have entered her head. If she suspected _any_ attachment elsewhere, it could not have been _there_. ‘Surely,’ she said, ‘I might have thought myself safe in _that_ quarter.’ She was in absolute anguish. We discussed what to do, and finally she decided to send for Edward. He came, but I am sorry to tell you what followed. Everything his mother said to make him end the engagement was useless, even with the help, as you can imagine, of my arguments and Fanny's pleas. Duty, affection, everything was ignored. I never imagined Edward could be so stubborn and unfeeling. His mother explained her generous plans if he married Miss Morton. She would settle the Norfolk estate on him, bringing in a full thousand a year after land tax. When matters grew desperate, she even offered to make it twelve hundred. On the other hand, if he persisted in this low connection, she showed him the poverty that must follow. His own two thousand pounds would be all he ever had, she declared. She would never see him again. Far from giving him the smallest help, if he entered any profession to support himself better, she would do everything she could to prevent his advancement.”
At this Marianne struck her hands together in a burst of indignation. “Good heavens!” she cried. “Can such a thing be possible?”
“You may well be astonished, Marianne,” her brother replied, “at the stubbornness that could resist arguments like these. Your exclamation is perfectly natural.”
Marianne was about to answer sharply, but remembered her promises and held back.

“Yet all this was urged in vain,” he continued. “Edward said little, but what he did say was absolutely firm. Nothing would persuade him to abandon his engagement. He would keep it, whatever it cost him.”

“Then he behaved like an honest man!” Mrs. Jennings cried with blunt sincerity, unable to remain silent. “Forgive me, Mr. Dashwood, but I would have thought him a scoundrel if he had done anything else. I have some interest in the matter too. Lucy Steele is my cousin, and I believe no better sort of girl exists, nor one more deserving of a good husband.”
John Dashwood was greatly astonished. But he had a calm nature, was not easily provoked, and never wanted to offend anyone, especially anyone wealthy. He therefore replied without resentment.

“I would never wish to speak disrespectfully of a relation of yours, ma'am. Miss Lucy Steele is no doubt a very deserving young woman. But in this case, you understand, the connection must be impossible. Entering a secret engagement with a young man in her uncle's care, the son, moreover, of a woman as wealthy as Mrs. Ferrars, is perhaps a little extraordinary altogether. In short, Mrs. Jennings, I have no wish to criticise the behaviour of anyone you value. We all wish her every happiness. Mrs. Ferrars, throughout, has behaved as any conscientious, good mother would in the same circumstances. She has shown dignity and generosity. Edward has chosen his own fate, and I fear it will be an unhappy one.”
Marianne sighed out the same fear. Elinor's heart ached for Edward, facing his mother's threats for a woman who could never reward his sacrifice.
“Well, sir,” Mrs. Jennings asked, “and how did it all end?”

“I am sorry to say, ma'am, in a most unhappy separation. Edward has been cast out of his mother's favour for ever. He left her house yesterday. Where he went, or whether he remains in London, I do not know. Naturally, _we_ cannot inquire.”
“Poor young man! What will become of him now?”

“What indeed, ma'am? It is a melancholy thought. Born with the prospect of such wealth! I cannot imagine a more deplorable situation. How can a man live on the interest from two thousand pounds? And remember that, but for his own foolishness, within three months he might have had two thousand five hundred a year, since Miss Morton has thirty thousand pounds. I cannot picture greater wretchedness. We must all feel for him, especially since it is entirely beyond our power to help.”

“Poor young man!” Mrs. Jennings cried. “He would certainly be welcome to a room and meals in my house. I would tell him so if I could see him. He ought not to be paying to live in lodgings and taverns now.”
Elinor thanked her inwardly for this kindness to Edward, though she could not help smiling at the form it took.

“If only he had treated himself as well as his friends wished to treat him,” John Dashwood said, “he could now be in his proper position and lack nothing. As it is, nobody can possibly help him. And something further is being prepared against him, worse than everything else. With a very natural spirit, his mother has decided to settle immediately on Robert _the very estate_ Edward might have had on the proper conditions. I left her discussing it with her lawyer this morning.”
“Well,” Mrs. Jennings said, “that is _her_ revenge. Everyone has their own way. But mine would hardly be to make one son independent of me because the other had annoyed me.”
Marianne rose and began walking about the room.
“What could wound a man's pride more,” John continued, “than to see his younger brother owning an estate that might have been his? Poor Edward! I sincerely feel for him.”

A few more minutes of similar expressions ended his visit. Repeatedly assuring his sisters that he believed Fanny's illness posed no serious danger, and that they therefore need not be very anxious, he finally took his leave and departed. He left the three ladies entirely agreed, at least in their opinions of Mrs. Ferrars's conduct, the Dashwoods', and Edward's.

The moment he left the room, Marianne's indignation burst out. Her vehemence made restraint impossible for Elinor and unnecessary for Mrs. Jennings, and all three joined in a spirited criticism of those involved.

chapters.title: Chapter 38
paragraphs: Mrs. Jennings praised Edward's behaviour warmly, but only Elinor and Marianne understood its true worth. Only _they_ knew how little temptation he had to defy his mother, and how little comfort, beyond knowing he had done right, could remain after losing friends and fortune. Elinor took pride in his honesty; pity for his punishment made Marianne forgive every offence. The public discovery restored full confidence between the sisters, but neither liked to dwell on the subject when they were alone. Elinor deliberately avoided it. Marianne's overly warm and certain assurances only fixed more firmly in her mind the belief that Edward still loved her, a belief she would rather have given up. Marianne, meanwhile, soon lost courage when trying to discuss something that always made her more dissatisfied with herself. It inevitably forced a comparison between her conduct and Elinor's.

She felt the full force of that comparison, but it did not, as Elinor had hoped, encourage her to make an effort now. Instead, it caused constant self-reproach and bitter regret that she had never made an effort before. It brought the pain of repentance without the hope of improvement. Her mind was so weakened that she still thought any present effort impossible, and the comparison only depressed her further.

For the next day or two, they heard no fresh news from Harley Street or Bartlett's Buildings. They already knew enough to keep Mrs. Jennings busy spreading the information without seeking more. Nevertheless, from the first she had intended to visit her cousins as soon as possible, both to comfort them and to find out more. Only an unusual number of callers had prevented her from going during those days.

The third day after they learnt the details was a Sunday so fine and beautiful that, although it was only the second week of March, many people were drawn to Kensington Gardens. Mrs. Jennings and Elinor went among them. Marianne, however, knew the Willoughbys had returned to London and lived in constant fear of meeting them. She chose to remain at home rather than venture into so public a place.

A close acquaintance of Mrs. Jennings joined them soon after they entered the gardens. Elinor was glad that she stayed and occupied all Mrs. Jennings's conversation, leaving her free to reflect quietly. She saw neither the Willoughbys nor Edward, and for some time nobody who could interest her for any reason, happy or sad. At last, to her surprise, Miss Steele addressed her. Looking rather shy, she nevertheless expressed great pleasure at meeting them. Encouraged by Mrs. Jennings's particular kindness, she left her own party briefly to join theirs. Mrs. Jennings immediately whispered to Elinor,
“Find out everything, my dear. She will tell you anything you ask. You see, I cannot leave Mrs. Clarke.”
Fortunately for Mrs. Jennings's curiosity, and Elinor's too, Miss Steele would tell everything _without_ being asked. Otherwise they would have learnt nothing.

“I am so glad to meet you,” Miss Steele said, familiarly taking her arm. “More than anything, I wanted to see you.” Then she lowered her voice. “I suppose Mrs. Jennings has heard the whole story. Is she angry?”
“Not with you at all, I believe.”
“That is a relief. And Lady Middleton—is _she_ angry with us?”
“I cannot imagine that she could possibly be angry.”

“I am tremendously glad to hear it. Good gracious, what a time I have had! I never saw Lucy so furious in my life. At first she swore she would never trim another bonnet for me, or do anything else for me as long as she lived. But she has quite recovered now, and we are as friendly as ever. Look, she made this bow for my hat and put the feather in last night. There, now _you_ are going to laugh at me too! But why shouldn't I wear pink ribbons? I don't care if it _is_ the Doctor's favourite colour. For my part, I would never have known he preferred it if he hadn't happened to say so. My cousins have teased me so much! Sometimes I hardly know where to look in front of them.”
She had strayed onto a subject about which Elinor had nothing to say. Before long, she therefore thought it advisable to return to the original one.

“Well, Miss Dashwood,” she said triumphantly, “people can say what they like about Mr. Ferrars declaring he wouldn't marry Lucy, but I can tell you it is not true. It is shameful to spread such unkind stories. Whatever Lucy herself may have thought, other people had no business to treat it as a certainty.”
“I assure you I have never heard anything of that sort even suggested before,” Elinor replied.

“Oh, haven't you? But I know very well it _was_ said, and by more than one person. Miss Godby told Miss Sparks that nobody in their senses could expect Mr. Ferrars to give up a woman like Miss Morton, with thirty thousand pounds, for Lucy Steele, who had nothing. Miss Sparks told me herself. Besides, my cousin Richard said he feared Mr. Ferrars would withdraw when it came to the point. When Edward stayed away for three days, I hardly knew what to think myself. I honestly believe Lucy thought everything was lost. We left your brother's on Wednesday, and saw nothing of him on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday. We had no idea what had become of him. Once Lucy thought of writing, but then her pride rose against it. This morning, though, he came just as we returned from church. Then he explained everything: how he had been summoned to Harley Street on Wednesday, how his mother and all of them had argued with him, and how he had declared in front of everyone that he loved nobody but Lucy and would marry nobody else. He had been so upset by it all that, as soon as he left his mother's house, he got on his horse and rode somewhere into the country. He stayed at an inn all Thursday and Friday to recover. After thinking everything over again and again, he said it seemed cruel to hold her to the engagement now he had no fortune, nothing at all. It could only harm her, for he had just two thousand pounds and no prospect of more. If he entered the church, as he was considering, he could expect only an assistant clergyman's post, and how could they live on that? He could not bear the thought of her doing no better. So he begged her, if she had the least wish for it, to end the engagement immediately and leave him to fend for himself. I heard every word as plainly as possible. He spoke of parting entirely for _her_ sake, on _her_ account, never his own. I would swear he never said a syllable about being tired of her, wanting Miss Morton, or anything of that kind. Of course Lucy would not listen to such talk. She told him at once—with a great deal of ‘sweet’ and ‘love’ and all that; oh dear, one cannot repeat such things!—she told him she had not the slightest wish to break it off. She could live with him on almost nothing, and however little he had, she would be happy to have it all, or something like that. Then he was enormously pleased, and they talked for some time about their plans. They agreed he should be ordained immediately, and they would wait to marry until he obtained a living of his own. Just then I could hear no more. My cousin called from downstairs that Mrs. Richardson had arrived in her carriage and could take one of us to Kensington Gardens. I had to go into the room and interrupt them to ask if Lucy wanted to go. She didn't want to leave Edward, so I ran upstairs, put on silk stockings, and came away with the Richardsons.”
“I don't understand what you mean by interrupting them,” Elinor said. “Weren't you all in the same room together?”

“Oh no, certainly not! Miss Dashwood, do you think people talk of love with someone else present? For shame! Surely you know better.” She gave an affected laugh. “No, no, they were shut in the drawing room together. I heard it all by listening at the door.”

“What!” Elinor exclaimed. “Have you been repeating a conversation you overheard at the door? I wish I had known sooner. I would certainly not have allowed you to tell me the details of a conversation you had no right to hear yourself. How could you treat your sister so unfairly?”

“Oh, there's nothing in _that_. I only stood at the door and heard what I could. Lucy would have done exactly the same to me. A year or two ago, when Martha Sharpe and I had so many secrets, she thought nothing of hiding in a cupboard or behind a fireplace board expressly to hear us talking.”
Elinor tried to change the subject. But Miss Steele could not be kept for more than a couple of minutes from what chiefly occupied her mind.

“Edward says he may go to Oxford soon,” she said. “At present he is lodging at No.—, Pall Mall. What an unpleasant woman his mother is, isn't she? Your brother and his wife weren't very kind either. Still, I won't say anything against them to _you_. And they did send us home in their own carriage, which was more than I expected. I was terribly afraid your sister-in-law might ask for the sewing cases back that she had given us a day or two earlier. But she said nothing about them, and I took care to keep mine out of sight. Edward says he has business at Oxford, so he must go there for a while. After _that_, as soon as he can find a bishop, he will be ordained. I wonder what curacy he will get! Good gracious!” She giggled. “I would stake my life on knowing what my cousins will say when they hear. They'll tell me to write to the Doctor and ask him to give Edward the assistant's post in his new parish. I know they will. But I wouldn't do it for the world. ‘Goodness,’ I shall say at once, ‘how could you imagine such a thing? _Me_, write to the Doctor, indeed!’”
“Well,” Elinor said, “it is comforting to be prepared for the worst. At least you have your answer ready.”
Miss Steele was about to continue on the same subject when her own party approached, making another topic more urgent.

“Oh, here come the Richardsons! I had so much more to tell you, but I mustn't stay away from them any longer. I assure you they are very genteel. He makes an enormous amount of money, and they have their own carriage. I have no time to tell Mrs. Jennings myself, but please say how glad I am to hear she isn't angry with us, or Lady Middleton either. And if anything should take you and your sister away, and Mrs. Jennings wanted company, we would be very happy to stay as long as she liked. I suppose Lady Middleton won't ask us again this time. Goodbye. I am sorry Miss Marianne wasn't here. Give her my kind regards. Goodness, you are wearing your spotted muslin! I wonder you weren't afraid of tearing it.”

That was her final concern. Afterwards she had only time to take leave of Mrs. Jennings before Mrs. Richardson reclaimed her. Elinor was left with enough information to occupy her thoughts for some time, though she had learnt little beyond what she had already anticipated. Edward's marriage to Lucy remained as firmly decided, and its date as wholly uncertain, as she had expected. Everything depended, exactly as she had foreseen, on his obtaining a church appointment for which there presently seemed not the smallest prospect.

Once they returned to the carriage, Mrs. Jennings eagerly asked for news. Elinor wanted to spread as little as possible of information so unfairly obtained. She therefore confined herself to a few simple facts that she was certain Lucy would want known for the sake of her own importance. She reported only that the engagement continued and what steps might bring about the marriage. Mrs. Jennings responded with the following natural observation.

“Wait until he has a living! Yes, we all know how _that_ ends. They'll wait a year, find nothing comes of it, then settle down on a curacy worth fifty pounds a year, the interest on his two thousand pounds, and whatever little Mr. Steele and Mr. Pratt can give her. Then they'll have a child every year, and heaven help them, how poor they will be! I must see what I can give them to furnish their house. Two maids and two menservants, indeed, as I was saying the other day! No, no, they will need one sturdy girl to do everything. Betty's sister would never suit them _now_.”
The next morning, the two-penny post brought Elinor a letter from Lucy herself. It read:
“Bartlett's Building, March.

“I hope my dear Miss Dashwood will forgive me for taking the liberty of writing. But I know your friendship will make you glad to hear such good news of me and my dear Edward, after all the troubles we have been through lately. So I will make no more apologies, but tell you that, thank God, although we have suffered dreadfully, we are both quite well now, and as happy as our love must always make us. We have faced great trials and persecution, but at the same time we are grateful for many friends. You are certainly not the least of them. I shall always remember your great kindness thankfully, and so will Edward, whom I have told about it. I know you will be pleased to hear, as will dear Mrs. Jennings, that I spent two happy hours with him yesterday afternoon. He would not hear of our parting, although I earnestly urged it, as I thought duty and prudence required. I would have parted from him for ever on the spot if he had agreed, but he said it could never be. While he had my love, he cared nothing for his mother's anger. Our prospects are not very bright, certainly, but we must wait and hope for the best. He will soon be ordained. If you can ever recommend him to anyone with a church living to give, I am sure you will remember us. I trust dear Mrs. Jennings will also put in a good word with Sir John, Mr. Palmer, or any friend who may be able to help. Poor Anne was very much to blame, but she meant well, so I say nothing. I hope Mrs. Jennings won't find it too much trouble to call if she is near here one morning. It would be a great kindness, and my cousins would be proud to know her. My paper reminds me to finish. Please give my most grateful and respectful regards to her, and to Sir John, Lady Middleton, and the dear children when you see them, and my love to Miss Marianne.
“I remain, etc.”
As soon as she finished reading, Elinor carried out what she believed to be the letter's real purpose: she handed it to Mrs. Jennings, who read it aloud with many approving and delighted comments.

“Very good indeed! How prettily she writes! Yes, it was quite proper to offer to release him if he wished. Just like Lucy. Poor soul, I heartily wish I _could_ find him a living. She calls me ‘dear Mrs. Jennings,’ you see. There never was a more good-hearted girl. Very good, upon my word. That sentence is beautifully put. Yes, yes, I shall certainly go and see her. How thoughtful, remembering everyone! Thank you for showing me, my dear. It is as pretty a letter as I ever saw, and does the greatest credit to Lucy's mind and heart.”

chapters.title: Chapter 39
paragraphs: The Miss Dashwoods had now spent a little over two months in London, and Marianne grew more impatient to leave every day. She longed for the country air, freedom, and quiet, imagining that if any place could give her relief, Barton would. Elinor was hardly less eager to go. She was less determined on leaving immediately only because she understood the difficulties of so long a journey, which Marianne refused to acknowledge. Nevertheless, she began seriously considering how to arrange it. She had already told their kind hostess of their wishes, and Mrs. Jennings was resisting them with all the eloquence of affection, when a plan was proposed which Elinor found much better than any alternative, though it would keep them from home a few weeks longer. The Palmers intended to go to Cleveland at the end of March for Easter. Charlotte warmly invited her mother and both her friends to accompany them. That alone would not have satisfied Elinor's sense of propriety. But Mr. Palmer himself supported the invitation with such genuine politeness that, together with the great improvement in his behaviour towards them since Marianne's unhappiness became known, it persuaded her to accept with pleasure.
When Elinor told Marianne what she had agreed to, however, her first response was far from promising.
“Cleveland!” she cried in great agitation. “No, I cannot go to Cleveland.”
“You forget,” Elinor said gently, “where it is. It is not near—it is not in the neighbourhood of—”
“But it is in Somersetshire. I cannot go to Somersetshire. The place I once looked forward to visiting—no, Elinor, you cannot expect me to go there.”

Elinor did not argue that she ought to overcome these feelings. Instead, she tried to counter them by appealing to others. This plan, she explained, would fix the date of their return to the dear mother Marianne so longed to see, and make the journey easier and more comfortable than any other arrangement, perhaps without any extra delay. Cleveland lay only a few miles from Bristol. From there Barton was no more than a day's journey, though a long one, and their mother's servant could easily come to escort them home. They need not stay at Cleveland longer than a week, so they might be back at Barton in little more than three weeks altogether. Marianne's love for her mother was real, and could therefore triumph without much difficulty over the imagined evils she had raised.

Far from tiring of her guests, Mrs. Jennings earnestly urged them to return with her from Cleveland. Elinor was grateful but would not change her plan. Their mother very readily gave her agreement, and every arrangement for their return was settled as far as possible. Marianne found some relief in calculating the number of hours that still separated her from Barton.

“Ah, Colonel, I don't know what you and I shall do without the Miss Dashwoods,” Mrs. Jennings said when he first called after their departure was settled. “They are quite determined to go home from the Palmers'. How lonely we shall be when I return! Lord, we shall sit yawning at one another, as dull as two cats.”

Perhaps this vivid picture of their future boredom was intended to provoke the Colonel into making the proposal that would provide him with an escape. If so, she soon had good reason to think she had succeeded. Elinor moved to the window to measure a print more easily before copying it for her friend. The Colonel followed with a particularly meaningful expression and spoke with her there for several minutes. Mrs. Jennings could not miss the effect on Elinor. She was too honourable to listen, and had even moved deliberately nearer the piano where Marianne was playing so that she _would not_ hear. But she could not help seeing Elinor change colour, listen with agitation, and become too absorbed in his words to continue her work. Her hopes received further confirmation when, between one piece of Marianne's music and the next, a few unavoidable words reached her. The Colonel seemed to be apologising for the poor quality of his house. That settled the matter beyond doubt. She wondered why he thought an apology necessary, but supposed it must be the proper form. She could not make out Elinor's reply, though from the movement of her lips she judged that _that_ was no serious objection. Inwardly she praised her honesty. They talked for several more minutes without Mrs. Jennings catching a syllable. Then another fortunate pause in Marianne's playing allowed her to hear the Colonel say calmly,
“I am afraid it will not be possible very soon.”
Astonished and shocked by words so unlike a lover's, she nearly exclaimed, “Lord, what could prevent it?” Restraining herself, she confined the outburst to a silent thought.
“How very strange! Surely he needn't wait until he is any older.”

Yet the delay the Colonel proposed did not seem to hurt or offend his companion at all. When they ended their conversation shortly afterwards and moved apart, Mrs. Jennings heard Elinor quite clearly say, in a voice that showed she meant every word,
“I shall always feel deeply grateful to you for this.”

Mrs. Jennings was delighted by her gratitude. She could only wonder how, after hearing such words, the Colonel could immediately take his leave with complete composure and go away without answering her. She had not imagined her old friend could be so indifferent a suitor.
What had actually passed between them was as follows.

“I have heard,” he said with great compassion, “of the injustice your friend Mr. Ferrars has suffered from his family. If I understand correctly, they have cast him off entirely because he insists on keeping his engagement to a very deserving young woman. Is my information right? Is that what has happened?”
Elinor confirmed that it was.

“The cruelty, and the short-sighted cruelty,” he replied with deep feeling, “of separating, or trying to separate, two young people who have loved each other for so long is terrible. Mrs. Ferrars does not know what she may be doing, or what she may drive her son to. I have met Mr. Ferrars two or three times in Harley Street and like him very much. He is not someone one can know intimately in a short time, but I have seen enough to wish him well for his own sake, and still more as your friend. I understand he intends to enter the church. Would you kindly tell him that the living of Delaford is his, if he considers it worth accepting? Today's post informed me that it has just fallen vacant. With his present unfortunate circumstances, it may be absurd to appear doubtful about _that_. I only wish it were worth more. It is a rectory, but a small one. I believe the last incumbent received no more than two hundred pounds a year. The income could certainly be improved, though I fear not enough to make him very comfortably off. Such as it is, however, I shall take the greatest pleasure in offering it to him. Please assure him of that.”

Elinor could hardly have been more astonished by this request if the Colonel really had proposed marriage to her. The church appointment she had thought beyond Edward's reach only two days earlier was already available to enable him to marry. And _she_, of all people, had been chosen to convey it to him! Her agitation was what Mrs. Jennings had attributed to a quite different cause. Yet whatever lesser, less generous and less agreeable feelings contributed to it, she deeply respected the general kindness and felt grateful for the particular friendship that together prompted Colonel Brandon's action. She expressed both warmly, thanked him with all her heart, and praised Edward's principles and character as she knew they deserved. If he truly wanted to pass so pleasant a task to someone else, she promised to undertake it gladly. At the same time, she could not help thinking that nobody could do it as well as he could himself. In truth, she would gladly have been spared the task, unwilling to give Edward the pain of receiving an obligation from _her_. But Colonel Brandon, for reasons of equal delicacy, also declined it. He seemed so anxious to make the offer through her that she would not oppose him further. She believed Edward was still in London; fortunately Miss Steele had told her his address. She could therefore promise to inform him that day. Once this was settled, the Colonel began speaking of his own advantage in gaining such a respectable, agreeable neighbour. _Then_ he regretted that the house was small and unimpressive. Elinor, exactly as Mrs. Jennings imagined, treated that as a very slight objection, at least as far as its size was concerned.
“I cannot imagine the small house troubling them,” she said. “It will suit the size of their household and their income.”

The Colonel was surprised to discover that _she_ regarded Edward's marriage as the inevitable result of the offer. He had not imagined that the Delaford living could provide an income on which anyone in Edward's position would venture to marry, and he said so.

“This small rectory _can_ do no more than support Mr. Ferrars comfortably as a single man. It cannot allow him to marry. I am sorry that I have no other living to offer, and little influence beyond this. If some unforeseen chance gives me the power to help him further, however, my opinion of him must change greatly before I could be less willing to help than I sincerely wish I could be now. Indeed, what I am doing seems almost nothing, since it takes him so little nearer what must be his chief, his only source of happiness. His marriage must still be a distant prospect. At least, I am afraid it will not be possible very soon.”

This was the sentence which, misunderstood, had so justly offended Mrs. Jennings's delicate feelings. But after this account of what actually passed between Colonel Brandon and Elinor at the window, her gratitude as they parted may perhaps seem no less reasonably felt, nor less appropriately expressed, than if it had answered a proposal of marriage.

chapters.title: Chapter 40
paragraphs: “Well, Miss Dashwood,” Mrs. Jennings said with a knowing smile as soon as the gentleman had left, “I won't ask what the Colonel has been saying. On my honour, I _tried_ not to hear, but I couldn't help catching enough to understand his purpose. I assure you, nothing has ever pleased me more. I wish you joy with all my heart.”

“Thank you, ma'am,” Elinor replied. “It _does_ give me great joy, and I feel Colonel Brandon's kindness very deeply. There are few men who would act as he has, few with such compassionate hearts. I have never been more astonished.”
“Lord, my dear, you are very modest. I am not in the least surprised. Lately I have often thought that nothing could be more likely to happen.”
“You judged from what you know of the Colonel's general generosity. Still, you could hardly have foreseen an opportunity coming so soon.”

“An opportunity!” Mrs. Jennings repeated. “Oh, once a man has made up his mind about something like that, he'll soon find an opportunity somehow. Well, my dear, let me wish you joy again and again. If ever there was a happy couple in the world, I think I shall soon know where to find them.”
“I suppose you mean to follow them to Delaford,” Elinor said with a faint smile.
“Yes, my dear, that is exactly what I mean. As for the house being a poor one, I cannot imagine what the Colonel means. It is as good a house as I ever saw.”
“He said it was in need of repairs.”
“Well, whose fault is that? Why doesn't he have it repaired? Who else should do it?”
A servant interrupted to announce that the carriage was waiting outside. Mrs. Jennings immediately prepared to leave, saying,

“Well, my dear, I must go before I have said half what I want to. But we can talk it all over this evening, since we shall be alone. I won't ask you to come with me. I expect your mind is too full to care for company. Besides, you must be longing to tell your sister everything.”
Marianne had left before their conversation began.
“Certainly, ma'am, I shall tell Marianne. But for the present I shall not mention it to anyone else.”
“Oh, very well,” Mrs. Jennings said, rather disappointed. “Then you don't want me to tell Lucy? I am thinking of going as far as Holborn today.”

“No, ma'am, not even Lucy, please. A day's delay will surely make very little difference. Until I have written to Mr. Ferrars, I don't think anyone else should be told. I shall do _that_ immediately. He must lose no time, since he will naturally have much to arrange concerning his ordination.”

At first this puzzled Mrs. Jennings considerably. She could not immediately understand why Mr. Ferrars needed such an urgent letter. A few moments' thought, however, produced a happy explanation, and she exclaimed,

“Oh, I see! Mr. Ferrars is to be the man. Well, so much the better for him. Yes, of course, he must be ordained in time. I am delighted your arrangements are so far advanced. But, my dear, isn't this rather unusual? Shouldn't the Colonel write himself? Surely he is the proper person.”
Elinor did not quite understand the beginning of this speech, but thought it unnecessary to inquire. She answered only the last part.
“Colonel Brandon is so sensitive about such things that he would rather anyone but himself tell Mr. Ferrars what he intends.”

“And so _you_ have to do it. Well, _that_ is an odd sort of delicacy! Still, I won't disturb you.” She saw Elinor preparing to write. “You understand your own affairs best. Goodbye, my dear. I haven't heard anything so pleasing since Charlotte's baby was born.”
She went away, but returned a moment later.

“I have just remembered Betty's sister, my dear. I should be very glad to find her such a good mistress. Whether she would do as a lady's maid, I cannot say. She is an excellent housemaid and very good with her needle. But you can consider all that when you have time.”
“Certainly, ma'am,” Elinor answered. She had heard little of the speech, being more anxious to be alone than to understand its subject.

All her concern now was how to begin, how to word her note to Edward. Their particular circumstances made difficult what would have been perfectly easy for anyone else. Equally afraid of saying too much or too little, she sat considering the paper with her pen in her hand, until Edward himself interrupted her by entering the room.

Coming to leave his farewell card, he had met Mrs. Jennings at the door as she went to her carriage. She apologised for not returning upstairs herself, then compelled him to go in by saying Miss Dashwood was above and wished to speak to him on very particular business.

In the middle of her uncertainty, Elinor had just been congratulating herself that, however difficult the right words might be to find in a letter, writing was at least better than speaking the news aloud. Then her visitor arrived and forced the greatest effort of all upon her. His sudden appearance astonished and confused her intensely. She had not seen him since his engagement became public, and therefore not since he knew that she knew of it. That, together with the awareness of her recent thoughts and of what she must tell him, made her especially uncomfortable for several minutes. He too was distressed, and they sat down in a most promising state of embarrassment. He could not remember whether he had apologised for intruding when he entered. To be safe, he made a formal apology as soon as he could speak after taking his chair.

“Mrs. Jennings told me you wanted to speak to me,” he said. “At least, that was what I understood. Otherwise I would certainly not have intruded like this. At the same time, I should have been very sorry to leave London without seeing you and your sister, especially as it will probably be some time—I am unlikely to have the pleasure of meeting you again soon. I leave for Oxford tomorrow.”

“You would not have gone without our good wishes,” Elinor replied, recovering herself and determined to finish what she dreaded as quickly as possible, “even if we could not give them in person. Mrs. Jennings was quite right. I have something important to tell you, which I was just about to put in a letter. I have been entrusted with a very pleasant task.” She breathed rather faster than usual. “Colonel Brandon was here only ten minutes ago. He asked me to tell you that, hearing you intend to enter the church, he has great pleasure in offering you the living of Delaford, which has just become vacant. He only wishes it were more valuable. Let me congratulate you on having so worthy and discerning a friend, and join him in wishing that the living—it brings in about two hundred a year—were worth much more, and better able to allow you to—that it might be more than temporary provision for you. In short, that it might secure everything you hope for in happiness.”

Since Edward could not express his feelings himself, nobody else can be expected to express them for him. His _face_ showed all the astonishment such unexpected, unimagined news must cause. But he said only two words:
“Colonel Brandon!”

“Yes,” Elinor continued, gaining courage now that some of the worst was over. “He intends it to show his sympathy for what has recently happened: for the cruel position your family's unjustifiable conduct has placed you in. I am sure Marianne, I, and all your friends share that sympathy. It is also a proof of his high opinion of your character, and his particular approval of your behaviour in these circumstances.”
“Colonel Brandon is offering _me_ a living? Can that really be possible?”
“Your relations' unkindness has made you surprised to find friendship anywhere at all.”

“No,” he replied, suddenly aware, “not to find it in _you_. I cannot fail to know that I owe it all to you, to your kindness. I feel it. I would express it if I could, but you know I am no great speaker.”

“You are quite mistaken. I assure you that you owe it entirely, or almost entirely, to your own worth and Colonel Brandon's recognition of it. I played no part. Until he told me his plan, I did not even know the living was vacant. Nor had it ever occurred to me that he might have such an appointment to offer. Because you are my friend and my family's, perhaps—indeed, I know—he takes still greater pleasure in giving it to you. But I promise you, I never asked him for anything.”

Truth required her to acknowledge some small share in the action. Yet she was so unwilling to appear Edward's benefactor that she admitted it hesitantly. That probably helped fix in his mind a suspicion which had recently entered it. For a little while after she finished, he sat deep in thought. At last, as though making an effort, he said,

“Colonel Brandon seems a man of great worth and respectability. That is how I have always heard him described. I know your brother thinks highly of him. He is certainly intelligent, and entirely a gentleman in his manners.”

“I believe,” Elinor answered, “that as you know him better you will find him everything you have heard. Since you will be such close neighbours—I understand the parsonage is almost beside the main house—it is particularly important that he _should_ be all those things.”

Edward did not answer. But when she turned her head away, he looked at her with such seriousness, intensity, and sadness that he seemed to be saying he might one day wish the parsonage much farther from the main house.
“Colonel Brandon lodges in St. James Street, I think,” he said shortly afterwards, rising from his chair.
Elinor gave him the number of the house.
“Then I must hurry to offer him the thanks you refuse to accept _yourself_, and assure him that he has made me a very—an exceedingly happy man.”

Elinor did not try to keep him. They parted with her earnest assurance that she would always wish him happiness, whatever changes life might bring. On _his_ side there was more an attempt to return the same goodwill than any ability to express it.
“The next time I see him,” Elinor told herself as the door closed behind him, “he will be Lucy's husband.”
With this pleasing prospect, she sat down to reconsider their meeting, recall Edward's words, and try to understand all his feelings—and, naturally, to reflect discontentedly on her own.

Mrs. Jennings came home from visiting people she had never met before, and must therefore have had much to say about them. But the important secret in her possession occupied her mind far more than anything else. As soon as Elinor appeared, she returned to it.
“Well, my dear,” she cried, “I sent the young man up to you. Wasn't that right of me? I suppose you had no great difficulty? He wasn't very unwilling to accept your proposal?”
“No, ma'am. _That_ was hardly likely to happen.”
“Well, how soon will he be ready? Everything seems to depend on that.”
“I know so little about these formalities,” Elinor said, “that I can scarcely guess how much time or preparation is needed. But I suppose his ordination can be completed in two or three months.”

“Two or three months!” Mrs. Jennings cried. “Lord, my dear, how calmly you speak of it! Can the Colonel wait two or three months? Bless me, _I_ should lose all patience. Of course one would be glad to do poor Mr. Ferrars a kindness, but I really don't think it worth waiting that long for him. Surely somebody else would do just as well—someone already ordained.”
“My dear ma'am,” Elinor said, “what can you be thinking? Colonel Brandon's sole purpose is to help Mr. Ferrars.”
“Bless you, my dear! Surely you don't expect me to believe the Colonel is marrying you only to give Mr. Ferrars ten guineas for performing the ceremony!”

The misunderstanding could not survive that. An explanation immediately followed, giving both women considerable amusement for the moment without substantially diminishing either woman's happiness. Mrs. Jennings merely exchanged one source of delight for another, while keeping her expectation of the first.

“Yes, yes, the parsonage is small,” she said when her first burst of surprise and satisfaction had passed, “and very likely _does_ need repairs. But to hear a man apparently apologising for a house which I know has five sitting rooms downstairs, and which the housekeeper told me, I think, could make up fifteen beds! And apologising to you, who have been living in Barton Cottage! It seems quite ridiculous. Still, my dear, we must encourage the Colonel to improve the parsonage and make it comfortable before Lucy moves in.”
“But Colonel Brandon does not seem to think the living provides enough income for them to marry.”

“The Colonel is a fool, my dear. Because he has two thousand a year himself, he thinks nobody can marry on less. Take my word for it: if I am alive, I shall visit Delaford Parsonage before Michaelmas. And I certainly won't go unless Lucy is there.”
Elinor entirely agreed that Edward and Lucy were unlikely to wait for any further improvement in their circumstances.

chapters.title: Chapter 41
paragraphs: After thanking Colonel Brandon, Edward took his happiness to Lucy. By the time he reached Bartlett's Buildings, it was apparently so great that she could assure Mrs. Jennings, who called the next day to congratulate her, that she had never seen him in such high spirits in her life.

Lucy's own happiness and high spirits, at least, were beyond doubt. She heartily shared Mrs. Jennings's expectation that they would all be comfortably together at Delaford Parsonage before Michaelmas. Far from resisting the credit Edward insisted on giving Elinor, she spoke with the warmest gratitude of her friendship for them both. She readily acknowledged their entire debt to her and openly declared that no effort Elinor made for their benefit, now or in future, could ever surprise her. She believed Miss Dashwood capable of doing anything for those she truly valued. As for Colonel Brandon, Lucy was not merely ready to worship him as a saint; she sincerely wanted him treated like one in worldly matters too. She wanted his tithes raised to the highest possible amount, and secretly resolved to make every possible use, once at Delaford, of his servants, carriage, cows, and poultry.

More than a week had passed since John Dashwood's visit to Berkeley Street. Since then they had taken no notice of Fanny's illness beyond one inquiry sent by word of mouth. Elinor began to feel she must visit her. The duty ran against her own wishes and received no encouragement from either companion. Marianne not only absolutely refused to go herself, but urgently tried to stop Elinor going at all. Mrs. Jennings always placed her carriage at Elinor's disposal, but disliked Mrs. John Dashwood so much that neither curiosity about her appearance after the discovery, nor a strong desire to offend her by defending Edward, could overcome her reluctance to meet her again. Elinor therefore set out alone for a visit nobody could have wished to make less, risking a private conversation with a woman whom neither of her companions had so much reason to dislike.

She was told Mrs. Dashwood was not receiving visitors. Before the carriage could turn away, however, John happened to come out. He expressed great pleasure at seeing Elinor, said he had just been going to Berkeley Street, and invited her in, assuring her that Fanny would be very pleased to see her.
They went upstairs to the drawing room and found it empty.

“I suppose Fanny is in her room,” he said. “I shall go to her shortly. I am sure she will not have the slightest objection to seeing _you_. Quite the opposite. Especially _now_, there can be no—but you and Marianne have always been great favourites. Why didn't Marianne come?”
Elinor made the best excuse she could for her sister.

“I am not sorry to find you alone,” he answered, “because I have a great deal to say. This living of Colonel Brandon's—can it be true? Has he really given it to Edward? I heard it by chance yesterday and was coming expressly to ask you more about it.”
“It is quite true. Colonel Brandon has given Edward the living of Delaford.”
“Really! Well, that is astonishing. No relationship, no connection between them! And when livings command such prices! What was this one worth?”
“About two hundred pounds a year.”

“Very well. For the right to appoint the next clergyman to a living of that value, assuming the previous holder was old and sick and likely to leave it vacant soon, he might have received—fourteen hundred pounds, I dare say. Why didn't he arrange that before the man's death? Of course it is too late to sell the appointment _now_. But a man of Colonel Brandon's intelligence! I am surprised he should show so little foresight in a matter of such ordinary, natural concern. I am convinced there is great inconsistency in almost every human character. Still, on reflection, perhaps _this_ explains it. Edward is to hold the living only until the person to whom the Colonel really sold the appointment is old enough to take it. Yes, that must be it. Depend upon it.”

Elinor firmly contradicted him. She explained that she had conveyed Colonel Brandon's offer to Edward herself and must therefore understand the exact terms on which it was offered. He was obliged to accept her authority.
“It is truly extraordinary!” he exclaimed when she finished. “What motive could the Colonel possibly have?”
“A very simple motive: he wanted to help Mr. Ferrars.”

“Well, whatever Colonel Brandon may be, Edward is a fortunate man. But don't mention it to Fanny. I have told her, and she is bearing it very well, but she will not like hearing much discussion of it.”
Elinor could hardly refrain from observing that Fanny ought to bear calmly an improvement in her brother's income which could not possibly make either herself or her child poorer.

“Mrs. Ferrars knows nothing yet,” he added, lowering his voice suitably for so important a subject. “I think it best to keep it entirely from her for as long as possible. When the marriage takes place, I fear she will have to hear everything.”

“But why take such precautions? Of course we cannot suppose Mrs. Ferrars could feel the slightest pleasure in knowing her son has enough to live on; _that_ is quite out of the question. But after her recent behaviour, why should we suppose she feels anything at all? She has finished with him, cast him off for ever, and made everyone under her influence do the same. Surely after that nobody can imagine she is open to either sorrow or joy on his account. Nothing that happens to him can interest her. She cannot be so weak as to throw away the comfort of a child while keeping all a parent's anxiety!”

“Ah, Elinor,” John said, “your reasoning is excellent, but it rests on ignorance of human nature. When Edward makes this unhappy marriage, his mother will feel it just as deeply as if she had never disowned him. So anything that might hasten that dreadful event must be kept from her as far as possible. Mrs. Ferrars can never forget that Edward is her son.”
“You surprise me. I should have thought it had nearly slipped her mind by _now_.”
“You do her a great injustice. Mrs. Ferrars is one of the most loving mothers in the world.”
Elinor said nothing.
“_Now_,” John said after a brief pause, “we are considering _Robert_ as a husband for Miss Morton.”
Smiling at the solemn, decisive importance of her brother's manner, Elinor calmly answered,
“I suppose the lady has no say in the matter.”
“No say? What do you mean?”
“Only that, from the way you speak, I suppose it makes no difference to Miss Morton whether she marries Edward or Robert.”

“Certainly it can make no difference. Robert will now be regarded as the eldest son for all practical purposes. As for anything else, they are both very agreeable young men. I don't know that either is better than the other.”
