Elinor said no more. John was silent for a little while too, then concluded his reflections as follows.

“There is _one_ thing I can assure you of, my dear sister.” He kindly took her hand and spoke in an awed whisper. “And I _will_ tell you, because I know it must please you. I have good reason to believe—indeed, I have it from the best authority, or I would not repeat it. Otherwise it would be very wrong to mention it. But my authority is the very best. Not that I actually heard Mrs. Ferrars say it herself, but her daughter _did_, and she told me. In short, whatever objections there might have been to a certain—a certain connection, you understand—it would have been much preferable to her. It would not have caused her half the distress _this_ does. I was extremely pleased that Mrs. Ferrars saw it that way. Very gratifying for all of us, you know. She said it would have been incomparably the lesser evil, and that she would gladly settle _now_ for nothing worse. Still, all that is entirely out of the question, not to be thought of or mentioned. Any attachment, you understand, could never be. That is all over. I merely wanted to tell you because I knew how much you would like to hear it. Not that you have anything to regret, dear Elinor. There is no doubt you will do extremely well—quite as well, perhaps better, taking everything into account. Has Colonel Brandon visited you lately?”

Elinor had heard enough, if not to gratify her vanity or increase her sense of importance, at least to unsettle her nerves and fill her thoughts. She was therefore glad when Robert Ferrars entered, sparing her a substantial reply and the risk of hearing more. After a little conversation, John remembered that Fanny still did not know Elinor was there and went to find her. Elinor was left to improve her acquaintance with Robert. His cheerful unconcern and happy self-satisfaction confirmed her worst opinion of both his mind and his heart. He enjoyed a grossly unfair share of his mother's love and generosity at his banished brother's expense—a preference earned by nothing except his own dissolute life and Edward's integrity.

They had been alone scarcely two minutes before he began speaking of Edward. He too had heard about the living and was very curious. Elinor repeated the details she had given John. Their effect, though quite different, was no less striking. Robert laughed extravagantly. The thought of Edward as a clergyman in a small parsonage delighted him beyond measure. When he added the picture of Edward in a white surplice reading prayers and announcing the marriage banns of John Smith and Mary Brown, he could imagine nothing more ridiculous.

Elinor waited silently, her face immovably serious, for this foolishness to end. She could not stop her eyes fixing on him with a look that expressed all her contempt. The look was usefully bestowed: it relieved her feelings and communicated nothing to him. What brought him back from wit to wisdom was not her disapproval, but his own sensitivity.

“We may laugh,” he said at last, recovering from the affected laughter that had considerably prolonged his genuine amusement, “but upon my soul, it is very serious. Poor Edward! He is ruined for ever. I am extremely sorry, because I know what a good-hearted creature he is, perhaps as well-meaning a fellow as any alive. You must not judge him, Miss Dashwood, from _your_ slight acquaintance. Poor Edward! His manners are certainly not the best. But we are not all born with the same abilities, the same ease. Poor fellow, to see him among strangers! It was pitiable enough. Yet I honestly believe he has as good a heart as anyone in the kingdom. I assure you I have never been so shocked as when all this came out. I could not believe it. My mother told me first. Feeling that I must act firmly, I immediately said, ‘My dear mother, I do not know what you intend to do, but I must say that if Edward marries this young woman, _I_ shall never see him again.’ Those were my very first words. I was extraordinarily shocked. Poor Edward! He has utterly destroyed himself, shut himself out of all respectable society for ever. But, as I told my mother at once, I am not in the least surprised. With his sort of education, it was always to be expected. My poor mother was half beside herself.”
“Have you ever met the young woman?”

“Yes, once. While she was staying here, I happened to call for ten minutes, and saw quite enough. Just an awkward country girl, without style or elegance and with scarcely any beauty. I remember her perfectly. Exactly the sort I would expect to captivate poor Edward. As soon as my mother told me, I offered to speak to him myself and persuade him against it. But I found it was too late _then_ to do anything. Unfortunately I was not there at the beginning and heard nothing until after the break, when it was not my place to interfere. Had I known a few hours earlier, I think we could probably have found some solution. I should certainly have put the matter to Edward very strongly. ‘My dear fellow,’ I would have said, ‘consider what you are doing. You are forming a most disgraceful connection, which your entire family opposes.’ In short, I cannot help believing some means could have been found. But now it is all too late. He must starve, you know. That is certain: absolutely starve.”

He had just settled this point with great composure when Mrs. John Dashwood entered and ended the discussion. Though _she_ never mentioned the affair outside her own family, Elinor could see its effect on her mind in the almost embarrassed expression with which she entered, and in her attempt at warmth towards Elinor. She even went so far as to express regret that the sisters were leaving London so soon, since she had hoped to see more of them. Her husband, who followed her into the room and listened adoringly to every word, seemed to find in this effort everything most affectionate and graceful.

chapters.title: Chapter 42
paragraphs: One more brief call in Harley Street completed the brother and sisters' meetings in London. During it, John congratulated Elinor on travelling so far towards Barton without expense, and on Colonel Brandon's intention to follow them to Cleveland a day or two later. Fanny offered a faint invitation to visit Norland whenever they happened to be nearby—the most unlikely thing imaginable. John gave Elinor a warmer, though less public, assurance of how promptly he would visit her at Delaford. These were the only signs of any future meeting in the country.

Elinor was amused that all her friends seemed determined to send her to Delaford, the place she would now least choose to visit or inhabit. Not only did her brother and Mrs. Jennings consider it her future home, but Lucy, when they said goodbye, warmly urged her to visit her there.

Very early in April, and reasonably early in the morning, the parties from Hanover Square and Berkeley Street left their respective houses to meet, as arranged, on the road. For Charlotte's comfort and the baby's, the journey would take more than two days. Mr. Palmer, travelling faster with Colonel Brandon, would join them at Cleveland shortly after their arrival.

Marianne had enjoyed few comfortable hours in London and had long been eager to leave. Yet when the moment came, she could not say goodbye without great pain to the house where she had last enjoyed the hopes and confidence in Willoughby now extinguished for ever. Nor could she leave the place where he remained, occupied with new commitments and new plans in which _she_ could have no part, without many tears.

Elinor's satisfaction at departing was more definite. She had no such object to hold her lingering thoughts, and left nobody behind from whom permanent separation would cause even a moment's regret. She was glad to escape the persecution of Lucy's friendship, grateful to be taking Marianne away without her having seen Willoughby since his marriage, and hopeful of what a few quiet months at Barton might do to restore her sister's peace of mind and strengthen her own.

Their journey was completed in perfect safety. On the second day they entered Somerset, the cherished or forbidden county, as Marianne's imagination alternately described it. Before noon on the third, they drove up to Cleveland.

Cleveland was a spacious house of modern construction, standing on a sloping lawn. It had no park, but fairly extensive ornamental grounds. Like every estate of similar importance, it possessed an open shrubbery and a more sheltered woodland walk. A smooth gravel drive curved round a plantation to the front. Trees dotted the lawn; firs, mountain ashes, and acacias guarded the house; and a dense screen of these, mixed with tall Lombardy poplars, concealed the service buildings.

Marianne entered with her heart full of feeling, conscious that she was only eighty miles from Barton and fewer than thirty from Combe Magna. Within five minutes, while the others busily helped Charlotte display her baby to the housekeeper, she slipped out again. She stole through the winding shrubberies, just beginning to show their beauty, towards a distant rise. From the Grecian temple there, her eyes could wander over a wide stretch of country to the south-east and rest fondly on the furthest ridge of hills. She imagined that Combe Magna might be visible from their summits.

In these moments of precious, priceless misery, she welcomed Cleveland with tears of anguish. Returning by another route, she felt all the happy privilege of freedom in the country, of wandering wherever she chose in unrestrained, luxurious solitude. She resolved to spend nearly every hour of every day with the Palmers indulging in these solitary walks.

She returned just in time to join the others as they set out to explore the grounds nearer the house. The rest of the morning passed easily: strolling round the kitchen garden, examining the blossom on its walls, and hearing the gardener lament blighted plants; lingering in the greenhouse, where Charlotte laughed over favourite plants carelessly exposed and damaged by the late frost; and visiting the poultry yard, where further amusement arose from her dairymaid's disappointments. Hens had abandoned nests or been carried off by a fox, and a promising young brood was rapidly dwindling.

The morning was fine and dry. In planning her outdoor occupations, Marianne had allowed for no change of weather throughout their stay. She was therefore greatly surprised to find that steady rain prevented another walk after dinner. She had counted on going to the Grecian temple at dusk, perhaps wandering over all the grounds. Mere cold or damp would not have stopped her. But even _she_ could not imagine heavy, persistent rain to be dry or pleasant walking weather.

Their company was small and the hours passed quietly. Mrs. Palmer had her baby, Mrs. Jennings her carpet-work. They discussed the friends left behind, arranged Lady Middleton's engagements, and wondered whether Mr. Palmer and Colonel Brandon would get beyond Reading that night. Elinor joined in, though the subjects concerned her little. Marianne had a talent for finding the library in any house, however thoroughly the family avoided it, and soon obtained a book.

Mrs. Palmer did everything that steady kindness and cheerful friendliness could do to make them welcome. The openness and warmth of her manner more than compensated for the lack of attention and elegance that often made her neglect the forms of politeness. Her kindness, enhanced by a pretty face, was engaging. Her foolishness was obvious but not offensive, because it was free of conceit. Elinor could have forgiven everything except her laugh.
The two gentlemen arrived the next day for a very late dinner. They pleasantly enlarged the party and brought welcome variety to a conversation much depleted by a long morning of continued rain.

Elinor had seen little of Mr. Palmer, and his behaviour towards her and Marianne had varied so much in that little, that she did not know what to expect of him at home. She found him entirely a gentleman towards his guests, and rude to his wife and her mother only occasionally. He could be a pleasant companion, and was kept from always being one chiefly by his readiness to imagine himself as superior to people generally as he must feel towards Charlotte and Mrs. Jennings. In the rest of his character and habits, Elinor noticed nothing unusual for a man of his age. He was particular about food, irregular in his hours, and fond of his child though he pretended to dismiss him. He wasted at billiards the mornings that ought to have been given to business. On the whole, however, she liked him much better than she had expected. Inwardly, she was not sorry she could like him no more: not sorry that his love of luxury, selfishness, and conceit made her turn with satisfaction to the thought of Edward's generosity, simple tastes, and modest feelings.

She now heard news of Edward, or at least of some of his affairs, from Colonel Brandon, who had lately visited Dorsetshire. Treating her both as Edward's impartial friend and his own kind confidante, he spoke often of Delaford Parsonage, described its shortcomings, and explained what he intended to do to put them right. His behaviour in this and every other matter could readily justify Mrs. Jennings's belief that he loved Elinor: his open pleasure in meeting her after only ten days apart, his eagerness to talk, his respect for her opinion. It might even have made Elinor suspect the same, had she not still believed, as she had from the beginning, that Marianne was his real favourite. As it was, the idea scarcely entered her mind except when Mrs. Jennings suggested it. She could not help thinking herself the more accurate observer. She watched his eyes; Mrs. Jennings considered only his behaviour. When Marianne began to feel a severe cold in her head and throat, the anxious concern in his face escaped Mrs. Jennings entirely because he expressed it in no words. Elinor, however, recognised the heightened sensitivity and unnecessary alarm of a lover.

Two delightful evening walks on the third and fourth days of their stay had given Marianne a violent cold. She had not confined herself to the dry gravel of the shrubbery, but wandered all over the grounds, especially the furthest, wilder parts, where the trees were oldest and the grass longest and wettest. The still greater carelessness of sitting afterwards in wet shoes and stockings had helped. For a day or two she denied or dismissed it, but her worsening symptoms forced themselves on everyone's concern and finally on her own notice. Remedies were recommended from every direction, and, as usual, she rejected them all. Though heavy and feverish, with aching limbs, a cough, and a sore throat, she expected a good night's sleep to cure her completely. When she went to bed, Elinor had difficulty persuading her to try even one or two of the simplest remedies.

chapters.title: Chapter 43
paragraphs: Marianne rose at her usual time the next morning, answered every inquiry by saying she was better, and tried to prove it by returning to her normal occupations. But a day spent shivering beside the fire with a book she could not read, or lying exhausted and listless on a sofa, gave little evidence of improvement. When she finally went early to bed, feeling worse and worse, Colonel Brandon could only wonder at Elinor's calm. She had cared for and nursed Marianne all day against her wishes, and insisted on proper medicine at night. Yet, like Marianne, she trusted in the certainty and healing power of sleep, and felt no serious alarm.

A restless, feverish night disappointed them both. Marianne insisted on getting up, then admitted she could not sit upright and willingly returned to bed. Elinor was now quite ready to follow Mrs. Jennings's advice and send for the Palmers' apothecary.

He came and examined Marianne. Although he encouraged Elinor to expect recovery within a few days, he described the illness as tending towards a putrid fever and let the word “infection” escape him. Mrs. Palmer was immediately alarmed for her baby. From the beginning, Mrs. Jennings had been inclined to take Marianne's illness more seriously than Elinor. She now looked grave at Mr. Harris's report, supported Charlotte's fears and caution, and urged her to leave with the infant at once. Mr. Palmer treated their fears as groundless, but could not withstand his wife's anxiety and insistence. Her departure was settled. Within an hour of Mr. Harris's arrival, she set off with her little boy and his nurse to stay with a close relation of her husband's a few miles beyond Bath. At her earnest request, Mr. Palmer promised to join her in a day or two. She was almost equally urgent that her mother should go with her. But Mrs. Jennings showed a kindness of heart that made Elinor truly love her: she declared she would not leave Cleveland while Marianne remained ill. By her own attentive care she would try to take the place of the mother from whom she had brought her away. In everything, Elinor found her a willing, active helper, eager to share every tiring duty and often giving substantial assistance through her greater experience of nursing.

Weakened and depressed by the illness, and feeling unwell throughout her body, poor Marianne could no longer hope to recover by the next day. The thought of what that day would have brought without this unlucky illness made every symptom harder to bear. They had been due to begin their journey home, escorted all the way by a servant of Mrs. Jennings, and surprise their mother the following morning. The little Marianne said consisted entirely of complaints about the unavoidable delay. Elinor tried to cheer her and persuade her, as she _then_ genuinely believed herself, that it would be very brief.

The following day brought little change. Marianne was certainly no better; apart from that lack of improvement, she did not seem worse. Their company was further reduced. Mr. Palmer was very reluctant to leave, both from genuine kindness and humanity and because he disliked appearing to have been frightened away by his wife. At last Colonel Brandon persuaded him to fulfil his promise to follow her. As he prepared to go, the Colonel himself, with much greater difficulty, began talking of leaving too. Here Mrs. Jennings's kindness intervened most welcome. In her opinion, sending him away while the woman he loved was so anxious about her sister would deprive them both of every comfort. She therefore told him directly that she needed him at Cleveland: he must play piquet with her in the evenings while Elinor was upstairs, and so on. She urged him so strongly to stay that he, whose deepest wish was satisfied by agreeing, could not even pretend to object for long. Mr. Palmer warmly supported her request, seeming relieved to leave someone so capable of helping or advising Elinor in an emergency.

Naturally, Marianne was kept entirely in ignorance of every one of these arrangements. She did not know she had caused Cleveland's owners to leave within about a week of arriving. Mrs. Palmer's absence did not surprise her. Since it did not trouble her either, she never mentioned her name.

Two days after Mr. Palmer left, her condition remained much the same, with little variation. Mr. Harris visited daily and still confidently predicted a rapid recovery. Elinor was equally hopeful. The others were far less cheerful. Mrs. Jennings had decided early in the illness that Marianne would never survive it. Colonel Brandon, whose main occupation was listening to her gloomy predictions, had no strength of mind to resist them. He tried to reason himself out of fears which the apothecary's different opinion seemed to make absurd. But the many hours he spent entirely alone each day were all too favourable to the admission of every melancholy thought. He could not shake the conviction that he would never see Marianne again.

On the morning of the third day, however, both their gloomy expectations nearly disappeared. Mr. Harris declared on arrival that Marianne was considerably better. Her pulse was much stronger and every symptom more favourable than at his previous visit. All Elinor's hopes were confirmed, and she became entirely cheerful. She was glad that, in writing to her mother, she had followed her own judgement rather than her friend's and treated the illness detaining them at Cleveland as slight. She was almost ready to fix the date when Marianne could travel.

But the day did not end as well as it began. Towards evening Marianne worsened again, becoming more heavy, restless, and uncomfortable than before. Still hopeful, Elinor attributed the change only to the exertion of sitting up while her bed was made. She carefully administered the prescribed cordials and was pleased when Marianne at last fell asleep, expecting the greatest benefit from it. The sleep was less peaceful than Elinor wished, but lasted a considerable time. Anxious to judge its effect herself, she decided to sit beside Marianne throughout. Mrs. Jennings, unaware of any change, went unusually early to bed. Her maid, one of the principal nurses, was taking a break in the housekeeper's room. Elinor remained alone with her sister.

Marianne's sleep became increasingly disturbed. Elinor watched every restless change of position and heard the frequent, indistinct sounds of complaint escaping her. She was almost wishing to wake her from such painful sleep when a sudden noise in the house startled Marianne awake. She sat up abruptly and cried out with feverish alarm,
“Is Mama coming?”
“Not yet,” Elinor answered, hiding her terror and helping Marianne lie down again. “But I hope she will be here before long. You know it is a great distance from here to Barton.”
“But she mustn't go round by London!” Marianne cried with the same hurried agitation. “I shall never see her if she comes through London.”

Elinor realised with alarm that her sister was not fully conscious of her surroundings. Trying to soothe her, she anxiously felt her pulse. It was weaker and faster than ever. Marianne continued speaking wildly about their mother, and Elinor's fear grew so quickly that she decided to send for Mr. Harris immediately and dispatch someone to Barton. She at once thought of consulting Colonel Brandon about the best way to bring their mother. As soon as she had rung for the maid to take her place, she hurried to the drawing room, where she knew he usually remained until much later than this.

There was no time to hesitate. She immediately told him her fears and difficulties. He had neither courage nor confidence to challenge the fears, and listened in silent despair. But he removed the practical difficulties at once. With a readiness suggesting he had already imagined the emergency and his own part in it, he offered to fetch Mrs. Dashwood himself. Elinor's objections were easily overcome. She thanked him briefly but fervently, then wrote a few lines to her mother while he hurried to send his servant to Mr. Harris and order fresh horses for immediate departure.

How grateful she felt for a friend like Colonel Brandon at such a moment, and for such a companion for her mother! His judgement would guide her, his care relieve her, and his friendship perhaps comfort her. As far as the shock of such a summons _could_ be softened, his presence, manner, and assistance would soften it.

Whatever _he_ felt, he acted meanwhile with the firmness of a composed mind. He made every arrangement with the greatest speed and calculated precisely when Elinor could expect him back. Not a moment was wasted. The horses arrived sooner than expected. He pressed her hand with a solemn look, spoke a few words too softly for her to hear, and hurried into the carriage. It was about midnight. Elinor returned to Marianne's room to wait for the apothecary and watch beside her through the rest of the night. Both sisters suffered almost equally. Hour after hour passed before Mr. Harris appeared: Marianne in sleepless pain and delirium, Elinor in the cruellest anxiety. Her fears, once roused, made up in their intensity for all her former confidence. The servant who sat with her—for she would not allow Mrs. Jennings to be woken—only increased her torment by hinting at what her mistress had thought all along.

At intervals, Marianne's confused thoughts still fixed on their mother. Every mention of her name pierced Elinor's heart. She blamed herself for having treated so many days of illness lightly, and desperately longed for immediate relief. Yet she imagined relief might soon be useless, that everything had been delayed too long. She pictured their distressed mother arriving too late to see her beloved child alive, or to find her able to recognise her.

She was about to send again for Mr. Harris, or for someone else if _he_ could not come, when he finally arrived after five o'clock. His opinion partly compensated for the delay. Though he admitted a very unexpected and unwelcome change in his patient, he would not call the danger serious. He spoke so confidently of the relief a different treatment must bring that some of his confidence reached Elinor. Promising to return within three or four hours, he left both patient and anxious attendant calmer than he had found them.

Mrs. Jennings heard the night's events in the morning with deep concern and many reproaches for not being called to help. Her earlier fears now returned with stronger justification, leaving her in no doubt of the outcome. She tried to comfort Elinor, but her certainty of Marianne's danger prevented her from offering hope. She was truly grieved. The rapid decline and early death of someone so young and lovely would have distressed a less interested person. Marianne had further claims on Mrs. Jennings's sympathy: she had been her companion for three months, remained under her care, and was known to have suffered a great wrong and long unhappiness. Elinor, a particular favourite, was visibly distressed before her. As for their mother, when Mrs. Jennings considered that Marianne might mean to _her_ what Charlotte meant to herself, her sympathy for _her_ suffering was wholly sincere.

Mr. Harris was punctual on his second visit, but found his hopes for the treatment disappointed. The medicines had failed, the fever remained, and Marianne was merely quieter, no clearer in her mind, lying in a heavy stupor. Elinor instantly caught all his fears and more, and proposed calling another medical adviser. He thought that unnecessary. There was another treatment to try, another application in whose success he felt as confident as before. He ended with encouraging assurances which Elinor heard but could not take to heart. Except when she thought of her mother, she was calm, but almost without hope. She remained like this until noon, scarcely leaving her sister's bedside. Her thoughts wandered from one image of sorrow and one suffering friend to another. Mrs. Jennings's conversation weighed heavily on her spirits. She openly attributed the severity and danger of the illness to the many weeks of poor health brought on by Marianne's disappointment. Elinor felt the explanation only too reasonable, and it added fresh misery to her thoughts.

Around noon, however, she began to imagine—to hope—that Marianne's pulse was slightly better. Caution and fear of disappointment kept her silent for some time, even with her friend. She waited, watched, and examined it repeatedly. At last she ventured to share her hope, with an agitation harder to conceal behind outward calm than any of her previous distress. On examining Marianne, Mrs. Jennings had to admit a temporary improvement, but tried to prevent Elinor from expecting it to last. Elinor repeated every warning to herself and told herself not to hope. It was too late. Hope had already entered. Feeling all its anxious excitement, she bent over her sister to watch, scarcely knowing what she watched for. Half an hour passed, and the favourable sign remained. Others appeared to support it: Marianne's breathing, skin, and lips all offered Elinor signs of recovery. She looked at her sister with eyes that were weak but clear and rational. Hope and anxiety now weighed on Elinor equally, giving her no peace until Mr. Harris arrived at four. His assurances and congratulations on a recovery beyond even his expectations brought her confidence, comfort, and tears of joy.

Marianne was substantially better in every respect, and he declared her entirely out of danger. Perhaps satisfied that the recent alarm had partly justified her predictions, Mrs. Jennings now allowed herself to trust his judgement. With genuine joy, soon becoming unmistakable cheerfulness, she accepted the likelihood of complete recovery.

Elinor could not be cheerful. Her joy was of another kind, leading to anything but gaiety. The thought of Marianne restored to life, health, friends, and her adoring mother filled her heart with exquisite comfort and deep gratitude. But it produced no outward display of happiness, no words, no smiles. Within her, everything was satisfaction, silent and strong.

She remained beside her sister almost without interruption throughout the afternoon, calming every fear, answering every question from her weakened mind, giving every help, and watching nearly every look and breath. At moments the possibility of a relapse naturally reminded her of anxiety. But frequent, careful examination showed every sign of recovery continuing. At six o'clock, Marianne sank into a quiet, steady sleep that seemed perfectly comfortable, and Elinor silenced every doubt.

The time when Colonel Brandon could be expected was approaching. By ten o'clock, she hoped, or not much later, their mother would be freed from the dreadful uncertainty in which she must now be travelling. And the Colonel too, perhaps scarcely less deserving of pity! How slowly time passed while it kept them ignorant of the happy change.

At seven, leaving Marianne still peacefully asleep, Elinor joined Mrs. Jennings for tea in the drawing room. Fear had kept her from eating much breakfast, and its sudden reversal had done the same at dinner. The refreshment was therefore especially welcome, with the contentment she brought to it. Afterwards Mrs. Jennings tried to persuade her to rest before her mother's arrival and let _her_ take over at Marianne's bedside. But Elinor felt no tiredness and could not possibly sleep just then. She would not be kept from her sister for an unnecessary moment. Mrs. Jennings accompanied her upstairs to assure herself that all remained well, then left her with her patient and her thoughts, retiring to her own room to write letters and sleep.

The night was cold and stormy. Wind roared round the house and rain beat on the windows, but Elinor, happy within, scarcely noticed. Marianne slept through every gust. As for the travellers, a rich reward awaited them for all their present discomfort.

The clock struck eight. If it had been ten, Elinor would have felt certain she heard a carriage approaching. Even though their arrival was _almost_ impossible so early, her conviction that she _did_ hear one was so strong that she went into the adjoining dressing room and opened a shutter to make sure. Her ears had not deceived her. The bright carriage lamps were immediately visible. In their wavering light she thought she could distinguish four horses. This suggested the intensity of her poor mother's alarm and helped explain the unexpected speed.

Never had Elinor found it harder to remain calm. She knew what her mother must feel as the carriage stopped: the uncertainty, the fear, perhaps despair. And she knew what news _she_ had to give. With that knowledge, calm was impossible. She could only be quick. Waiting just long enough to leave Mrs. Jennings's maid with Marianne, she hurried downstairs.
As she crossed an inner passage, the commotion in the entrance hall told her they were already inside. She rushed into the drawing room, opened the door, and found only Willoughby.

chapters.title: Chapter 44
paragraphs: Elinor recoiled at the sight of him, her face filled with horror. Following her first impulse, she immediately turned to leave. Her hand was already on the door handle when he hurried towards her and stopped her with a voice that sounded more like an order than a plea.
“Miss Dashwood, stay for half an hour—for ten minutes. I beg you.”
“No, sir,” she answered firmly. “I shall _not_ stay. You can have no business with _me_. I suppose the servants neglected to tell you that Mr. Palmer is away.”
“If they had told me that Mr. Palmer and every relation he has were at the devil,” he exclaimed vehemently, “I would not have turned away. My business is with you alone.”
“With me!” She was utterly astonished. “Very well, sir. Be quick, and if possible, less forceful.”
“Sit down, and I shall do both.”

She hesitated, uncertain what to do. She thought of Colonel Brandon arriving and finding her there. Yet she had promised to listen, and her curiosity was engaged as well as her honour. After a moment she decided that prudence required speed, and that agreeing would best secure it. She silently approached the table and sat down. He took the chair opposite. For half a minute neither spoke.
“Please be quick, sir,” Elinor said impatiently. “I have no time that I can spare.”
He sat absorbed in deep thought and seemed not to hear what she said.
“Your sister is out of danger,” he said abruptly a moment later. “The servant told me. Thank God! But is it true? Is it really true?”
Elinor would not answer. He repeated the question with even greater urgency.
“For God's sake, tell me! Is she out of danger or not?”
“We hope she is.”
He got up and walked across the room.

“If I had known that half an hour ago! But since I _am_ here”—he returned to his chair with forced liveliness—“what does it matter? For once, Miss Dashwood, perhaps for the last time, let us be cheerful together. I am in an excellent mood for gaiety. Tell me honestly”—his cheeks flushed more deeply—“do you think me more a villain or a fool?”

Elinor looked at him in greater astonishment than ever. She began to suspect he was drunk. Neither this strange visit nor his strange behaviour seemed otherwise explicable. Believing that, she immediately rose and said,
“Mr. Willoughby, I advise you to return to Combe for now. I cannot spare any more time. Whatever business you have with me, you will remember and explain it better tomorrow.”
“I understand,” he answered with a meaningful smile, his voice perfectly steady. “Yes, I am very drunk. A pint of porter with my cold beef at Marlborough was enough to overcome me.”
“At Marlborough!” Elinor exclaimed, increasingly unable to understand what he was trying to say.
“Yes. I left London at eight this morning. The only ten minutes I have spent outside my carriage since then gave me a bite to eat at Marlborough.”

The steadiness of his manner and the intelligence in his eyes convinced Elinor that, whatever other inexcusable folly had brought him to Cleveland, drunkenness had not. After a moment's consideration, she said,

“Mr. Willoughby, you _ought_ to feel, as I certainly _do_, that after everything that has happened, coming here like this and forcing your presence on me needs a very particular excuse. What do you intend by it?”

“I intend,” he said with serious intensity, “if possible, to make you hate me a little less than you do _now_. I want to offer some explanation, some apology for the past, to lay my whole heart before you. If I can persuade you that, though I have always been an idiot, I have not always been a scoundrel, perhaps I may gain something like forgiveness from Ma—from your sister.”
“Is that really why you have come here?”
“Upon my soul, it is.” His warmth recalled the former Willoughby so vividly that, against her will, she began to believe him sincere.
“If that is all, you can be satisfied already. Marianne _does_ forgive you. She has forgiven you for a _long_ time.”
“Has she?” he cried as eagerly as before. “Then she forgave me before she should have. But she shall forgive me again, and with better reason. Will you listen to me _now_?”
Elinor bowed to show her agreement.

“I don't know,” he said after a pause in which she waited and he reflected, “how _you_ have explained my behaviour to your sister, or what monstrous motive you have assigned me. Perhaps you will think no better of me, but it is worth trying, and you shall hear everything. When I first became close to your family, I had no purpose beyond spending the time pleasantly while I had to remain in Devonshire—more pleasantly than I ever had before. Your sister's beauty and engaging manner naturally attracted me. Her behaviour towards me almost from the beginning was such—it astonishes me now, when I remember what it was, and what _she_ was, that my heart could have remained so untouched. But I must admit that at first it merely flattered my vanity. I did not consider her happiness, only my own amusement. Yielding to feelings I had always indulged too freely, I used every means I could to make her like me, without intending to return her love.”
At this point, Elinor turned her eyes on him with the angriest contempt and stopped him by saying,

“Mr. Willoughby, there is hardly any further point in your continuing this account, or in my listening to it. Nothing that follows can excuse such a beginning. Please spare me the pain of hearing any more about the matter.”

“I insist that you hear it all,” he replied. “My fortune was never large, and I had always spent extravagantly, always mixed with people richer than myself. Every year since I came of age—and probably before—had increased my debts. My old cousin Mrs. Smith's death was to free me, but that was uncertain and might be far off. For some time I had therefore intended to repair my finances by marrying a wealthy woman. Loving your sister was out of the question. With a pettiness, selfishness, and cruelty which no angry or contemptuous look, even yours, Miss Dashwood, can condemn too much, I tried to win her affection without any thought of returning it. One thing may be said for me: even in that dreadful state of selfish vanity, I did not understand the full harm I planned, because _then_ I did not know what love was. But have I ever known? You may well doubt it. If I had truly loved, could I have sacrificed my feelings to vanity and greed? Still worse, could I have sacrificed hers? Yet I did. To escape a relative poverty which her love and company would have stripped of every terror, I made myself rich and lost everything that could make wealth a blessing.”
“Then you did once believe yourself in love with her?” Elinor asked, a little softened.

“Who could have resisted such attractions, such tenderness? Is there a man alive who could? Yes, little by little, without noticing, I became sincerely attached. The happiest hours of my life were those I spent with her knowing my intentions were honourable and my feelings innocent. Even _then_, though fully determined to propose, I wrongly allowed myself to postpone it day after day. I disliked committing myself while my finances were so troubled. I won't argue the point, or wait for _you_ to explain the absurdity—and worse than absurdity—of hesitating to give my word when my honour was already pledged. Events have proved me a calculating fool, carefully preserving an opportunity to make myself contemptible and miserable for ever. At last, though, I made up my mind. As soon as I could find her alone, I would justify my constant attentions and openly declare the love I had already taken such pains to display. But in the interval, in the few hours before I could speak to her privately, something happened—an unlucky event that destroyed my resolution and all my happiness. A discovery was made.” He hesitated and looked down. “Mrs. Smith had somehow been told, I suppose by a distant relation interested in depriving me of her favour, about an affair, a connection—but I needn't explain further.” He looked at Elinor, his colour rising, his eyes questioning. “Your close acquaintance—you have probably known the whole story for some time.”

“I have,” Elinor answered, colouring too and hardening her heart again against pity. “I have heard everything. I confess I cannot understand how you could explain away any part of your guilt in that dreadful affair.”

“Remember who told you,” Willoughby cried. “Could his account be impartial? I admit I should have respected her position and her character. I am not trying to justify myself. But I cannot let you suppose I have nothing to say, that because she was wronged she was beyond reproach, or that because _I_ was dissolute, _she_ must be a saint. The violence of her passions, the weakness of her understanding—but I do not mean to defend myself. Her love deserved better treatment. I often remember with deep self-reproach the tenderness that briefly made me feel something in return. I wish, sincerely, that it had never happened. But she is not the only person I have hurt. I have hurt someone whose love for me—may I say it?—was scarcely less warm, and whose mind was infinitely superior!”

“Your indifference towards that unfortunate girl is no excuse for cruelly abandoning her. I must say it, however unpleasant such a subject is to discuss. Do not imagine that any weakness or natural lack of understanding on her part excuses the deliberate cruelty so clear on yours. You must have known that while you enjoyed yourself in Devonshire, pursuing new schemes, always cheerful and happy, she had been reduced to utter poverty.”
“But I swear I did _not_ know,” he answered heatedly. “I had forgotten that I neglected to give her my address. And ordinary common sense might have shown her how to discover it.”
“Well, sir, what did Mrs. Smith say to you?”

“She accused me directly, and you can imagine my embarrassment. Her pure life, rigid ideas, ignorance of the world—everything was against me. I could not deny the facts, and every attempt to soften them failed. I think she was already inclined to question my conduct generally. She was also displeased by how little attention and time I had given her during this visit. In short, it ended in a complete break. I could have saved myself in one way. At the height of her morality, the good woman offered to forgive everything if I married Eliza. That was impossible, and she formally dismissed me from both her favour and her house. I was to leave the next morning. I spent the night considering what to do. The struggle was great, but ended too soon. My love for Marianne, my certainty that she loved me, could not outweigh my fear of poverty or overcome my false belief that wealth was necessary—a belief to which I was naturally inclined and which extravagant company had strengthened. I had reason to believe my present wife would accept me if I proposed, and persuaded myself that ordinary prudence left no other course. But a painful scene awaited me before I could leave Devonshire. I was due to dine with you that very day and had to offer some apology for cancelling. I debated for a long time whether to write it or deliver it myself. Seeing Marianne would be dreadful. I even doubted whether I could see her again and keep my resolution. In that respect, however, I underestimated my own greatness of spirit, as events proved. I went, saw her, saw her miserable, left her miserable—and left hoping never to see her again.”
“Why did you call, Mr. Willoughby?” Elinor asked reproachfully. “A note would have served every purpose. Why did you need to come yourself?”

“My pride required it. I could not bear to leave in a way that might make you or the neighbours suspect any part of what had happened between Mrs. Smith and me. I therefore decided to call at the cottage on my way to Honiton. But seeing your dear sister was truly dreadful. To make it worse, I found her alone; the rest of you had gone somewhere, I don't know where. Only the previous evening I had left her absolutely determined to do right. Within a few hours she was to be engaged to me for ever. I remember how happy and cheerful I felt walking back from the cottage to Allenham, pleased with myself and delighted with everyone. Yet in this last friendly meeting I approached her so guilty that I could hardly pretend otherwise. Her sorrow, her disappointment, her deep distress when I said I must leave Devonshire immediately—I shall never forget it. And all combined with such trust, such confidence in me! Oh God, what a heartless scoundrel I was!”
For a few moments they were both silent. Elinor spoke first.
“Did you tell Marianne that you would return soon?”

“I don't know what I told her,” he answered impatiently. “Certainly less than the past deserved, and probably much more than the future justified. I cannot think about it. I cannot. Then your dear mother came to torment me further with all her kindness and trust. Thank heaven it _did_ torment me. I was miserable. Miss Dashwood, you cannot imagine the comfort I find in remembering my misery. I resent myself so bitterly for the stupid, wicked foolishness of my heart that all the suffering it caused me is now a source of triumph and satisfaction. Well, I left everything I loved and went to people towards whom I felt, at best, indifference. The journey to London, using my own horses and therefore moving so slowly, with nobody to speak to! Such cheerful thoughts; such delightful prospects when I looked ahead; such a soothing picture when I looked back towards Barton! Oh, it was a blessed journey.”
He fell silent.
“Well, sir,” Elinor said, pitying him but increasingly impatient for him to leave, “is that everything you have to say?”
“Everything? No. Have you forgotten what happened in London? That infamous letter? Did Marianne show it to you?”
“Yes. I saw every note exchanged between you.”

“When her first letter reached me—which it did immediately, because I had been in London all along—what I felt was, in the usual phrase, beyond expression. More simply, perhaps too simply to move anyone, my feelings were very, very painful. Every line and word was a dagger to my heart, to use a worn-out metaphor its dear writer would forbid if she were here. The news that Marianne was in London struck like a thunderbolt. Thunderbolts and daggers! How she would have rebuked me! Her tastes and opinions are, I believe, better known to me than my own, and certainly dearer.”
Elinor's heart had changed repeatedly through this extraordinary conversation, and softened again now. Yet she felt obliged to check the kind of thoughts he had just expressed.
“This is wrong, Mr. Willoughby. Remember that you are married. Tell me only what you honestly believe I need to hear.”

“Marianne's note assured me that I was as dear to her as ever. Despite our many weeks apart, her feelings had not changed, and she trusted mine as completely as before. It woke all my remorse. I say woke, because time, London, business, and pleasure had partly quieted it. I was becoming a fine hardened villain, imagining I no longer cared for her and choosing to suppose she no longer cared for me. I told myself our attachment had been an idle, trivial affair, and shrugged my shoulders to prove it. I silenced every reproach and overcame every scruple by occasionally telling myself, ‘I shall be heartily glad to hear she has married well.’ Her note made me understand myself better. I knew she was infinitely dearer to me than any other woman, and that I was treating her shamefully. But everything between Miss Grey and me was just settled. I could not retreat. I could only avoid you both. I sent Marianne no answer, hoping to prevent any further notice from her. For a while I even decided not to call in Berkeley Street. At last I thought it wiser to behave like a cool, ordinary acquaintance. One morning I watched until you were all safely out, then left my card.”
“You watched until we had left the house?”

“Exactly. You would be surprised how often I watched you, and how often I nearly met you. Many times I went into a shop to avoid being seen as your carriage passed. Living in Bond Street, I scarcely went a day without glimpsing one of you. Only constant vigilance and an unchanging determination to keep out of sight could have separated us so long. I avoided the Middletons as far as possible, and anyone else likely to be a mutual acquaintance. But not knowing they were in London, I stumbled into Sir John, I think on his first day, and the day after I called at Mrs. Jennings's. He invited me to a dance that evening. Even if he had _not_ mentioned you and Marianne as an attraction, I should have been too certain you would be there to venture near him. The next morning came another note from Marianne, still loving, open, innocent, trusting—everything that made _my_ behaviour most hateful. I could not answer. I tried, but could not form a sentence. Yet I think I thought of her every moment of the day. If you _can_ pity me, Miss Dashwood, pity my position _then_. With my head and heart full of your sister, I had to act the happy lover to another woman. Those three or four weeks were the worst of all. At last, as you know, I was forced to meet you. What a fine figure I made! What an evening of agony! Marianne, lovely as an angel, on one side, calling me Willoughby in that voice! Oh God, holding out her hand, asking for an explanation, those beautiful eyes fixed so anxiously and eloquently on my face! And Sophia on the other side, jealous as the devil, looking all that—well, it doesn't matter. It is over. Such an evening! I escaped as soon as I could, but not before I saw Marianne's dear face white as death. _That_ was the last, the very last sight I had of her. That is how I last saw her. It was dreadful. Yet today, thinking she was really dying, I found a sort of comfort in believing I knew exactly how she would appear to the last people to see her alive. All through my journey she was before me, constantly, with that same expression and colour.”
They paused briefly, each absorbed in thought. Willoughby roused himself first and broke the silence.
“Well, I must be quick and go. Your sister is certainly better, certainly out of danger?”
“We have been assured she is.”
“And your poor mother, so devoted to Marianne!”
“But your letter, Mr. Willoughby—your own letter. Have you anything to explain about that?”

“Yes, yes, _that_ especially. As you know, your sister wrote again the very next morning. You saw her words. I was breakfasting at the Ellisons', and her letter came there from my lodgings with several others. Sophia noticed it before I did. Its size, the fine paper, and the handwriting immediately made her suspicious. She had already heard some vague report that I was attached to a young woman in Devonshire. What she saw the previous evening identified the woman and increased her jealousy. Adopting a playful manner, so delightful in a woman one loves, she immediately opened and read it. Her impudence was well rewarded: what she read made her miserable. I could have endured her misery, but her rage, her malice—those had to be soothed at any cost. In short, what do you think of my wife's letter-writing style? Delicate, tender, truly feminine, wasn't it?”
“Your wife! But the letter was in your own handwriting.”

“Yes, my sole credit was obediently copying sentences I was ashamed to sign. The original was entirely hers: her happy ideas, her gentle language. But what could I do? We were engaged, everything was being prepared, the date almost fixed—but I am talking foolishly. Preparations! Dates! The plain truth is that I needed her money. In my position, I had to do anything to prevent a break. Besides, what difference did the wording make to my character in Marianne's eyes, or her friends'? The result could only be the same. My task was to declare myself a scoundrel; whether I did it with a bow or a shout mattered little. ‘I am ruined in their opinion for ever,’ I told myself. ‘I can never see them again. They already think me unprincipled; this letter will only make them think me a brute as well.’ That was how I reasoned, with a kind of desperate recklessness, while copying my wife's words and parting with the last reminders of Marianne. Her three notes were, unfortunately, all in my pocketbook. Otherwise I would have denied having them and treasured them for ever. I had to pack them up without even kissing them. And the lock of hair, which I had always carried in the same pocketbook—Madam was now searching it with the most charming spite—that dear lock too. Everything, every keepsake, was torn from me.”

“You are very wrong, Mr. Willoughby, very much to blame,” Elinor said, though her voice betrayed compassion despite herself. “You should not speak like this about either your wife or my sister. You made your choice; nobody forced it upon you. Your wife has a right to your courtesy, at least to your respect. She must care for you, or she would not have married you. Treating her unkindly and speaking contemptuously of her does nothing to make amends to Marianne. Nor can I imagine it eases your own conscience.”

“Do not speak to me of my wife,” he said with a deep sigh. “She does not deserve your pity. She knew I did not love her when we married. Well, we married, went to Combe Magna to be happy, and then returned to London to enjoy ourselves. Now do you pity me, Miss Dashwood? Or has all this been useless? Am I even a little less guilty in your eyes than before? My intentions were not always bad. Have I explained away any part of my guilt?”

“Yes, certainly something—a little. You have shown yourself less blameworthy on the whole than I believed. Your heart has proved less wicked, much less wicked. But I hardly know—the misery you have caused—I can scarcely imagine what could have made it worse.”

“When your sister recovers, will you repeat what I have told you? Let me be a little less condemned in her opinion as well as yours. You say she has already forgiven me. Let me imagine that knowing more of my heart and my feelings now might bring a more spontaneous, natural, gentle, less dignified forgiveness. Tell her how miserable and repentant I am. Tell her my heart never changed towards her, and, if you will, that she is dearer to me at this moment than ever.”
“I shall tell her everything necessary to what we may comparatively call your defence. But you have not explained why you came at this particular time, or how you heard she was ill.”

“Last night I met Sir John Middleton in the lobby at Drury Lane. Recognising me, he spoke for the first time in two months. I had noticed without surprise or resentment that he had ignored me since my marriage. But now his kind, honest, foolish soul was so full of anger with me and concern for Marianne that he could not resist telling me something he knew ought to hurt me terribly, though he probably doubted that it _would_. As bluntly as possible, he said Marianne Dashwood was dying of a putrid fever at Cleveland. A letter received that morning from Mrs. Jennings described her danger as extreme; the Palmers had all fled in fright, and so on. I was too shocked to pretend indifference even to someone as unobservant as Sir John. Seeing my suffering softened his heart. So much resentment disappeared that, when we parted, he nearly shook my hand while reminding me of an old promise about a pointer puppy. What I felt on hearing your sister was dying—dying while she believed me the greatest villain alive, despising and hating me in her final moments, for how could I know what dreadful intentions I had been accused of? I knew _one_ person would paint me capable of anything. What I felt was terrible. I quickly decided what to do, and at eight this morning I was in my carriage. Now you know everything.”

Elinor made no reply. Her thoughts fixed silently on the irreparable damage that independence granted too young, with its habits of idleness, dissipation, and luxury, had done to this man's mind, character, and happiness. He combined every advantage of looks and ability with a naturally open, honest disposition and a sensitive, affectionate heart. Society had made him extravagant and vain; extravagance and vanity had made him cold and selfish. Seeking a guilty triumph over someone else's feelings, vanity had drawn him into genuine love. Extravagance, or its child necessity, had then demanded the sacrifice of that love. Every fault that led him into wrongdoing had also led him to punishment. The attachment from which he had outwardly torn himself, against honour, feeling, and every better interest, now ruled his thoughts when it was no longer permissible. The marriage for which he had so readily abandoned Marianne to misery would probably bring him unhappiness far less curable than hers. After several minutes, Willoughby recalled her from these reflections. Emerging from thoughts at least as painful, he sprang up to leave and said,
“There is no point in remaining here. I must go.”
“Are you returning to London now?”
“No, to Combe Magna. I have business there, then London in a day or two. Goodbye.”
He offered his hand. She could not refuse her own, and he pressed it affectionately.
“And you _do_ think a little better of me?” he asked, releasing her hand and leaning against the mantelpiece as though forgetting he meant to leave.

Elinor assured him she did: she forgave him, pitied him, wished him well, and even cared about his happiness. She added some gentle advice about the conduct most likely to secure it. His answer offered little encouragement.

“As for that,” he said, “I must struggle through the world as best I can. Happiness at home is impossible. But if I may believe that you and your family care about my fate and actions, perhaps it may help, perhaps keep me on my guard. At least it may give me something to live for. Marianne is certainly lost to me for ever. Even if some blessed chance left me free again—”
Elinor interrupted him with a rebuke.
“Well,” he answered, “goodbye once more. Now I shall go away and live in fear of one event.”
“What do you mean?”
“Your sister getting married.”
“You are very wrong. She can never be more completely lost to you than she is already.”

“But she will be gained by someone else. And if that person is the very man I could least bear—but I shall not stay and destroy your compassion by showing that I forgive least where I have wronged most. Goodbye. God bless you!”
With those words, he hurried from the room almost at a run.

chapters.title: Chapter 45
paragraphs: For some time after he left, even after the sound of his carriage had faded, Elinor remained overwhelmed by a crowd of very different thoughts whose common effect was sadness. She could not, for a while, think even of her sister.

Willoughby, whom only half an hour earlier she had despised as the most worthless of men, now aroused her pity for the suffering his faults had brought upon him. Thinking of him permanently separated from her family, she felt a tenderness and regret which, she soon admitted to herself, answered his wishes rather than his deserts. She knew his influence over her was strengthened by things that ought, reasonably, to carry no weight: his exceptional attractiveness; the open, warm, lively manner for which he deserved no moral credit; and his still-passionate love for Marianne, which he could no longer even innocently indulge. But she recognised all this long before she could feel his influence weaken.

When she finally returned to Marianne, who knew nothing of what had happened, she found her just waking. The long, peaceful sleep had refreshed her as much as Elinor had hoped. Elinor's heart was full. Past, present, future, Willoughby's visit, Marianne's safety, and their mother's expected arrival combined to keep her intensely agitated, banishing every sign of tiredness. She feared only that her sister might notice. That fear had little time to trouble her, however. Within half an hour of Willoughby's departure, another carriage brought her downstairs again. Eager to spare her mother every unnecessary moment of dreadful uncertainty, she ran straight into the hall and reached the outer door just in time to welcome and support her as she entered.

As the carriage approached, Mrs. Dashwood's terror had almost convinced her that Marianne was dead. She had no voice to ask about her, none even to greet Elinor. But her daughter waited for neither greeting nor question and immediately gave the joyful news. Receiving it with all her usual intensity, Mrs. Dashwood was instantly as overwhelmed by happiness as she had been by fear. Between them, her daughter and her friend supported her into the drawing room. Still unable to speak, she wept for joy and embraced Elinor again and again, turning now and then to press Colonel Brandon's hand. Her look expressed both gratitude and certainty that he shared her happiness. He did share it, though in an even deeper silence than hers.

As soon as she recovered herself, Mrs. Dashwood wanted to see Marianne. Within two minutes she was beside her beloved child, dearer than ever through absence, suffering, and danger. Elinor's delight at their reunion was checked only by fear that it might prevent Marianne from sleeping again. But Mrs. Dashwood could be calm, even prudent, when her child's life was concerned. Marianne was content to know her mother was near, and understood that she was too weak to talk. She willingly accepted the silence and quiet urged by every nurse around her. Mrs. Dashwood insisted on staying up all night. At her mother's request, Elinor went to bed. Yet the rest that an entirely sleepless night and many hours of exhausting anxiety seemed to demand was denied her by her restless mind. Willoughby—“poor Willoughby,” as she now allowed herself to call him—occupied her thoughts constantly. She would not for anything have missed hearing his defence. Now she blamed herself, now excused herself, for judging him so harshly before. But the promise to tell Marianne was always painful. She dreaded carrying it out, dreaded its effect, and doubted whether, after hearing it, Marianne could ever be happy with anyone else. For a moment she wished Willoughby a widower. Then she remembered Colonel Brandon and reproached herself. _His_ suffering and _his_ faithfulness deserved the reward of her sister's love far more than his rival's did. She wished anything rather than Mrs. Willoughby's death.

Mrs. Dashwood's own previous anxiety had greatly softened the shock of Colonel Brandon's message at Barton. Her concern for Marianne was already so intense that she had decided to leave for Cleveland that very day, without waiting for further news. Her arrangements were so advanced before he arrived that the Careys were expected at any moment to collect Margaret. She was unwilling to take her youngest daughter somewhere there might be infection.

Marianne improved daily. The brightness of Mrs. Dashwood's face and spirits proved the truth of her repeated declaration that she was one of the happiest women alive. Elinor could not hear it, or see its evidence, without sometimes wondering whether her mother ever remembered Edward. But Mrs. Dashwood had trusted the restrained account Elinor sent of her own disappointment. The abundance of her joy now carried her towards thoughts that would only increase it. Marianne had been restored to her from a danger which, she was beginning to realise, her own mistaken encouragement of the attachment to Willoughby had helped to cause. Her recovery also gave Mrs. Dashwood another source of happiness which Elinor had not imagined. At their first chance to talk privately, she revealed it.
“At last we are alone. My dear Elinor, you don't yet know all my happiness. Colonel Brandon loves Marianne. He told me himself.”
Elinor felt by turns pleased and pained, surprised and unsurprised. She listened silently to every word.

“You are never like me, dear Elinor, or I should wonder at your calmness now. If I had sat down to wish for every possible good for my family, I should have chosen Colonel Brandon's marriage to one of you as the most desirable thing. And I believe Marianne is the one who will be happiest with him.”

Elinor almost asked why she thought so. She was certain no reason could arise from an impartial comparison of their ages, characters, or feelings. But her mother's imagination always carried her away on any interesting subject. Instead of questioning her, Elinor therefore answered with a smile.

“He opened his whole heart to me yesterday as we travelled. It came out quite unexpectedly, without any intention. Naturally I could speak only of my child. He could not hide his distress; I saw it was equal to mine. Perhaps he thought ordinary friendship, in this world of ours, would not explain such warm sympathy. Or rather, I suppose he was not thinking at all. Irresistible feeling made him tell me of his earnest, tender, constant love for Marianne. He has loved her, my Elinor, from the first moment he saw her.”

Here, however, Elinor recognised not Colonel Brandon's words or declarations, but the natural embellishments of her mother's lively imagination, which shaped everything delightful according to its own wishes.

“His love infinitely surpasses anything Willoughby ever felt or pretended: warmer, more sincere, more constant, whatever we should call it. It has endured through full knowledge of dear Marianne's unfortunate love for that worthless young man. And without selfishness, without allowing himself any hope! If he could have seen her happy with someone else—what a noble mind! Such openness, such honesty! Nobody can be deceived in _him_.”
“Colonel Brandon's reputation as an excellent man is firmly established,” Elinor said.

“I know it,” her mother replied seriously. “Otherwise, after such a warning, _I_ should be the last to encourage this affection, or even take pleasure in it. But coming for me as he did, with such prompt and active friendship, is enough to prove him one of the best of men.”

“His character does not depend on _one_ act of kindness,” Elinor answered, “which his love for Marianne would have prompted even without humanity. Mrs. Jennings and the Middletons have known him closely for years. They all love and respect him. Even my own knowledge of him, though recent, is considerable. _I_ value and esteem him so highly that, if Marianne can be happy with him, I shall be as ready as you to call the connection our greatest blessing. What did you say to him? Did you let him hope?”

“Oh, my dear, I could not speak of hope then, either to him or to myself. Marianne might have been dying at that moment. But he asked for neither hope nor encouragement. His confession was involuntary, feeling that could not be restrained, shared with a comforting friend, not an appeal to a parent. Still, after a while I _did_ say—for at first I was quite overcome—that if she lived, as I trusted she would, nothing would make me happier than helping their marriage forward. Since arriving, since this wonderful certainty of her safety, I have said it more fully and given him every encouragement I can. Time, very little time, I tell him, will do everything. Marianne's heart cannot be wasted for ever on a man like Willoughby. His own good qualities must soon win it.”
“Judging by the Colonel's spirits, though, you have not yet made him as hopeful as yourself.”

“No. He thinks Marianne's love too deeply rooted to change for a long time. Even if her heart becomes free again, he is too modest to believe he could win it with such differences of age and temperament between them. But there he is entirely mistaken. He is only enough older to make it an advantage, to give him settled character and principles. I am convinced his temperament is exactly what will make your sister happy. His appearance and manners also favour him. Affection does not blind me: he is certainly not as handsome as Willoughby. Yet there is something much more pleasing in his face. You remember, there was always something in Willoughby's eyes at times that I disliked.”
Elinor could _not_ remember any such thing. Without waiting for agreement, her mother continued.

“And the Colonel's manners please me more than Willoughby's ever did. I also know they will win Marianne's affection more deeply. Their gentleness, their genuine consideration for others, their manly, unaffected simplicity suit her true nature far better than Willoughby's liveliness, which was often artificial and often badly timed. I am quite certain that even if he had proved as truly good as he has proved the opposite, Marianne could never have been as happy with _him_ as she will be with Colonel Brandon.”
She paused. Elinor could not entirely agree, but her disagreement remained unspoken and therefore caused no offence.

“At Delaford she will be an easy distance from me,” Mrs. Dashwood added, “even if I stay at Barton. And very probably—I hear it is a large village—there must surely be some small house or cottage nearby that would suit us just as well as our present home.”
Poor Elinor! Another plan to send her to Delaford. But her determination remained stubborn.
“And his fortune too! At my age, you know, everyone cares about _that_. Although I neither know nor wish to know its actual size, I am sure it must be a good one.”
Someone else entered and interrupted them. Elinor withdrew to consider it all privately, to wish her friend success, and yet, even while wishing it, to feel a pang for Willoughby.

chapters.title: Chapter 46
paragraphs: Although Marianne's illness was weakening by nature, it had not lasted long enough to make her recovery slow. Helped by youth, natural strength, and her mother's presence, she improved steadily. Within four days of Mrs. Dashwood's arrival, she could move into Mrs. Palmer's dressing room. There, at Marianne's express request, Colonel Brandon was invited to visit. She was eager to thank him for bringing her mother.

His emotion on entering, seeing her changed appearance, and taking the pale hand she immediately offered seemed to Elinor to arise from more than his love for Marianne or his knowledge that others knew of it. In his melancholy eyes and changing colour as he looked at her, Elinor soon recognised the probable return of many painful memories. The resemblance between Marianne and Eliza, which he had already acknowledged, was now strengthened by her hollow eyes, sickly skin, reclining weakness, and warm gratitude for an exceptional obligation.

Mrs. Dashwood watched no less closely than her daughter. But her mind was influenced quite differently, and her observations produced quite different results. She saw nothing in the Colonel's behaviour beyond the simplest, most obvious feelings. In Marianne's words and actions, meanwhile, she persuaded herself that something beyond gratitude was already beginning.

After another day or two, with Marianne visibly stronger every twelve hours, Mrs. Dashwood began to speak of returning to Barton, urged equally by her own wishes and her daughter's. The plans of their two friends depended on _hers_. Mrs. Jennings could not leave Cleveland while the Dashwoods stayed. Their united requests soon persuaded Colonel Brandon to regard his own stay as equally fixed, if not equally essential. In return, he and Mrs. Jennings together persuaded Mrs. Dashwood to use his carriage for the journey home, for the greater comfort of her recovering child. The Colonel gladly agreed to collect it by visiting the cottage in a few weeks. This invitation came jointly from Mrs. Dashwood and Mrs. Jennings, whose active kindness made her generous and hospitable on other people's behalf as readily as her own.

The day of parting arrived. Marianne took an unusually attentive, prolonged farewell of Mrs. Jennings, full of earnest gratitude, respect, and good wishes, as though her own heart required it in private acknowledgement of past neglect. She said goodbye to Colonel Brandon with the warmth of a friend. He carefully helped her into the carriage, anxious, it seemed, that she should occupy at least half of it. Mrs. Dashwood and Elinor followed. The others were left to discuss the travellers and feel their own dullness until Mrs. Jennings was called to her chaise. Her maid's gossip must now comfort her for losing her two young companions. Immediately afterwards, Colonel Brandon set out alone for Delaford.

The Dashwoods travelled for two days, and Marianne bore both without serious fatigue. Each watchful companion did everything devoted love and anxious care could suggest to make her comfortable. Both found their reward in her physical ease and calm spirits. Elinor particularly welcomed the latter. She had watched her sister suffer week after week, burdened by a misery she had neither courage to discuss nor strength to hide. Now she saw an apparent peace of mind with a joy nobody else could equally share. If, as she trusted, it came from serious reflection, it must eventually lead to contentment and cheerfulness.

As they approached Barton, however, every field and tree recalled something particular and painful. Marianne grew quiet and thoughtful, turning her face away and gazing intently through the window. Elinor could neither wonder nor blame her. Helping her from the carriage, she saw that Marianne had been crying. The emotion was too natural to inspire anything less tender than pity, and its quietness deserved praise. Everything in her subsequent behaviour suggested a mind awakened to reasonable effort. The moment they entered the sitting room, Marianne looked firmly around, apparently determined to accustom herself at once to every object connected with Willoughby. She spoke little, but every sentence attempted cheerfulness. A sigh sometimes escaped, yet was always followed by a compensating smile. After dinner she tried the piano. The first music she saw, however, was an opera Willoughby had obtained for her, containing some of their favourite duets and bearing her name on the cover in his handwriting. That would not do. Shaking her head, she put it aside. After running her fingers over the keys for a minute, she complained that they were weak and closed the instrument. As she did so, however, she firmly declared that she would practise a great deal in future.

The next morning brought no weakening of these encouraging signs. Rest had strengthened body and mind alike. She looked and spoke with more genuine animation, anticipating Margaret's return and the restoration of their dear family circle. Their shared pursuits and cheerful companionship were, she said, the only happiness worth wishing for.

“When the weather settles and I have my strength back,” she said, “we shall take long walks together every day. We shall go to the farm beside the down and see how the children are getting on, to Sir John's new plantations at Barton Cross, and to Abbeyland. Often we shall visit the old Priory ruins and try to trace the foundations as far as we are told they once extended. I know we shall be happy. I know the summer will pass happily. I intend never to rise later than six, and from then until dinner I shall divide every minute between music and reading. My plan is formed: I mean to undertake serious study. I know our own library too well to use it for anything beyond amusement. But there are many worthwhile books at the Park, and more recent works I know I can borrow from Colonel Brandon. Reading only six hours a day, I shall gain a great deal of the knowledge I now lack within a year.”

Elinor respected a plan arising from such worthy intentions. Still, she smiled to see the same eager imagination which had carried Marianne to extremes of idle listlessness and selfish complaint now introducing excess into a scheme of sensible occupation and virtuous self-control. Her smile became a sigh when she remembered her unfulfilled promise to Willoughby. She feared she must communicate something that might unsettle Marianne again and destroy, at least temporarily, this promising prospect of peaceful activity. Wanting to postpone the painful moment, she decided to wait until her sister's health was stronger. But she made the resolution only to break it.

Marianne had been home two or three days before the weather became fine enough for someone recovering from illness to go out. At last a mild, pleasant morning encouraged both her desire and her mother's confidence. Leaning on Elinor's arm, she was permitted to walk in the lane outside the house for as long as she could without tiredness.

The sisters walked slowly, as Marianne's weakness required in exercise she had not attempted since her illness. They had gone only far enough for a full view of the hill behind the house—that important hill—when Marianne paused, looked towards it, and calmly said,
“There, just there”—she pointed with one hand—“on that jutting mound. That is where I fell, and where I first saw Willoughby.”
Her voice faded on his name, but she soon recovered it and continued.
“I am grateful that I can look at the place with so little pain. Shall we ever speak about it, Elinor?” She hesitated. “Or would it be wrong? I hope I _can_ talk about it now in the way I ought.”
Elinor gently encouraged her to speak freely.

“As for regret,” Marianne said, “I have finished with that, where _he_ is concerned. I do not want to tell you what my feelings for him were, but what they are _now_. If I could be satisfied about one thing, if I could believe that he was not _always_ playing a part, not _always_ deceiving me—and, above all, if I could be certain he was never as _terribly_ wicked as I have sometimes feared since hearing about that unfortunate girl—”
She stopped. Elinor treasured the words with joy and answered,
“If you could be sure of that, you think you would find peace?”

“Yes. My peace depends on it in two ways. It is terrible to suspect someone who meant what _he_ meant to _me_ of such intentions. But what does that make me in my own eyes? In my position, what but shamefully unguarded love could have exposed me to—”
“How, then,” her sister asked, “would you explain his behaviour towards you?”
“I would think him—oh, how gladly I would think him—only changeable, very, very changeable.”
Elinor said nothing further. She was considering whether to begin her story immediately or wait until Marianne was stronger. For several minutes they moved slowly on in silence.
“I do not wish him too much happiness,” Marianne said at last with a sigh, “when I wish his private reflections no more painful than mine. Those will make him suffer enough.”
“Are you comparing your behaviour with his own?”
“No. I compare it with what it should have been. I compare it with your behaviour.”
“Our circumstances have been very different.”

“Less different than our conduct. Dearest Elinor, don't let your kindness defend what I know your judgement must condemn. Illness has made me think. It gave me time and quiet for serious reflection. Long before I was well enough to talk, I could think perfectly clearly. I looked back. From the beginning of our acquaintance with him last autumn, I saw in my own behaviour only a succession of recklessness towards myself and unkindness towards others. I saw that my feelings had prepared my suffering, and that my lack of courage in bearing it had nearly taken me to the grave. I knew I had brought the illness entirely on myself by neglecting my health in ways I understood, even then, to be wrong. If I had died, I would have destroyed myself. I did not know my danger until it had passed. But remembering what those reflections made me feel, I wonder that I recovered.
